title: Introduction to motion
text:
Laws of Motion › Introduction to motion › introduction to motion — Revision note (part 1/1)

Motion : An object is said to be in motion if its position relative to its surroundings changes with time. Conversely, if an object's position remains constant in relation to its surroundings, it is considered at rest.

Example: A car moving down a road, a ball rolling on the ground, leaves falling from a tree, a swing moving back and forth, the Earth revolving around the Sun,

Frame of Reference: When describing motion, we need a reference point. This reference point is called the frame of reference. We compare the object's position to this frame of reference to determine whether it's moving or at rest.

Example: A person sitting in a stationary bus is at rest relative to the bus (frame of reference) but moving relative to a stationary observer outside the bus (different frame of reference).

Types of Motion:

Uniform Motion: An object is in uniform motion if it covers equal distances in equal intervals of time. In simpler terms, its speed remains constant throughout the motion.

Example: A car traveling at a constant speed of 60 km/hr on a highway is in uniform motion.

Non-uniform Motion: An object is in non-uniform motion if it covers unequal distances in equal intervals of time. This means its speed keeps changing throughout the motion.

Example: A car accelerating from rest at a traffic light is in non-uniform motion.

title: Distance and displacement
text:
Laws of Motion › Distance and displacement › distance and displacement — Revision note (part 1/1)

Distance is the total path covered by the object in motion, irrespective of the direction of the path. Distance is known as a scalar quantity as only the path length covered is measured and the direction of motion is not considered. The distance can never be zero or negative, it is only be positive.

title: Distance, Displacement, Speed and Velocity
text:
Laws of Motion › Displacement, distance, speed And velocity › displacement, distance, speed and velocity — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Distance**: The length of the route actually traversed by a moving body, irrespective of the direction is called distance. Distance is a scalar quantity. S.I. unit of distance is $m$.

**Displacement**: The shortest straight-line distance from the initial position to the final position of a body, along with its direction, is called displacement. Displacement is a vector quantity. S.I. unit of displacement is $m$.

**Speed**: Speed of the moving body is defined as the distance travelled by a body per unit of time.

$Speedofthebody=\frac{Distancetravelledbythebody}{Timeoftravel}$

The average speed of an object is obtained by dividing the total distance travelled by the total time taken. That is,
$averagespeed=\frac{Totaldistancetravelled}{Totaltimetaken}$

If an object travels a distance s in time t then its speed v is, $v=\frac{s}{t}$

The $S.I.$ unit of speed is $m/s$.

**Velocity**: Velocity is the displacement of a body per unit time in a specified direction.

$Thevelocityofthebody=\frac{Displacement}{Timerequiredfordisplacement}=\frac{∆s}{∆t}$

The $S.I.$ unit of velocity is $m/s$.

In case the velocity of the object is changing at a uniform rate, then average velocity is given by the arithmetic mean of initial velocity and final velocity for a given period of time. That is, $averagevelocity=\frac{initialvelocity+finalvelocity}{2}$

Mathematically,
${v}_{avg}=\frac{u+v}{2}$

where ${v}_{avg}$ is the average velocity, u is the initial velocity and v is the final velocity of the object.
Speed and velocity have the same units that is $m{s}^{–1}orm/s.$

text:

**Uniform linear motion:**

An object is said to be in uniform motion if its velocity is constant. In this type of motion, the object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time. The time interval in this motion should be small.

**Non- uniform linear motion:**

An object is said to be in non-uniform motion if its velocity is not constant. In this type of motion, the object covers unequal distances in equal intervals of time.

Examples of motions where objects cover unequal distances in equal intervals of time are -

1. When a car is moving on a crowded street.

2. A person is jogging in a park.

A body can have

1. Zero velocity and still be accelerated.

2. Constant speed and still have a varying velocity.

The direction of the velocity of a body can change, even when its acceleration is constant.

title: Acceleration
text:
Laws of Motion › Acceleration › acceleration — Revision note (part 1/1)

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. It describes how quickly an object's speed or direction is changing over time.

Example: A car speeding up from a traffic light or a ball rolling down a hill is experiencing acceleration.

Units of Acceleration:

The SI unit of acceleration is meter per second squared (m/s²). This signifies how much an object's velocity changes every second.

Positive acceleration: When an object's speed increases (even if it starts from rest) or when its direction changes towards a shorter path (e.g., turning a corner), it has positive acceleration.

Examples: A car accelerating from 0 km/hr to 60 km/hr in 10 seconds experiences positive acceleration.

Negative acceleration (deceleration): When an object's speed decreases (including coming to a complete stop) or when its direction changes towards a longer path (e.g., braking), it has negative acceleration.

Examples: A train slowing down from 80 km/hr to 40 km/hr in 5 seconds experiences negative acceleration (deceleration).

title: uniform circular motion
text:
Laws of Motion › Uniform circular motion › uniform circular motion — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Uniform Circular Motion** is a motion of an object in a circular path with uniform speed.

[Figure 1]

The direction of the velocity of the particle will be tangent to the position of the particle at every point on the circumference of the circle.

The velocity of a particle in circular motion is variable or the circular motion is accelerated even though the speed of the particle is uniform.

**Difference between the uniform circular motion and uniform linear motion.:**

In uniform linear motion, the speed and velocity are constant and acceleration is zero i.e., the uniform linear motion is an unaccelerated motion, while in a uniform circular motion the velocity is variable, so it is an accelerated motion

In UCM, the angular speed of the particle is constant.

Speed along a circular path is given by

$v=\frac{2πr}{t}$, where **r** is the radius of the circle and **t** is the time taken to travel along the circle.

There are many familiar examples of objects moving under uniform circular motion, such as the motion of the moon around the earth, the motion of a satellite in a circular orbit around the earth, a cyclist on a circular track at a constant speed etc.

Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement with time. It is given by, $\omega=\frac{d\theta}{dt}$

Angular velocity and linear velocity are related by the equation, $v=Rω$

The centripetal acceleration of the body is given by $a=\frac{{v}^{2}}{R}={\omega}^{2}R$

Centripetal acceleration acts along the radius and towards the centre of the circle.

Laws of Motion › Determining the direction of velocity in uniform circular motion › determining the direction of velocity in uniform circular motion — Revision note (part 1/1)

Determining the direction of velocity in uniform circular motion:

The direction of velocity of a particle performing uniform circular motion is along the tangent to the circle at the position of the particle, in the sense of motion of the particle.

Image

In uniform circular motion, speed is uniform, velocity is not uniform.
The magnitude of velocity remains constant, but the direction of velocity changes continuously with time.
It follows that the motion is accelerated, i.e., the acceleration is not zero.
The magnitude of acceleration remains constant, but the direction of acceleration changes continuously with time.
Acceleration is always directed towards the centre of the circle. It is called centripetal acceleration. The corresponding force is called centripetal force.

title: balanced and unbalanced forces
text:
Laws of Motion › Balanced and unbalanced forces › balanced and unbalanced forces — Revision note (part 1/1)

According to Newton's first law of motion, only a net external unbalanced force can change the state of motion. Balanced forces do not cause a change in motion of an object.

When the balanced forces act on an object at rest, the object will not move it will continue to be in the rest state. For example, a book kept on a table is acted upon by two forces, one the force of gravity pulling the object down and the other force of normal reaction by the table on the book. These two forces balance out each other and hence there is no change in motion of the book.

When the balanced forces act on an object in uniform motion, the object will continue to move in uniform motion without changing its speed or direction. When a ball is rolling with uniform speed on a flat floor there are two forces acting on the ball, one the force of gravity pulling the ball down and the other force of normal reaction by the floor on the ball. These two forces balance out each other and hence there is no change in motion of the ball.

Forces that cause a change in the motion of an object are called unbalanced forces. The forces would no longer be equal. When we push an object at rest, the object is made to move with an acceleration. This happens because the push given by us is an unbalanced force.

[Figure 1]

The above diagram is an example of a balanced force. As forces on both the sides are same, hence the net force on the system is equal to zero.

[Figure 2]

The above diagram is an example of unbalanced force. As both the forces are different, the net force on the system is not equal to zero.

title: newton’s first law of motion
text:
Laws of Motion › Newton’s first law of motion › newton’s first law of motion — Revision note (part 1/3)

**Statement of Newton's first law of motion:**
Newton's first law of motion states that everybody continues to be in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external unbalanced force.

Explanation of Newton's first law:

1) Without the application of an external force, a body continues to be at rest. For example, a book kept on a table continues to remain there unless we move it.

2) Without the application of an external force, a body in uniform motion continues to move uniformly. In everyday life, we see that bodies in motion eventually come to rest. For example, a ball rolled on a floor eventually comes to rest. Now, the ball stops because external forces are pushing the ball in the opposite direction; in this case, it is the force of friction from the ground. But if no force acts on the body, the body will continue its motion till eternity.

3) Without the application of an external force, a body cannot change its direction of motion, i.e. it continues to move in the same straight line. For example, a bike moving along a straight road cannot change its direction on its own. We have to turn its handle.

If an object is at rest or in uniform linear motion, it does not mean that no forces are acting on it. It means that all the forces acting on the body cancel each other out and the net external force on the body is zero. For example, a book kept on a table is stationary not because no force acts on it. Two forces are acting on the book viz., the force of gravity in the downward direction and the normal reaction by the table on the book. Now, these two forces cancel each other out. Hence, there is no external unbalanced force in the book.

Newton's first law defines force

title: newton’s first law of motion
text:
Laws of Motion › Newton’s first law of motion › newton’s first law of motion — Revision note (part 2/3)

The law indirectly says that only an external unbalanced force can change the state of motion of the body. Hence, we can define force as an external push or pull that tries to move a body at rest or tries to stop a body in motion or tries to increase the speed of the moving body or tries to change the direction of motion of the body.

Newton's first law defines inertia

One of the conclusions of the law is the body cannot change its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line on its own. Only some external entity can make that change. This inability of the body to change its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line by itself is called inertia of the body. Hence, Newton's first law of motion is also called the law of inertia.

Quantitatively, the inertia of a body in linear motion is measured by the mass of the body. The heavier the body, the greater the force required to change its state and hence greater its inertia. The reverse is also true.

**Types of inertia:**

1) Inertia of rest:
The body at rest remains at rest and cannot move on its own. This inability of the body is called inertia of rest. A body tries to oppose any force that tries to move the body. For example, when the bus starts suddenly, the passengers inside the bus feel a backward jerk. This is because their feet which are in touch with the bus moves forward and the upper body is still in its state of rest hence the passengers feel a backward push on account of the inertia of rest.

title: newton’s first law of motion
text:
Laws of Motion › Newton’s first law of motion › newton’s first law of motion — Revision note (part 3/3)

2) Inertia of motion:
The body in uniform motion can neither accelerate nor retard on its own. This inability of the body is called inertia of motion. A body in uniform motion tries to oppose any force that tries to accelerate or stop it. For example, when a bus moving at a uniform speed tries to stop the passengers inside the bus feel a forward jerk. This is because their feet which is in touch with the bus retard when brakes are applied but the upper body continues to move at the same speed, and hence passenger feel a forward push on account of inertia of motion.

3) Inertia of direction:
The body in uniform motion cannot change the direction of motion on its own. This inability of the body is called inertia of direction. A body opposes the force that tries to change its direction of motion. For example, when a car moves along a curved road, the passengers inside the car are thrown outwards. This is because the person inside the car tries to move in a straight line due to the inertia of direction.

title: newton's second law of motion
text:
Laws of Motion › Newton's second law of motion › newton's second law of motion — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Newton's second law of motion :**

According to Newton's second law of motion, the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the force applied on it and it acts in the direction of applied force.

$F=\frac{∆p}{∆t}=\frac{∆(mv)}{∆t}\ F=\frac{dp}{dt}=\frac{d(mv)}{dt}\ F=m\frac{dv}{dt}=ma⋯⋯⋯⋯\left{a=\frac{dv}{dt}\right}$

For this relation to hold :

1. The velocities are needed to be much smaller than the velocity of light
2. Mass should remain constant

**Importance of Newton’s Second Law of Motion :**

- It gives mathematical formulation for the quantitative measure of force as the rate of change of linear momentum.
- It defines momentum $p=mv$ instead of velocity as the fundamental quantity related to motion. What is changed by a force is the momentum and not necessarily the velocity.
- Aristotle’s fallacy is overcome by considering resultant unbalanced force

**To obtain Newton's first law of motion from the second law of motion :**

From Newton's second law of motion, F=ma

If F=0, a=0

It means that if no force is applied on the body, its acceleration will be zero.

title: newton’s third law of motion
text:
Laws of Motion › Newton’s third law of motion › newton’s third law of motion — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Newton's Third Law**

- Newton's third law states that, to every action, there is always an equal and opposite reaction.
- Action and reaction forces are always on different objects.
- This means that if body A exerts a force on body B, then body B also exerts equal and opposite force on body A. simultaneously.

[Figure 1]

Vectorially, it can be written as

${\vec{F}}_{AB}+{\vec{F}}_{BA}=0\ ∴{\vec{F}}_{AB}=-{\vec{F}}_{BA}$

Here (-ve) sign indicates both the forces act in an opposite direction

**Some points to remember**

1. Action and reaction always occur in pairs.
2. Action and reaction are always on different objects and hence never cancel each other.
3. Action and reaction occur at the same instant of time.
4. The action-reaction pairs can be contact or non-contact force

**Example :**

1. Repulsive forces between two magnets are a pair of action-reaction forces
2. The gravitational force between Earth and Moon or between Earth and Sun are also similar pairs of non-contact action-reaction forces

title: Newton’s Third Law of Motion
text:
Laws of Motion › Newton’s third law of motion › Introduction to newton's third law of motion — Revision note (part 1/1)

Study Notes: Newton's Third Law of Motion

1. The Law — Definition

- Whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object simultaneously exerts a force, which is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
- Key phrase: "Every action has an equal and opposite reaction

2. Everyday Examples

- Kicking a ball: Your foot pushes the ball forward and the ball pushes your foot backward
- Sitting on a wheeled chair pushing a table. If you push table forward , the chair moves backward. If you pull table backward, the chair moves forward
- Walking: You push the ground backward and then friction pushes you forward

3. Rockets — A Powerful Example

- A rocket does not push against the ground to fly
- It expels gas downward at high speeds
- Reaction force: gas pushes rocket upward → this is thrust
- This reaction force is what carries the rocket into space

4. The Role of Mass

- Equal forces produce different accelerations depending on mass
- Gun & bullet example: The gun exerts force on the bullet, the bullet flies far (small mass = huge acceleration). The bullet exerts equal force on the gun, the gun only recoils slightly (large mass = small acceleration)
- Remember: Force = Mass × Acceleration (Newton's 2nd Law connects here)

5. Key Takeaways

- Forces always come in pairs — you cannot have an action without a reaction
- The two forces act on different objects, never on the same one
- Motion is described as a "conversation" between two objects
- Newton's Third Law applies everywhere — from walking to rocket launches

title: How do you keep bouncing when you jump on a trampoline?
text:
Laws of Motion › Newton’s laws of motion › how do you keep bouncing when you jump on a trampoline? — Revision note (part 1/2)

Statement of Newton's first law of motion:
Newton's first law of motion states that everybody continues to be in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external unbalanced force.

Explanation of Newton's first law:

1) Without the application of an external force, a body continues to be at rest. For example, a book kept on a table continues to remain there unless we move it.

2) Without the application of an external force, a body in uniform motion continues to move uniformly. In everyday life, we see that bodies in motion eventually come to rest. For example, a ball rolled on a floor eventually comes to rest. Now, the ball stops because external forces are pushing the ball in the opposite direction; in this case, it is the force of friction from the ground. But if no force acts on the body, the body will continue its motion till eternity.

**Newton's second law of motion:**

Momentum p=mv where m is the mass of the object and v is the velocity.

Momentum is a vector quantity.

Kilogram-metre per second ($kg.{ms}^{-1}$) is the S.I. unit of momentum.

Suppose an object of mass, m is moving along a straight line with an initial velocity, u. It is uniformly accelerated to velocity, v in time, t, by the application of a constant force, F throughout the time, t.

The initial and final momentum of the object will be,

${p}_{1}=mu$ and ${p}_{2}=mv$respectively.
The change in momentum is directly proportional to ${p}_{2}-{p}_{1}$.

Thus, the change in momentum $∝mv–mu\ ∝m\times(v–u)$

$∴$The rate of change of momentum $∝\frac{m\times\left(v-u\right)}{t}$

Newton's second law of motion states that the rate of change of momentum of an object is proportional to the applied unbalanced force in the direction of the force.

title: law of conservation of momentum
text:
Laws of Motion › Law of conservation of momentum › law of conservation of momentum — Revision note (part 1/2)

Law of conservation of momentum states that the momentum of the system remains constant or conserved when no external force is applied

or the momentum of a system before collision is equal to momentum of the system after collision when no external force is applied

When there is no external force acting on the system,

$\vec{F}=0\ \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}=0\ ⇒\vec{p}=constant$

So if we are considering two bodies of masses ${m}_{1}$ & ${m}_{2}$ initially moving with a velocity of ${u}_{1}$ & ${u}_{2}$ respectively, now if they collide and after collision, they have velocities ${v}_{1}$ & ${v}_{2}$, Their momentums before and after collision are given as

[Figure 1]

Momentum of mass 1 before collision = ${m}_{1}{u}_{1}$

Momentum of mass 2 before collision = ${m}_{2}{u}_{2}$

Momentum of mass 1 after collision = ${m}_{1}{v}_{1}$

Momentum of mass 2 after collision = ${m}_{2}{v}_{2}$

$∴$ The rate of change of its momentum (or ${F}_{12}$) of mass 1 during the collision will be $\frac{{m}_{1}({v}_{1}-{u}_{1})}{t}$

Similarly, the rate of change of its momentum (or ${F}_{21}$ ) of mass 2 during the collision will be $\frac{{m}_{2}({v}_{2}-{u}_{2})}{t}$

According to Newton's third law of motion, ${F}_{12}=-{F}_{21}$

$∴\frac{{m}_{1}({v}_{1}-{u}_{1})}{t}=-\frac{{m}_{2}({v}_{2}-{u}_{2})}{t}$

After solving this we get,

${m}_{1}{u}_{1}+{m}_{2}{u}_{2}={m}_{1}{v}_{1}+{m}_{2}{v}_{2}$

This is the mathematical formulation of the law of conservation of linear momentum.

Thus, the principle of conservation of linear momentum can be stated as, "The total momentum of an isolated system is conserved during any interaction".

The plot shows that the object has a variable velocity that is increasing from u to v as the slope is positive velocity is increasing in a positive direction.

= u × t

Also, from the first equation of motion, v – u = at

title: definition of work
text:
Work And Energy › Work › definition of work — Revision note (part 1/1)

The work done by the force is defined as the product of the component of the force in the direction of the displacement (F) and the magnitude of this displacement (d).

Thus, $W=(F\cos\theta)d=\vec{F.}\vec{d}$

It is a scalar quantity. Its S.I unit is joule.

When the displacement is done in the direction of the applied force then the work is said to be positive.

When the displacement is done in the opposite direction of the applied force then the work is said to be negative.

[Figure 1]

Conditions for no work done:

1) When an applied force causes no displacement then work done is zero. A person pushing a heavy rock which does not move is an example of no work done even when force is applied.

2) When no force is applied but there is displacement happening. A block moving smoothly on a floor with uniform velocity is an example of no work done.

3) When force and displacement are perpendicular to each other. In this case, the angle between force and displacement is $\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\cos\frac{\pi}{2}$ becomes zero. Hence, the work done is zero. Assuming moon to be moving around earth in a perfectly circular orbit, earth's gravitational force does no work on the moon because the displacement in a circular orbit is always perpendicular to the centripetal force, which in this case is the gravitational force of attraction.

Note : The work done by centripetal force is always zero. (Centripetal force and velocity are always perpendicular to each other)

title: Formula to calculate work done
text:
Work And Energy › Formula to calculate work done › formula to calculate work done — Revision note (part 1/1)

Work is said to be done when we apply a force on an object and the object experiences displacement. If the displacement in the direction of force is zero then the work done becomes zero. The formula for work is used to calculate work done in moving an object.

The formula for work is used to calculate the work done to displace any object. Work is the product of the force applied and displacement in the direction of the force applied. Work is the dot product of the two vectors: force and displacement. Thus work is a scalar quantity. SI unit of work is Joule (J).

The formula for Work can be expressed as,

W = F.d

W = (Fcos θ)d

Where,

W = Work done
F = Magnitude of the force applied
d = Magnitude of the displacement in the direction of the force.
θ = is the angle between the vectors: force and displacement
SI unit of work is Joule (J). If 1 joule of work is done then the formula for work comes out to be 1 J = 1 N.m

title: expression for kinetic energy
text:
Work And Energy › Energy › expression for kinetic energy — Revision note (part 1/1)

Let the force **F** be applied to a stationary object of mass **m**. The applied force sets the object in motion. Let **u** be its initial velocity (here u = 0). Let a be the acceleration of the object, and, after time t, the velocity of the object becomes equal to v. The displacement
during this time is s. The work done on the object, W = F . s

$W=F\timess$ ____(1)

According to Newton’s second law of motion,
F = ma -------- (2)

From the second equation of motion, we get,
$s=ut+\frac{1}{2}{at}^{2}$

However, as the initial velocity is zero, u = 0.
$s=0+\frac{1}{2}{at}^{2}$

$s=\frac{1}{2}{at}^{2}$

Using equations (1) and (2), we get,

$W=ma\times\frac{1}{2}{at}^{2}\ ∴W=\frac{1}{2}m{(at)}^{2}$ ___________ (3)

According to Newton’s first equation of motion,
$v=u+at\ v=0+at\ ∴v=at⇒{v}^{2}={(at)}^{2}$ ____________(4)

Using equations (3) and (4), we get,

$W=\frac{1}{2}{mv}^{2}$

The kinetic energy gained by an object is the amount of work done on the object.
$∴K.E.=W$

Thus the kinetic energy gained by an object due to its motion is given by

KE =$\frac{1}{2}{mv}^{2}$

where 'm' is the mass of the object and v is the velocity with which the object is moving.

text:

To raise an object of mass ‘**m**’ to a height ‘**h**’ above the earth’s surface, a force equal to the weight ‘**mg**’ of an object has to be used against the gravitational force.

The amount of work done can be calculated as follows.
Work = force x displacement
$W=mg\timesh\ ⇒W=mgh$

The amount of potential energy stored in the object because of its displacement is given as
P.E. = mgh

$(W=P.E.)$

Displacement to height **h** causes energy equal to **mgh** to be stored in the object.

Potential Energy is the energy stored in an object when it is at a certain height ($h$) w.r.t. the ground.

Thus the equation of Potential Energy is given by:

$PE=mgh$

where,

$'m'isthemassoftheobject\ 'h'istheheightoftheobjectfromtheground\ 'g'istheaccelerationduetogravity.$

title: law of conservation of energy
text:
Work And Energy › Energy › law of conservation of energy — Revision note (part 1/1)

The Law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor be destroyed, it can only be converted from one form to another. Thus, the total amount of energy in the universe remains constant.

[Figure 1]

This law of conservation of energy is valid in all situations and for all kinds of transformations.

The Law of conservation of mechanical energy states that sum total of potential and kinetic energy does not change with time as long as the forces are conservative. The total potential energy at the top will be equal to the total kinetic energy at the bottom in a free fall.

Total Energy at any point will always be equals to the sum of Kinetic Energy and Potential Energy:

$T.E.=K.E.+P.E.$

$T.E.=\frac{1}{2}{mv}^{2}+mgh$

Thus, every object has potential energy when it is at a height above the ground and it keeps getting converted to kinetic energy as the object falls towards the ground. On reaching the ground (point C), all the potential energy gets converted to kinetic energy. But at any point during the fall the total energy remains constant.
i.e., T.E. = P.E. + K.E.
T.E. at A = mgh + 0 = mgh
T.E. at B = mgx + mg (h - x) = mgh
T.E. at C = 0 + mgh = mgh

title: free fall
text:
Work And Energy › Free fall › free fall — Revision note (part 1/1)

When an object falls towards the earth solely under the influence of gravitational force then it is said to be in free fall.

Due to earth's attraction there will be an acceleration involved.

This acceleration is due to gravity and is called acceleration due to gravity which is denoted by 'g'

S I unit of g is $m/{s}^{2}$ .

Acceleration due to gravity is directed downwards towards the centre of the earth.

'g' is given by $g=\frac{GM}{{R}^{2}}$

Magnitude of force F will be equal to product of mass and acceleration due to gravity and is given by

$F=mg$

The kinematical equations under gravity can be expressed as :

$v=u-gt\ s=ut-\frac{1}{2}{gt}^{2}\ {v}^{2}={u}^{2}-2gs$

In the above equation, the acceleration is replaced by gravity i.e. $a=-g$

here the negative sign indicates, the acceleration due to gravity always acts downwards, hence considered (-ve).

true free fall is possible only in vacuum.

For free fall, the initial velocity u = 0 and the acceleration a = g. Thus we can write the equations as

$v=-gt\ s=-\frac{1}{2}{gt}^{2}\ {v}^{2}=-2gs$

The moon and the artificial satellites are moving only under the influence of the gravitational field of the earth. Thus they are in free fall.

subconcept_name: does skydiving feel like free falling?
title: Does skydiving feel like free falling?
text:
Work And Energy › Free fall › does skydiving feel like free falling? — Revision note (part 1/2)

Skydivers and wingsuit flyers may call what they do as free falling?? But words mean a little more specific in physics.

So, let’s explore what free fall is all about

free fall is what an object does when it is only under the influence of one force, gravity.

We have to go back to history to understand this concept

For thousands of years scientists believed that how fast something fell depended on how heavy it was. It seemed logical too.

But in 16th century, Galileo had hypothesized that if air resistance and friction are negligible, all objects regardless of their mass fell at the constant acceleration towards earth. That constant acceleration is the acceleration due to gravity.

Galileo, using the instruments available to him, measured the acceleration that was due to Earth’s gravity, as about 10 meter per second square. We now know that it's 9.8 meter per second square near the surface of the earth.

He wasn’t far off and that is impressive!!

If we were to take two objects, one light and other heavy and drop them from a height, they would both hit the ground at the same time. This indicates that the acceleration is independent of the mass. It verifies Galileo’s point.

This even works on the moon!!

The best way to see the basic features of free fall, that is the motion involving gravity is to start by considering straight up and down motion with no air resistance or friction.

For instance, if we drop a stone from a height without giving a force upon dropping it, the stone is in the state of free-fall. It has zero initial velocity.

Under these circumstances, the motion is one-dimensional and has constant acceleration, g.

title: numerical problems on work and energy
text:
Work And Energy › Numerical problems on work and energy › numerical problems on work and energy — Revision note (part 1/1)

The energy possessed by a body on account of its motion is called Kinetic Energy.

The kinetic energy gained by an object due to its motion is given by:

$KE=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}$

where '**m**' is the mass of the object and '**v**' is the velocity in which object is moving.

The form of mechanical energy stored in an object because of its specific state or position is called its potential energy.

The potential energy stored in an object at height (h) is given by $P.E.=mgh$

where, '**m**' is the mass of the object, '**h**' is the height of the object from the ground and '**g**' is the acceleration due to gravity.

The work done by the force is defined as the product of the component of the force in the direction of the displacement (F) and the magnitude of this displacement (s).

Thus, $W=(F\cos\theta)s=\vec{F.}\vec{s}$

The rate of doing work is called power. It is also defined as the rate of change of energy per unit time.

The power is measured as the amount of work done by the source in one second.

We can write power as $P=\frac{W}{t}$ where W is work done and t is time taken.

S.I. unit of power is watt.

If 1 joule of work is done in 1 second then, power spent is said to be 1 watt.

Bigger units of power are kilowatt(kW), megawatt(MW) and gigawatt (GW).

title: potential and potential difference
text:
Current Electricity › Potential and potential difference › potential and potential difference — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Potential :**

Potential is said to be the quantity determining the energy of charge in an electric field.

The difference in the potential between the positive and negative terminals of a cell is called as potential difference.

The potential at a point is defined as the amount of work done per unit charge in bringing a positive test charge from infinity to that point. It is denoted by symbol $V$. it is a scalar quantity.

[Figure 1]

If $Wjoule$ is the work done in bringing the test charge $Qcoulomb$ from infinity to the point $P$, the electric potential $V$ at the point null is given by

$V=\frac{W}{Q}$

The $S.I.$ unit of electric potential is ${JC}^{-1}$ or $Volt(V)$.

The potential at a point is said to be $1Volt$ when $1joule$ of work is done in bringing $1coulomb$ charge from infinity to that point.

$1Volt=\frac{1joule}{1coulomb}=1{JC}^{-1}$

**Potential Difference :**

The work done by the external force in moving a unit positive test charge from one point to the other point in an electric field is called the potential difference between those points.

[Figure 2]

If $W$ be the work done in carrying a test charge ${q}_{0}$ from $B$ to $A$, then the potential difference between $A$ and $B$ is given by

$Potentialdifference(V)=\frac{Workdone(W)}{Totalchargetransfered(Q)}$

${V}_{A}-{V}_{B}=\frac{W}{{q}_{0}}$

The $S.I.$ unit of potential difference is $volt$ and it is a scalar quantity.

In an electric field, a free positive test charge moves from a region of higher potential to a region of lower potential. A free negative charge moves from lower potential to the higher potential.

$Electron-volt$ is a very small unit of work (or energy), which is used in atomic physics.

title: conventional current
text:
Current Electricity › Free electrons and current › conventional current — Revision note (part 1/1)

Conventional current

When the two charged conductors are joined by a metal wire, the direction of the flow of electrons is determined by the electric potential of the conductor.

A conductor having more number of electrons is said to be at negative potential or lower potential, while a conductor having the deficiency of the electrons is said to be at positive potential or the higher potential.

When a positively charged conductor (having deficiency of electrons) is joined by the metal wire to a negatively charged conductor (having more number of electrons). The electrons will flow from the negatively charged conductor to the positively charged conductor. Thus, the electrons will flow from a higher to a lower level.

The flow is always from the higher level to the lower level, this is the conventional direction of any flow.

The electric current is said to flow from a body at the higher potential to a body at lower potential i.e., in the direction opposite to the direction of the flow of electrons.

Thus, in any circuit, the direction of flow of current is always from the positive terminal of the battery to the negative terminal. This is the conventional direction of the current flow.

The rate of flow of charge across a cross-section is called current.

The amount of charge is given by :

$Charge=current\timestime$

$Q=I\timest$

If $n$ is the number of electrons and $e$ is the charge on one electron, then the total charge passed through the cross-section is

$Q=n\timese$

The unit of charge in S.I. units is Coulomb (C). Current is expressed in Ampere (A). The charge of one electron is $1.6x{10}^{-19}$ C.

Ampere: One-ampere current is said to flow in a conductor if one Coulomb charge flows through it every second.

$∴1A=\frac{1C}{1S}$

title: resistance and Ohm's law
text:
Current Electricity › Resistance & Ohm's law › resistance and Ohm's law — Revision note (part 1/1)

A measure of opposition to the flow of electric current induced by a voltage is called resistance.

Ohm's law states that if the physical state of a conductor remains constant, the current (I) flowing through it is directly proportional to the potential difference (V) between its two ends.

i.e $I∝V$

I=kV

where k= constant of proportionality

Therefore, $I\times\frac{1}{k}=V$

where $\frac{1}{k}$= R = Resistance of the conductor

Therefore $I\timesR=V$

Hence,V=IR

At given temperature, the resistance (R) of a conductor is directly proportional to its length (L) and inversely proportional to its area of cross-section (A)

Resistance R=$\frac{ρL}{A}$

where L= Length of the wire.

$\rho$= Resistivity of the wire.

A= Area of the cross-section of the wire.

The unit of resistance is Ohm. It is indicated by the symbol $\Omega$.

$1Ohm(\Omega)=\frac{1Volt}{1Ampere}$

title: Electric circuit and circuit components
text:
Current Electricity › Resistance & Ohm's law › electric circuit and circuit components — Revision note (part 1/1)

An electric circuit is composed of electrical components that form a continuous conducting path connected to the terminals of a power source. In simple circuits, the power source is usually a dry cell or a series of dry cells commonly called a battery. It is connected to a load or a device, which can be a light bulb, a resistor, a heater, etc. A complete or closed circuit is formed when current flows continuously in the circuit. However, any break on the circuit that stops the flow of current creates an open circuit.

The basic components of electric circuits include a voltage source, a load, and a conductive pathway.

A voltage source is an electrical component that supplies energy. It provides a potential difference for the charges to flow. Examples of voltage sources are a battery and a generator.
The load in a circuit is a device that uses electrical energy. A load can be a resistor, a light bulb, or a motor.
A conductive pathway provides a path for the current to flow and is used to connect the electrical components to each other and the power source.

The three basic components of an electric circuits.

Besides these three basic elements, most electrical circuits also employ a switch to easily turn on or off the circuit. Other common passive electrical components are resistors, capacitors, and inductors.

title: Conductors and Insulators
text:
Current Electricity › Conductors & Insulators › insulators and conductors — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Conductors and Insulators**:

**CONDUCTORS**

Conductors are those through which the electric charge can easily flow. They have resistance. e.g., the human body, metals, earth, mercury and electrolytes are conductors of electricity.

In metals, free electrons are the actual charge carriers and these are free to move throughout the volume of the metal. In electrolytes, both positive and negative charges are the actual carriers. The charges in the electrolyte are carried by ions that move in an electrolyte.

**INSULATORS**

The substances through which the electric charge cannot flow are called insulators or dielectrics. These substances have extremely high electrical resistance.

e.g., Glass, hard rubber, plastic, and dry wood are insulators. Practically, insulators do not have free electrons.

If a charge is given to a conductor, it is readily transferred over its entire surface. On the other hand, if some charge is given to an insulator it stays at the place where it is placed. These charges are called static charges.

title: resistance in series
text:
Current Electricity › System of resistors & Effective resistance › resistance in series — Revision note (part 1/1)

When the resistances ${R}_{1,}{R}_{2},{R}_{3},......{R}_{n}$ are connected in series, the effective resistance is equal to the sum of the individual resistances.

[Figure 1]

Then the effective series resistance ${R}_{S}$ is given by ${R}_{S}={R}_{1}+{R}_{2}+{R}_{3}+......+{R}_{n}$.

The equivalent resistance in series combination is larger than the largest resistance.

If $n$ resistors of resistance $R$ each are connected in series then the effective resistance of the combination is $nR$.

The voltages across the resistances are ${V}_{1,}{V}_{2},{V}_{3},......{V}_{n}$ then, the total voltage is given by

$V={V}_{1}+{V}_{2}+{V}_{3}+......+{V}_{n}$.

In the series combination, the current through each resistance remains the same.

The potential difference between the two extremes of the arrangement is equal to the sum of the potential differences across individual resistors.

This arrangement is used to increase the resistance in a circuit.

When resistors are connected in series, they are connected one after another. If any of them does not function, the circuit breaks and there is no flow of electricity.

title: Resistance in parallel

The current flowing through an individual resistor is proportional to the inverse of its resistance and the total current flowing through the circuit is the sum of the currents flowing through individual resistors.

This arrangement is used to reduce the resistance in a circuit.

Even if any of the several bulbs connected in parallel becomes non-functional, the circuit does not break as the current flows through the other paths, and the rest of the bulbs light up. When several bulbs are connected in parallel, they emit the same amount of light as when they are connected individually in the circuit, while bulbs connected in series emit less light than when connected individually.

title: Domestic electric connections (household electric circuit)
text:
Current Electricity › System of resistors & Effective resistance › domestic electric connections (household electric circuit) — Revision note (part 1/1)

Domestic electrical connections : The electricity in our homes is brought through the main conducting cable either from the electric pole or from underground cables.

Usually, there are three wires in the cable.
One is called the live wire which brings in the current. It has a red or brown insulation.
The other wire is called neutral wire through which the current returns. It is blue or black.
In India, the voltage difference between the live and neutral wires is about 220 V. Both these wires are connected to the electric meter tough a fuse.
Through a main switch, they are connected to all the conducting wires inside the home so as to provide electricity to every room.
In each separate circuit, various electrical appliances are connected between the live and neutral wires.
The different appliances are connected in parallel and the potential difference across every appliance is the same.
The third wire is called the earth wire and is of yellow or green colour. This is connected to a metal plate buried deep underground near the house and is for safety purposes.

subconcept_name: electric fuse and precautions to be taken while using electricity
title: Electric Fuse and Precautions to be taken while using electricity
text:
Current Electricity › System of resistors & Effective resistance › electric fuse and precautions to be taken while using electricity — Revision note (part 1/1)

Fuse wire : Fuse wire is used to protect domestic appliances.

It is made of a mixture of substances and has a speciﬁc melting point.
It is connected in series to the electric appliances.
If for some reason, the current in the circuit increases excessively, the fuse wire gets heated up and melts. The circuit gets broken and the ﬂow of current stops, thus protecting the appliance.
This wire is ﬁtted in a groove in a body of porcelain-like non-conducting material. For domestic use, fuse wire with upper limits of 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 4 A, 5 A and 10 A are used.

Rubber gloves and rubber soled shoes should be used while working with electrical appliances.

Electric switches and sockets should be fitted at a height at which small children cannot reach and put pins or nails inside. Plug wires should not be pulled while removing electrical plug from its socket.
Before cleaning an electrical appliance, it should be switched off and its plug removed from the socket.
One’s hands should be dry while handling an electrical appliance, and as far as possible, one should use footwear with rubber soles. As rubber is an insulator, it prevents the current from ﬂowing through our body, thereby protecting it.
If a person gets an electric shock, you should not touch that person. You should switch off the main switch and if the switch is too far or you do not know where it is located, then you should remove the plug from the socket if possible. If not, then you should use a wooden pole to push the person away from the electric wire.

title: Measurement of Matter
text:
Measurement of Matter › Laws of chemical combination › measurement of matter — Revision note (part 1/2)

**What is matter?**

- Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass. Matter is everything that we see around us. Actually, it’s not only things we see but also it is perceived by all our senses.

**What is matter made up of?**

- Let’s us take an example to understand that. If we take a piece of chalk and keep breaking it and crushing it, the smallest particle is obtained. If the particle is broken further, the smallest indivisible particle is obtained called atom. Atom is the smallest indivisible (that cannot be broken further) particle of matter.
- Atoms combine to form molecules. Molecules have independent existence. Example- two oxygen atoms forms oxygen molecule, three atoms of oxygen forms ozone molecule, etc.
- Hence all the matter around us is made up of particles (atoms and molecules).

**Maharishi Kanad’s view on Atom**

- Matter consists of indestructible particles called paramanus ( 'param' means ultimate and 'anu' means particle), now called as atoms.
- A paramanu does not exist in free state but it combines with other paramanus to form a bigger particle (molecules).

**Dalton's Atomic Theory**

- Matter consists of very small indivisible particles called atoms.
- Atom can neither be created nor be destroyed.
- The atoms of an element are identical in all respects.
- Atoms of an element combine in small whole numbers to form molecules of that element.
- Atoms of one element combine with atoms of another element in a simple whole-number ratio to form molecules of compounds.

**Dalton's Atomic Theory: Contradictions**

title: Different Laws of Chemical Combinations
text:
Measurement of Matter › Laws of chemical combination › different laws of chemical combinations — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Laws of Chemical Combination:**Chemical combination- Atoms of different elements combine to form compounds. The formation of compounds is governed by various Laws called the laws of chemical combination.
Lavoisier and Joseph L. Proust. gave the following two laws of chemical combination :

1. **Law of conservation of mass**

The law of conservation of mass states that “mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction”.

**"Mass can neither be created nor destroyed"**

**e.g.**$NaCl+{AgNO}_{3}\rightarrowAgCl+{NaNO}_{3}$
In the above experiment, the total mass of $NaCland{AgNO}_{3}$ consumed is equal to the total mass of $AgCland{NaNO}_{3}$ produced.
Mass is conserved as the matter is neither created nor destroyed.

1. **Law of constant proportions**

Lavoisier noted that many compounds are composed of two or more elements. Such compounds had the same elements in the same proportions, irrespective of where the compound came from or who prepared it.

Example: Water, the ratio of the mass of hydrogen to the mass of $oxygen$ is always 1:8, irrespective to the source of water. Thus, if 9 $mg$ of water is decomposed, 1 $mg$ of hydrogen and 8 $mg$ of $oxygen$ are always obtained.

In ammonia, nitrogen and hydrogen are always in the ratio $14:3$ by mass, irrespective of the source or the method from which it is obtained.

This shows the law of constant proportions is also known as the law of definite proportions.

This law was given by **Proust** as “In a chemical substance the elements are always present in definite proportions by mass”.

title: Different Laws of Chemical Combinations
text:
Measurement of Matter › Laws of chemical combination › different laws of chemical combinations — Revision note (part 2/2)

To give appropriate explanations of these laws was also the problem faced by scientists. John Dalton gave the basic theory about the nature of matter; a theory based on the divisibility of matter, which was just a philosophy till then. He termed it as ‘atoms’ from Greek and said the smallest particles of matter are atoms. His theory was based on the laws of chemical combination. Dalton’s atomic theory explained the law of conservation of mass and the law of definite proportions,

According to**Dalton’s atomic theory;** all matter, whether an element, a compound, or a mixture is composed of small particles called atoms.

The postulates of this theory may be stated as follows:

(i) All matter is made of very tiny particles called atoms, which participate in chemical reactions.

(ii) Atoms are indivisible particles, which cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.

(iii) Atoms of a given element are identical in mass and chemical properties.

(iv) Atoms of different elements have different masses and chemical properties.

(v) Atoms combine in the ratio of small whole numbers to form compounds.

(vi) The relative number and types of atoms are constant in a given compound.

title: Atomic size, atomic mass and molecular mass
text:
Measurement of Matter › Measurement of matter - Atom › atomic size, atomic mass and molecular mass — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Atom:**
• An atom consists of a massive and positively charged nucleus and electrons revolving around it.
• Positively charged protons and electrically neutral neutrons make up the nucleus, whereas, electrons are negatively charged particle. $\begin{matrix} Particle & Symbol \\ 1.Neutron & a)n \\ 2.Proton & c){p}^{+} \\ 3.Electron & b){e}^{-} \end{matrix}\$
• The size of an atom is determined by its radius which is the distance between the nucleus of an atom and its outermost orbit.
• Atomic radius is expressed in nanometres.
• The atomic size depends upon the number of electron orbits in the atom. Atomic size increases with an increase in the number of orbits.
**Example:**Atom of $K$ is bigger than the atom of $Na$ because $K$ (2,8,8,1) have 4 orbits while $Na$ (2,8,1) have 3 orbits.
• If two atoms have the same outermost orbit, then the atom having the larger number of electrons in the outermost orbit is smaller than the one having fewer electrons in the same outermost orbit.
**Example:** An atom of $Mg$ is smaller than an atom of $Na$.

**Atomic mass:**
• Atomic mass is the sum of number of protons and neutrons together, ignoring the electrons because of their small size.
• Daltons are the standard units used for measuring **atomic mass**.
• Example: In Sodium $(Na)$, number of protons = 11 and number of neutrons = 12. Therefore, atomic mass of sodium = 11 + 12 = 23u

**Molecular mass:**
• The molecular mass of a substance is the sum of atomic masses of all the atoms in a single molecule of that substance.
• Molecular mass is expressed in the unit **Dalton $\left(u\right)$ or atomic mass unit $(amu)$.**
• Mathematically it can be written as:
**Molecular mass = sum of constituent atomic masses**

**Example**:

Therefore, the valency of sodium is 1, and the valency of chlorine is also 1.

- Elements belonging to the same group possess the same valency.

• Mole is used to expressing the amount of a chemical substance in chemistry.
• **A mole** is the amount of substance containing the same number of chemical units(atoms, ions, molecules) as there are atoms in exactly 12 grams of the **carbon-12**isotope. Symbol is$mol$.
• Mass of 1 mole of a substance (element/compound) in grams is known as its **molar mass. ($M.M$)**• Molar mass of any element in grams is numerically equal to the atomic mass of that element in u.
• The molar volume of a gas is the volume of one mole of a gas at STP. At STP, one mole ($6.022\times{10}^{23}$ particles) of any gas occupies a volume of $22.4L.$[STP = standard temperature =${0}^{^{\circ}}C$, and standard pressure = $1atm$]

• The number of particles present in one mole of any substance = $6.022\times{10}^{23}$units.
• This is called Avogadro's number or Avogadro’s constant. It is denoted by**${N}_{A}$.**

• **The number of particles in 1 mole:**$6.022\times{10}^{23}$particles.
• 1 mole of hydrogen atoms represents hydrogen hydrogen$6.022\times{10}^{23}$hydrogen atoms.
• 1 mole of hydrogen molecules represents hydrogen hydrogen$6.022\times{10}^{23}$hydrogen molecules.

• **Gram atomic mass/Gram molecular mass**

• The gram atomic mass of an element is the mass of one mole of atoms of that element.
• The gram molecular mass of a compound is defined as the mass of a mole of the molecules of that compound.
Example- The gram atomic mass of hydrogen is $1g$ and the gram molecular mass of water is approximately $18grams.$

• The number of moles in a given sample of an element/compound can be calculated by dividing the total mass of the sample by the molar mass of the element/compound by the following formula.

title: Valency and variable Valency
text:
Measurement of Matter › Valency, variable valency › valency and variable valency — Revision note (part 1/1)

Valency is defined as the combining capacity of an element.
It represents the number of chemical bonds formed by one atom of that element with other atoms.
The valency of an element can be determined from its electronic configuration.
**Example**: $Na$ (2,8,1) $\overset{-1{e}^{-}}{\rightarrow}$ ${Na}^{+}$ (2,8)
Sodium atom gives away one electron to form a complete octet. So, the valency of sodium is 1.

$Cl$ (2,8,7) $\overset{+1{e}^{-}}{\rightarrow}$ ${Cl}^{-}$ (2,8)
Chlorine atom accepts one electron to form a complete octet. So, the valency of chlorine is 1.

A chemical bond is formed between ${Na}^{+}$ and ${Cl}^{-}$ ions which results in the formation of an ionic compound $NaCl$.
**The electronic definition of valency**: The number of electrons that an atom of an element gives away or takes up while forming an ionic bond, is called the valency of that element.
Valence electrons are those electrons that are present in the outermost orbit of the atom. It is always represented as a whole number.

Sometimes, under different conditions, the valency of the same element changes i.e. the elements exhibit more than one valency. This property is known as variable valency.
**Example**: Copper exhibits variable valencies 1 $({Cu}^{+})$ and 2 $({Cu}^{2+})$.

Similarly, Iron can also show variable valencies 2 $({Fe}^{+2})$ and 3 $({Fe}^{+3})$.

text:
Acids, Bases and Salts › Acid, bases & salts - Arrhenius theory › arrhenius theory of acids and bases — Revision note (part 1/2)

• **Arrhenius acid-base theory:** In the year 1887, the Swedish scientist Arrhenius suggested a theory of acids and bases.
His definition of acids and bases is as follows:
Acid is a substance which produces ${H}^{+}$ ions when dissolved in water.
Example: $HCl,{H}_{2}{SO}_{4},{H}_{2}{CO}_{3}$, etc.

$HCl\left(g\right){\rightarrow}_{Dissociation}^{water}{H}^{+}\left(aq\right)+{Cl}^{-}\left(aq\right)$

A base is a substance which produces ${OH}^{-}$ ions when dissolved in water.
Example: $NaOH,Ca{\left(OH\right)}_{2},etc.$

$NaOH\left(s\right){\rightarrow}_{Dissociation}^{water}{Na}^{+}\left(aq\right)+{OH}^{-}\left(aq\right)$
Arrhenius theory of acids and bases works well for aqueous solutions.

text:
Acids, Bases and Salts › Acid, bases & salts - Arrhenius theory › arrhenius theory of acids and bases — Revision note (part 2/2)

**Classification of acids and bases and alkali:**
• On the basis of the extent of dissociation of acids and bases in an aqueous solution, they are classified into the following categories:
1. **Strong acid**: Strong acids are those in which, complete dissociation of the compound takes place into ${H}^{+}$ ions.
Example: $HCl,HBr,{HNO}_{3},{H}_{2}{SO}_{4}$,etc.
2. **Strong base**: Strong bases are those in which, complete dissociation of the compound takes place into ${OH}^{-}$ ions.
Example: $NaOH,KOH,Ca{\left(OH\right)}_{2},$ etc.
3. **Weak acid**: Weak acids partially dissociate and the resulting aqueous solution contains a small proportion of ${H}^{+}$ ion and the corresponding acidic radical.
Example: ${H}_{2}{CO}_{3},{CH}_{3}COOH$, etc.
4. **Weak Base**: Weak bases partially dissociate and the resulting aqueous solution contains a small proportion of ${OH}^{-}$ ion and the corresponding basic radical. Example: ${NH}_{4}OH$.
**Alkali:**The bases which show high solubility in water are termed as alkali.
Example: $NaOH,KOH,$etc.
**The basicity of acids**: It is defined as the number of ${H}^{+}$ ions that can be obtained by the dissociation of one molecule of an acid.
**The acidity of bases:**It is defined as the number of ${OH}^{-}$ ions that can be obtained by the dissociation of one molecule of a base.
**For example**: **HCl is a monobasic acid** as it produces one ${H}^{+}$ ion in aqueous solution.
**NaOH is monoacidic base** as it produces one ${OH}^{-}$ ion in aqueous solution.

title: The pH of solution and universal indicators
text:
Acids, Bases and Salts › Acids, bases and salts - pH of a solution › the pH of solution and universal indicators — Revision note (part 1/4)

**$pH$ of Acid**• $pH$ stands for the **"power of hydrogen"** in any solution. Measurements of $pH$ is important in many fields which include medicine, chemistry, water treatment, and many other applications.
• If a solution has more number of $[{H}^{+}]$ ions, then the solution is the more acidic solution.
• The $pH$ scale extends from **1 to 14** and the $pH$ of an acid lies in the range between **1-6**. As this number increases, the acidic nature of a solution decreases.
• According to this scale, the $pH$ value of water is 7 meaning pure water has $[{H}^{+}]$= $1x{10}^{-7}mol/L$.
• $pH$ 7 indicates a neutral solution.
• Therefore, lesser the $pH$ number, more will be its acidity.
• $pH$ can be measured easily using $pH$ papers.
• Strong acids have lesser $pH$ values and they are defined as those acids which dissociate completely in an aqueous solution to produce ${H}^{+}$ ions.
• Examples of strong acids include hydrochloric acid (HCl), sulphuric acid $({H}_{2}{SO}_{4})$ and nitric acid $({HNO}_{3})$.
• Weak acids have greater $pH$ values than strong acids and they are defined as those acids which do not dissociate completely in an aqueous solution, the concentration of ${H}^{+}$ ions produced is low.
Examples of weak acids include acetic acid $({CH}_{3}COOH)$ and carbonic acid ${H}_{2}{CO}_{3}$.

**Calculation of $pH$:**
• $pH$ of an acid can be calculated using formula: $pH=-{\log}_{10}[{H}^{+}]\ and\ pH+pOH=14$

title: The pH of solution and universal indicators
text:
Acids, Bases and Salts › Acids, bases and salts - pH of a solution › the pH of solution and universal indicators — Revision note (part 2/4)

**$pH$ of Base**
• If a solution has more number of $[{OH}^{-}]$ ions, then it is called a Basic solution.
• $pH$ of a base lies in the range between **8-14**. As the number increases, the basicity of a solution also increases.
• Example of strong bases are: Sodium hydroxide and calcium hydroxide.
The equation is: $pH$ = $-{\log}_{10}[{H}^{+}]$
Similarly, $pOH=-{\log}_{10}[{OH}^{-}]$
• The relationship between $pH$ and $pOH$ of the solution at room temperature is $pH+pOH=14$.

**Neutralization:** When $NaOH$ is added to $HCl$, the resulting solution contains only ${Na}^{+}and{Cl}^{-}$ ions, that is $NaCl$, salt and the solvent water.
The only source of ${H}^{+}$ and ${OH}^{-}$ ions in the solution is the dissociation of water.
Hence, this reaction is called the neutralisation reaction.
The reaction is also represented as follows:

$\underset{Acid}{HCl}+\underset{Base}{NaOH}\rightarrow\underset{Salt}{NaCl}+\underset{Water}{{H}_{2}O}\$
Basically, in a neutralisation reaction, an acid reacts with a base to form salt and water.

text:
Acids, Bases and Salts › Acids, bases and salts - pH of a solution › the pH of solution and universal indicators — Revision note (part 3/4)

$pH$ **of Solution**• Acids and bases when dissolved in water undergo dissociation to a small or a large extent resulting in the formation oaf $[{H}^{+}]$ and $[{OH}^{-}]$ ions. These $[{H}^{+}]$ and $[{OH}^{-}]$ ions are present in different proportions in all the natural aqueous solutions, which thereby determines the properties of those solutions.
• Pure water dissociates to a very small extent resulting in the formation of $[{H}^{+}]$ and $[{OH}^{-}]$ ions in equal proportion. Because of this property of water to undergo dissociation, any aqueous solution consists of both $[{H}^{+}]$ and $[{OH}^{-}]$ ions.
${H}_{2}O\overset{dissociation}{\rightarrow}{H}^{+}+{OH}^{-}$
• A Danish scientist **Sorenson** in **1909** introduced a convenient new scale for expressing the $[{H}^{+}]$ ion concentration. It is the $pH$ scale.
• $pH$ stands for the **"power of hydrogen"** in any solution. $pH$ of any solution is an important piece of information while understanding the **nature of a solution**.
• The relationship between $pH$ and $pOH$ of the solution at room temperature is $pH+pOH=14$.
• If a solution has more number of $[{H}^{+}]$ ions $≡$ Acidic solution, $pH$ < 7
• If a solution has more number of $[{OH}^{-}]$ ions $≡$ Basic solution, $pH$ > 7
• If a solution has an equal number of $[{H}^{+}]$ and $[{OH}^{-}]$ ions $≡$ Neutral solution, $pH$ = 7
• The $pH$ scale extends from **1 to 14,** and the $pH$ of an acid lies in the range between **1-6**. As this number increases, the acidic nature of a solution decreases.

• If a solution has more number of $[{OH}^{-}]$ ions, then it is called a Basic solution.
• $pH$ of a base lies in the range between **8-14**. As the number increases, the basicity of a solution also increases.
• According to this scale, the $pH$ value of water is 7, meaning pure water has $[{H}^{+}]$= $1x{10}^{-7}mol/L$. $pH$ 7 indicates a neutral solution.
• The $pH$ of an aqueous solution can be measured with a glass electrode and a $pH$ meter, or an indicator.
• $pH$ of solution can be measured easily using $pH$ papers.
• $pH$ indicator and $pH$ meter is used for accurate measurement of $pH$ in labs.

[Figure 2]

**Universal indicators:**
• These are the mixture of dyes, which will change its color to indicate the acidity or alkalinity of solution over a range of $pH$ values.
• A universal indicator is made by mixing several synthetic indicators in a specific manner.
• They are used for the determination of $pH$ of a solution as they show different colours at different $pH$ values.
• However, the most reliable method for measuring the $pH$ value of a solution is to use an instrument called $pH$ meter.
• Examples: Phenolpthalein, Methyl red etc.

title: pH Scale and Indicators
text:
Acids, Bases and Salts › Acids, bases and salts - pH of a solution › pH Scale and indicators — Revision note (part 1/1)

pH Scale and Indicators:

Indicators are substances that change colour when added to acids or bases. This colour change helps identify the nature of a solution.One commonly used indicator is litmus. Litmus is a natural indicator obtained from lichens. It shows different colour changes in acids and bases. Blue litmus turns red in acids, while red litmus turns blue in bases. Using litmus, it is easy to determine whether a solution is acidic or basic.

It does not indicate how strong or weak the acid or base is. A universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators. Instead of giving just one colour change, it shows different colours for solutions of different acidic or basic strength. Each colour corresponds to a value on the pH scale.

pH scale:

The pH scale shows how acidic or basic a solution is. The scale generally ranges from 0 to 14.

pH >7 = Alkaline solution

pH<7 = Acidic solution

pH = 7 = Neutral solution

Universal indicator paper is often used to measure pH. When the paper is dipped into a solution, it changes colour. This colour is compared with a pH colour chart to estimate the pH value.

Acids produce hydrogen ions, H⁺, in aqueous solutions whereas bases produce hydroxyl ions,OH-. If an acid produces a large number of hydrogen ions, it is called a strong acid. If it produces fewer hydrogen ions, it is called a weak acid.

For example, Hydrochloric acid (HCl) - strong acid

Acetic acid (${CH}_{3}COOH$) -- weak acid

Bases that produce a large number of hydroxide ions are called strong bases, while those producing fewer hydroxide ions are called weak bases.

For example, Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) - strong base

Ammonium hydroxide (${NH}_{4}OH$) - weak base

title: Reactivities of Acids and Bases
text:
Acids, Bases and Salts › Reactions of acids & bases › reactivities of acids and bases — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Acids are the compound that produces hydronium ion(s) [ ${H}_{3}{O}^{+}$] when dissolved in water.
Bases are substances that produce Hydroxyl ions [${OH}^{-}$] when dissolved in water.
Reactivity of acids and bases
1. Neutralization:**
Acids and bases react with each other to form salt and water. This reaction is known as **the neutralization reaction**
$Acid+Base\rightarrowSalt+Water$
For Example, $HCl+NaOH\rightarrowNaCl+{H}_{2}O$

**2. Reaction of an acid with metals:**
Acids react with metals to give corresponding salt and liberation of hydrogen gas.
$Metal+dil.Acid\rightarrowSalt+Hydrogen↑$
$2NaOH+Zn\rightarrow{Na}_{2}{ZnO}_{2}+{H}_{2}↑$

**3. Reaction of acids with oxides of metals:**
Acids react with oxides of metals to give corresponding salt and water.
$Metaloxide+dil.Acid\rightarrowSalt+Water$
${Na}_{2}O+2HCl\rightarrow2NaCl+{H}_{2}O$

**4. Reaction of bases with oxides of non-metals:**
Bases react with oxides of non-metals to give corresponding salt and water.
$Ca{(OH)}_{2}+{CO}_{2}\rightarrow{{CaCO}_{3}}_{(s)}+{H}_{2}O$
${SO}_{3}+2NaOH\rightarrow{Na}_{2}{SO}_{4}(aq)+{H}_{2}O$

**5. Reaction of an acid with carbonates and bicarbonates of metals:**
The reaction of an acid with carbonates and bicarbonates of metals results in corresponding salt, carbon dioxide, and water.
$Metalcarbonate/metalhydrogencarbonate+Acid\rightarrowSalt+Carbondioxide+Water$
${Na}_{2}{CO}_{3}+HCl\rightarrowNaCl+{H}_{2}O+{CO}_{2}$

title: Demonstrating Neutralization reaction
text:
Acids, Bases and Salts › Reactions of acids & bases › demonstrating neutralization reaction — Revision note (part 1/2)

Aim: To demonstrate neutralization reaction

Materials Required: 250ml beaker, Dilute hydrochloric acid, 2 glass rods, pH paper, pH indicator strip, dilute NaOH

We are aware of acids and bases. But how do we identify acids and bases? Yes! By using indicators. But how do determine the strength of an acid or base? Can you recall? Yes. The pH of any solution gives us information about the nature of a solution. Well! Today we will be using pH paper to identify the pH.

Here I have a beaker in which I have taken 10ml of dilute HCl. Now I am going to take a glass rod. Let us dip this glass rod in this beaker containing dilute HCl. With the help of this glass rod, we will put a drop of this solution on pH paper. Observe the colour change of the pH paper. Now let us take a pH indicator strip and match the colour of the paper with the colour on the pH indicator paper. So now as you can see the colour indicates the pH. So what is the pH of the solution? It is _______.

Now here I have another beaker containing dilute NaOH solution. With the help of a dropper, we will add some drops of dilute NaOH solution into this beaker containing dilute HCl solution. Let us now stir the solution using the glass rod. Now let us take another piece of pH paper. With the help of glass rod, let us add two-three drops of this solution and observe the change in the colour of the pH paper. Now let us record the pH. What is the pH? It is _______. What do you observe? The pH of the solution decreases. Now we will keep on adding dilute NaOH drop by drop and we will keep recording the pH.

Well! What do you observe? The pH of the solution goes on decreasing as we add more and more drops of dilute HCl.

title: Demonstrating Neutralization reaction
text:
Acids, Bases and Salts › Reactions of acids & bases › demonstrating neutralization reaction — Revision note (part 2/2)

We will stop adding NaOH as soon as the pH paper turns green. The green colour of the pH paper indicates that the pH of the solution is 7. That is neutral pH.

But why does the pH of the HCl solution decrease on adding NaOH solution? Well! We know that acids and bases on dissolving in water dissociate to give respective cation and anion. An aqueous solution of HCl contains dissociated ${H}^{+}$ ions and ${Cl}^{-}$ ions. An aqueous solution of NaOH contains dissociated ${Na}^{+}$ ions and ${OH}^{-}$ ions. When we add dilute NaOH solution to HCl solution, a large concentration of ${OH}^{-}$ ions are added to a large concentration of ${H}^{+}$ ions. On the other hand, water dissociates to a very small extent to give ${H}^{+}$ and ${OH}^{-}$ ions. On adding, dilute NaOH to HCl solution, the excess of ${OH}^{-}$ ions combine with the excess of ${H}^{+}$ ions resulting in the formation of water molecules. These water molecules formed mix with the solvent water molecules. So when sufficient amount of NaOH is added to HCl solution, the resulting solution will have only ${Na}^{+}$ and ${Cl}^{-}$ ions that thereby combine to form salt that is NaCl and solvent water. As a result, the pH of the solution goes on decreasing. When the pH becomes 7, it indicates that the solution now is neutral. So here HCl which is an acid reacts with base that is NaOH to give salt NaCl and water. This reaction is called the Neutralizaion reaction.

Aim: To demonstrate the reaction of acids with metals

Materials required: Metal pieces - magnesium, zinc, iron, aluminium, dilute hydrochloric acid, spatula, stand, cork, delivery tube, , candle, 4 test tubes

We all know that Metals are reactive in nature. Metals react with acids resulting in the formation of salt and the liberation of hydrogen gas. However, the reaction of acids with metals depends upon certain factors. The first is the strength and the concentration of the acid with which the metal reacts and the other factor is the reactivity of the metal and the temperature. Let us understand the reaction of metals with acid by carrying out a simple activity.

We will take 4 test tubes containing an equal amount of dilute hydrochloric acid. In the first test tube, we are going to add magnesium metal in the second test tube we are going to add aluminium metal in the third test tube we are going to add Zinc metal in the fourth Test tube, we are going to add iron metal. Now, as soon as you add metal into the test tube containing dilute hydrochloric acid you will observe the formation of bubbles. What do these bubbles indicate? These bubbles indicate the liberation of some gas. So which is the gas that is liberated? Well! The gas liberated is hydrogen gas. When a metal reacts with dilute acid it results in the liberation of an inflammable gas that is hydrogen gas. During this reaction, the reactive metal displaces hydrogen from the acid to liberate hydrogen gas. Thereby, the metal is converted into a basic radical which then combines with the acidic radical from the acid resulting in the formation of salt.

title: salts and its types
text:
Acids, Bases and Salts › Acid, bases & salts- salts › salts and its types — Revision note (part 1/1)

$⇒Acidsarethesubstancesthatproducehydroniumion(s)[{H}_{3}{O}^{+}]whendissolvedinWater.$

$⇒BasesarethesubstanceswhichproduceHydroxylion\left[{OH}^{-}\right]whendissolvedinwater.$

Acids and bases react with each other to form salt and water. This reaction is known as the**Neutralization reaction**

$1.Acid+Base\rightarrowSalt+Water$

For Example: $HCl+NaOH\rightarrowNaCl+{H}_{2}O$

- Salts are classified into three types: Acidic, basic and neutral.
- **Acidic Salts:**
- Formed by the neutralization reaction between a strong acid and a weak base.
- The aqueous solution of an acidic salt has a pH of less than 7.

Example: ${NH}_{4}Cl$

- **Basic Salts:**
- Formed by the neutralization reaction between strong base and weak acid.
- The aqueous solution of a basic salt has a pH greater than 7.

Example: ${NaHCO}_{3}$

- **Neutral Salts:**
- Formed by the neutralization reaction between a strong acid and a strong base.
- The aqueous solution of a neutral salt has a pH equal to 7.

Example: NaCl

- **Water of crystallization:**
- It is the number of water molecules present in one formula unit of a salt.

Example: Copper sulphate crystals contain water of crystallization. One formula unit of copper sulphate contains five water molecules. These blue crystals on heating lose the water molecules present and become colourless. Hydrated copper sulphate has the chemical formula ${CuSO}_{4}.5{H}_{2}O$

**Electronic conduction:**When electrons conduct electricity through electrical wires it is known as electronic conduction.[ in metals]
Electrons leave the battery at the negative terminal, and once they complete the electric circuit, they enter the battery at the positive terminal.
This flow of electron constitutes the flow of current.

**Ionic Conduction:**When the transfer of ions conducts electricity through a liquid or a solution, it is known as**Ionic conduction.**
When there is a liquid or solution connected to the circuit. The two rods, wire, and plates that are immersed in it are called **electrodes.**
Electrodes are generally made up of a conducting solid i.e. metals.
The electrode connected to the negative terminal of a battery is known as **Cathode**
The electrode connected to the positive terminal of a battery is known as an **Anode**.

**• Dissociation of ions and electrical conductivity:**
**•**Aqueous solutions of the compounds such as $NaCl,{CuSO}_{4},{H}_{2}{SO}_{4}andNaOH$ are electrical conductors.
**•**The substances which conduct electricity in their molten or aqueous solutions are called electrolytes
**•**Out of these $NaCland{CuSO}_{4}$ are salts, ${H}_{2}{SO}_{4}$ is a strong acid and $NaOH$ is a strong base.
**•**These Salts, Strong acids and Strong bases dissociate completely in their aqueous solutions.
**•**The aqueous solutions of all these contain large numbers of cations and anions which help in the flow of current.
**•**The positively charged cations in the solution are attracted to the negative electrode or cathode and move towards the cathode;
**•**The negatively charged anions move in the direction of the anode.
**•**The movement of ions in the solution towards the respective electrodes results in the conduction of electricity through the solution.
**•**Therefore, those solutions which contain a large number of dissociated ions conduct electricity.
**• S**uch solutions are known as **Electrolytic solutions.**

Aim: To demonstrate the electrical conductivity of ionic compounds

Materials required: beaker, electrodes, water, sodium chloride, 1g copper sulphate, 1g glucose, 1g urea, 5ml dilute ${H}_{2}{SO}_{4}$ and 5ml dilute NaOH

Hello dear students. We have learnt about the formation of Ionic compounds. Ionic compounds are formed by the electrostatic force of attraction between a cation and an anion. But do these ionic compounds conduct electricity? Well! Lets find that out by carrying out a simple experiment.

For this we will be taking 6 beakers filled with 50ml of water. In the first beaker we will add 1g sodium chloride, in second beaker we will add 1g copper sulphate, in third beaker we will add 1g glucose, in the fourth beaker we will add 1g urea, In the fifth beaker, we will add 5ml dilute ${H}_{2}{SO}_{4}$ and in the 6th beaker we will add 5ml dilute NaOH. Stir each of the solutions with a glass rod.

Now here I have two electrical wires. Let us connect one wire to the positive terminal of a 6V battery and the other wire to the negative terminal of the battery. As you can see, one switch and one holder with an electric bulb is included in the assembly setup.

We will now repeat the same procedure with the other solutions as well. While doing so, we need to make sure that we clean the uncovered part of the wires with water everytime we change the solution. We con observe that the bulb glows when aqueous solutions of ${CuSO}_{4}$ , ${H}_{2}{SO}_{4}$ and NaOH is used. But in case of glucose and urea solution the bulb does not glow. What does this indicate? Well! We all know that the bulb will glow only when the electric circuit is complete. The movement of these dissociated ions in the solution towards the respective electrodes amounts to the conduction of electricity through the solution. As a result, Ionic compounds conduct electricity. But what about glucose and urea? Glucose and urea do not consuct electricity as they do not undergo dissociation and hence do not give cations and ions. Now you understand that ionic compounds are good conductors of electricity.

title: electrolysis
text:
Acids, Bases and Salts › Acid, bases & salts- salts › electrolysis — Revision note (part 1/3)

• **Electrolysis** is a process by which ionic substances are decomposed into simpler substances i.e. into their respective ions when an electric current is passed through them.
• In metallic conductors, electrons are the current-carrying particles or conductor of electricity. they conduct by flowing through a metal wire.
• Ions conduct electricity by flowing through the solution or molten metals.
• The ion that migrates towards the cathode is called the **cation** and the one which moves towards the anode is known as the **anion.**
• A solution of ionic compounds contains a large number of cations and anions.
• An aqueous solution of $NaCl$ contains positive and negative ions which are formed by the dissociation of $NaCl$ into ${Na}^{+}$ and ${Cl}^{-}$ ions.
• Strong electrolytes are good conductors of electricity because they completely dissociate in their aqueous solution.
• Weak electrolytes do not completely dissociate into its ions.
**The procedure of electrolysis:**In order to carry out electrolysis,Let us take 1 g of copper sulphate in 50 ml of water in a beaker.

title: electrolysis
