• As soon as the electric current starts flowing through the circuit, the cations, that is, ${Cu}^{++}$ ions in the solution get attracted towards the negatively charged cathode.

• The decomposition of the metal took place due to the electric current. This is known as **electrolysis.**
• Electrolysis contains two parts: Reaction at the cathode [reduction] and the reaction at the anode. [oxidation]

${{Cu}^{2+}}_{(aq)}+2{e}^{-}\rightarrow{Cu}_{(s)}.....................cathodehalfreaction\ Cu(s)\rightarrow{{Cu}^{2+}}_{(aq)}+2{e}^{-}....................AnodeHalfreaction$

title: Ionic Compounds: Reacapitulation and Dissociation of Ionic compounds
text:
Acids, Bases and Salts › Ionic compounds: Reacapitulation and dissociation of ionic compounds › ionic compounds: reacapitulation and dissociation of ionic compounds — Revision note (part 1/1)

- An ionic compound consists of a positively charged cation and negatively charged anion.
- An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between two oppositely charged ions. The force of attraction between a positively charged cation and negatively charged anion results in the formation of an ionic bond.
- The ionic compound $NaCl$ is formed by the interaction between sodium and chlorine atoms. The outermost shell of sodium ($Na$) and chlorine ($Cl$) is not a complete octet whereas the outermost shell of ${Na}^{+}$ ion and ${Cl}^{-}$ ion is a complete octet. Therefore, an ionic bond is formed between the positively charged sodium ion and negatively charged chlorine ion. This results in the formation of a highly stable ionic compound $NaCl$.
- When ionic compounds are dissolved in water, it forms an aqueous solution. The oppositely charged ions constituting the ionic compound are placed adjacent to each other in its solid-state. On dissolving the ionic compound in water, the water molecules separate the ions from each other. Thus, the ionic compound dissociates in water to form aqueous solution. This is called **dissociation of ionic compounds**.
- In the aqueous solution, each of the dissociated ions gets surrounded by water molecules. The aqueous state is represented by writing $(aq)$ on the right of the symbol of the ion ${NaCl}_{(s)}{\rightarrow}_{dissociation}^{water}{{Na}^{+}}_{(aq)}+{{Cl}^{-}}_{(aq)}$

text:
Classification of Plants › Introduction to plants and plant kingdom › basis of classification with flow chart — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Basis of classification**

The environment consists of several animals and plants. Each organism is different from others in terms of structure and function. Classification is essential for the identification and evolutionary study of organisms. Each organism shows different characteristics, E.g., prokaryotes are unicellular, and eukaryotes are multicellular.
• Aristotle classified animals based on whether they lived on land or water. But, this classification was misleading. Hence, it is essential to decide the unique characteristics to classify the organisms in specific groups.
• The complete hierarchy can be prepared by putting organisms with related characters under one group.
• Five Kingdom classification system proposed by Robert Whittaker (1969) includes kingdoms Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia.
[Figure 1]

Unicellular Eukaryotes are included in the kingdom Protista.

Multicellular eukaryotes with cell wall include the kingdom Fungi (heterotrophs) and Plantae (autotrophs) while those without cell wall is the kingdom Animalia.

[Figure 2]

text:
Classification of Plants › Introduction to plants and plant kingdom › basis of classification with flow chart — Revision note (part 2/2)

**Examples of characteristics used for hierarchical classification:**
**Prokaryotes:** Prokaryotes are called single-celled. It lacks a membrane-bound nucleus, mitochondria, and other cell organelles. Archaea and bacteria are the two main domains of it.
**Eukaryotes:** A eukaryotic cell has a membrane-bound nucleus. The nucleus divides itself to form different cells. The group of cells forms tissues and tissues form organs and organs form the organ system.
**Plants**: These are multicellular and can prepare their food by the process of photosynthesis. Some of the characteristics for the basis of plants classification are as follows:
1) The presence or absence of organs
2) The plants either have or do not have vascular tissues: Vascular tissues help in the conduction of water and food.
3) The presence or absence of seeds.
4) If seeds are present, then whether they are enclosed or naked.
4) Presence of a number of cotyledons in the seeds: one or two cotyledons.
5) Eichler (1883) classified Kingdom Plantae into two kingdoms, namely, Cryptogams and Phanerogams.
6) Cryptogams (absence of flowers, seeds, and fruits) are further classified as algae, bryophytes, and pteridophytes.
7) Phanerogams (the presence of flowers, seeds, and fruits) are classified as gymnosperms and angiosperms.
8) Depending upon the number of cotyledons in seeds angiosperms are divided into monocots (one cotyledon) and dicots (two cotyledons).

[Figure 3]

text:
Classification of Plants › Introduction to plants and plant kingdom › introduction to plants and plant kingdom — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Introduction to plants and plant kingdom:**

• Kingdom Plantae includes all types of land and aquatic plants.
• They are multicellular and eukaryotic (have a well-developed nucleus).
• Plants are autotrophic, as they can perform photosynthesis with the help of chlorophyll.

Kingdom Plantae is further classified on the basis of characteristics like absence or presence of seeds, vascular tissues, differentiation of plant body, etc.

**Phanerogams -**

1. Phanerogams are commonly called seed-producing plants.

2. They produce unique reproductive structures which are visible (Phaneros – visible, gamos: marriage).

**Cryptogams -**

1. Cryptogams are spore-producing plants and do not produce seeds and flowers.

2. They reproduce sexually by gametes but sex organs are concealed/obscured (kryptos: hidden, gamos: marriage).

[Figure 1]

**Algae:**

• Most algal plants are aquatic (marine or freshwater) while few grow in moist, terrestrial habitats (wet rocks, tree trunks, etc.).
• The plant body is not differentiated into root, stem, and leaves.
It has three types-
1) **Rhodophyceae -** Red due to pigment phycoerythrin. e.g., _Chondrus, Gelidium,_etc.
2) **Phaeophyceae -**Brown due to pigment fucoxanthin. e.g., _Sargassum, Laminaria,_etc.
3) **Chlorophyceae -**Green due to pigment chlorophyll. e.g., _Spirogyra, Chlorella,_etc.

**Bryophyta**:

text:
Classification of Plants › Introduction to plants and plant kingdom › introduction to plants and plant kingdom — Revision note (part 2/2)

• These are mostly terrestrial and nonvascular plants. They occur in moist shady places and need water for fertilization, hence they are called 'amphibious plants'.
• They show the presence of rhizoids for water and mineral absorption, and also help in the fixation of thallus on the substratum.
• They are classified into Liverworts, Hornworts, and mosses.
• **Liverworts**and**Hornworts** are lower members of Bryophytaasthey possess a flat plant body called a thallus. _Riccia_ is an example of liverwort, while _Anthoceros_ is an example of hornwort.
• **Mosses** are advanced members of Bryophyta as they possess erect plant bodies. e.g., _Funaria_.

**Pteridophyta:**

• They are commonly known as ferns.
• They are the first vascular, true terrestrial, and seedless plants.
• They are differentiated into root, stem, and leaves.
• Examples: _Nephrolepis_, _Selaginella,_ etc.

**Gymnosperms:**

• These plants have naked seeds (ovules not enclosed in the ovary).
• They do not give rise to flowers.
• Examples: _Cycas_, Conifers, etc.

**Angiosperms**:

• These plants have seeds enclosed within an ovary.
• They are flower-producing plants that are divided into two types:
1)**Monocotyledons:** They have a single cotyledon in their embryo. e.g., grasses, cereals, etc.
2)**Dicotyledons:** They have two cotyledons in their embryo. e.g., Sunflower, China rose, etc.

title: Introduction to cryptogams, thallophyta
text:
Classification of Plants › Cryptogams › introduction to cryptogams, thallophyta — Revision note (part 1/2)

A cryptogam is a plant or plant-like organism that reproduces through spores rather than seeds or blooms.

These include Thallophyta, Bryophyta, and Pteridophyta.

The plants with hidden reproductive organs are called cryptogams. Kryptos: hidden, gams: reproductive organs.
The thallophytes, bryophytes, and pteridophytes are cryptogams because their reproductive organs are not visible.

**Thallophyta:**
• They do not have a proper differentiation of body design.
• The plants of this group are known as 'algae'.
• They mainly grow in water (aquatic).
• They do not have roots, stems, leaves, or flowers. They may be unicellular or multicellular, and microscopic or large.

Some of these are found in freshwater, while some are found in saline water.
• They have chlorophyll, so they can prepare their food (autotrophic).
Examples: _Spirogyra_, _Ulothrix_, _Ulva_, _Sargassum_, etc.

**Activity**:

In a pond with greenish water, green fibers from water can be collected. After placing them in a Petri dish and carefully washing them with clean water, we can spread them on a glass slide and observe them under a compound microscope by putting a coverslip on them.

**Observation:**

1. The linear arrangement of cells.
2. Spirally arranged green thread-like chloroplasts in the cells in that straight fiber.
3. Cell walls could be seen.
4. The centrally placed nucleus can be seen.

**Conclusion**: _Spirogyra_, an algae present in freshwater bodies like ponds and rivers, is seen with spiral chloroplasts and a centrally placed nucleus.

**Pyrenoids**are seen in algae like _Spirogyra,_ and their main function is to act as centres of carbon dioxide fixation. They generate and maintain a carbon dioxide-rich environment around the photosynthetic enzyme ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCO).

title: Bryophyta
text:
Classification of Plants › Cryptogams › bryophyta — Revision note (part 1/2)

These are the first Terrestrial and Non-Vascular plants.

They form a green kind of mat on rocks, walls, and on the bark of trees which can be commonly observed during the monsoon season.

There are around 960 genera and 25,000 species of bryophytes.

**General characters of Bryophytes:**

1. The structure of the plant body of bryophytes is flat, ribbon-like long, without true roots, stem, or leaves.
2. These plants are thalloid, multicellular, and autotrophic.
3. The structure of the plant body of bryophytes is flat, ribbon-like long, without true roots, stem, or leaves.
4. Show differentiation in the body design, with stem, leaf-like structures, and root-like structures.
5. Root-like structures are referred to as Rhizoids (Root-like). They help in the absorption of water and minerals as well as binding to a substratum.
6. They are known as "Amphibious plants" or amphibians because they grow in moist soil but need water for reproduction.
7. They need water for the process of fertilization.
8. They do not have specific tissues for the conduction of food and water.
9. Examples are Moss _(Funaria), Marchantia, Anthoceros, Riccia_, etc
10. They reproduce by spore formation.
11. A structure used by bryophytes to produce spores is called a capsule. Inside the capsule, spores develop to maturity by meiosis and are shed by wind currents and breezes.

[Figure 1]

**Economic importance of bryophytes:**

a. In nursery and transportation:

Sphagnum, commonly known as bog moss or peat moss, usually occurs on the edges of bogs.

It can absorb large quantities of water similar to its own weight.

It is used during transportation and propagation to keep the excised parts/tissues of the crop moist.

title: Bryophyta
text:
Classification of Plants › Cryptogams › bryophyta — Revision note (part 2/2)

b. Medicinal uses: Sphagnum was used during the second world war as an anti-septic for surgical dressings.

c. Ecological importance: They aid in weathering of rocks which is the formation of soil.

d. Soil erosion: It creates a dense mat on soil, that prevents soil erosion.

title: Pteridophyta
text:
Classification of Plants › Cryptogams › pteridophyta — Revision note (part 1/1)

1. Pteridophyta are the first true terrestrial, vascular plants.
2. There are about 400 genera and 12,000 species of pteridophytes.
3. They have a primitive conducting system i.e xylem and phloem for the conduction of food and water.
4. These plants are also called ferns as they appear like a feather.
5. Their body is differentiated into roots, stems, and leaves.
6. They do not bear flowers and fruits.
7. They reproduce with the help of spores formed along the back or posterior surface of their leaves.
8. Sporangia are present in sori on leaflets.

[Figure 1]

7. Examples are ferns like _Nephrolepis, Marsilea, Pteris, Adiantum, Equisetum, Selaginella, Lycopodium,_ etc.

8. **Reproduction**: These plants reproduce asexually by spore-formation and sexually by zygote formation.

**Similarity between Thallophyta, Bryophyta, and Pteridophyta:**

Thallophyta, Bryophyta, and Pteridophyta are cryptogams and besides all the differences, one thing is common between them.

They all reproduce by spore formation and their reproductive organs are hidden. (cryptos: hidden, gams: reproductive organs)

**Economic importance of Pteridophytes:**

1. Ornamental value: Due to their beautiful leaves, ferns are grown as ornamental plants.
2. Food: Marsilea is a rich source of starch.
3. Soil binding: It binds to soil and prevents soil erosion.
4. Scouring: Stems of Equisetum are used in the polishing of metals.
5. Bio-fertilizer: _Azolla_ has a symbiotic association with nitrogen-fixing bacteria. It acts as a biofertilizer in paddy fields.

title: introduction to phanerogams- Gymnosperms
text:
Classification of Plants › Phanerogams › introduction to phanerogams- gymnosperms — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Phanerogams**:

1. Phanerogams are called spermatophytes and they consist of those plants which produce seeds.
2. These have special structures for reproduction which produce seeds. In these plants, after the process of reproduction, seeds are formed which contain the embryo and stored food.
3. During the germination of the seed, the stored food is used for the initial growth of the embryo.

Depending upon whether seeds are enclosed in a fruit or not, phanerogams are classified into gymnosperms and angiosperms.

**Division I- Gymnosperms:**

1. Gymnosperms are mostly evergreen, perennial, and woody.
2. Their stems are without branches.
3. The leaves form a crown.
4. Seeds of these plants do not have natural coverings, i.e. these plants do not form fruits and are therefore called gymnosperms. (gymnos: naked, sperms: seeds).
Examples are Cycas, Picea (Christmas tree), Thuja (Morpankhi), Pinus (Deodar), etc.
5. All gymnosperms are heterosporous- Heterosporous refers to the plants producing different types of spores that are different in structure, size, and function.
6. The male and female reproductive organs can form in cones or strobili. Male and female sporangia are produced either on the same plant, described as monoecious (one home or bisexual), or on separate plants, referred to as dioecious (two homes or unisexual) plants.

Monoecious gymnosperms:

These plants bear male and female flowers on different sporophylls of the same plant.

Tsuga and Pinus

Dioecious gymnosperms:

These plants bear male and female flowers on different sporophylls of different plants.

Ginkgo and Gnetum

**Garden plants:**

Cycas, Christmas trees, Hibiscus, lilies, etc. are commonly seen in our surroundings.

title: introduction to phanerogams- Gymnosperms
text:
Classification of Plants › Phanerogams › introduction to phanerogams- gymnosperms — Revision note (part 2/2)

Cycas and Christmas trees are examples of gymnosperms while hibiscus and lily are examples of angiosperms.

Similarities:

All of these come under phanerogams meaning they have special structures for reproduction and seeds are also produced in them.

Differences:

1. In gymnosperms, reproductive organs have cones whereas in angiosperms reproductive organs have flowers.
2. In gymnosperms, seeds are without natural coverings whereas in angiosperms seeds are enclosed in natural coverings called fruits.

title: angiosperms: Monocots and dicots
text:

3. Flowers develop into fruits and seeds are formed within fruits. Thus, these seeds are covered; hence, they are called angiosperms (angios: cover, sperms: seeds).

The plants whose seeds can be divided into two equal halves or dicotyledons are called dicotyledonous plants and those whose seeds cannot be divided into equal parts are called monocotyledonous plants.

title: Monocots vs Dicots
text:
Classification of Plants › Classification of plants › monocots vs dicots — Revision note (part 1/1)

Seeds are the fertilized matured ovule that contains the embryo of a plant and nutritive material.

Seeds are of 2 types viz: Monocots and Dicots

The monocot seeds have one cotyledon while the dicot seeds have 2 cotyledons or coats.

- To visualize this difference, soak grams, peas, wheat, rice, jowar, and groundnut in water for 3 to 4 hours and then press them using gentle force.
- Grams, peas, and groundnuts break open into two equal halves but we are not getting equal halves in the case of wheat, jowar, and rice.
- Dicot seeds have 2 cotyledons and they can be divided into 2 equal halves like in the case of peas, grams, and groundnuts.
- Monocots on the other hand have only one cotyledon and hence can’t be divided into two equal halves like in the case of wheat, jowar, and rice.

title: Energy Flow in an Ecosystem- Introduction
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Energy flow in an ecosystem › energy flow in an ecosystem- introduction — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Ecosystem:**

1. The functional unit of nature, where living organisms interact with each other (biotic factors) and with the surrounding physical environment (abiotic factors).
2. Biotic and abiotic components interact with each other in an ecosystem. Exmaple: in photosynthesis, the biotic components (plants) of an ecosystem use the abiotic components( sunlight, water, carbon dioxide, etc.) to produce chemical energy to survive.
3. The term ecosystem was first coined by A.G. Tansley.

Types of ecosystems:

**Natural ecosystem:**
Natural ecosystem are naturally formed and operates under natural condition, and there is little or no interference of human activities

Terrestrial ecosystem - It is a land-based ecosystem. It includes forests, grassland, and deserts ecosystem.

Aquatic ecosystem- An aquatic ecosystem is an ecosystem formed by surrounding a body of water. It is further divided into Freshwater (rivers, ponds, and lakes) and Marine ecosystems (seas, oceans, and estuaries).

**Artificial ecosystem:**

Man-made and artificially engineered ecosystems are also known as anthropogenic ecosystems.

They are made by humans.

Agroecosystem or simply stated as cropland is the best example of an artificial ecosystem.

Other examples are zoos, Botanical gardens, and Aquariums.

**The ecosystem comprises of following events:**

1. Input - It involves the Productivity in an ecosystem mainly the producers.

Autotrophs are organisms producing their own food such as plants and photosynthetic microorganisms.

2. Transfer of Energy - Energy always flows from the Primary Producers to Consumer (Primary consumer) then to the Secondary Consumer and so on.

It forms a Food Chain. Multiple Food Chains when interconnected are known as Food Web.

title: Energy Flow in an Ecosystem
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Classification of organisms according to mode of nutrition › energy flow in an ecosystem — Revision note (part 1/1)

All living organisms require nutrients for proper growth and development.
The process of taking in food, its digestion, absorption, and distribution to different parts of the body is called nutrition.
• The mode of nutrition differs in various organisms.
• According to the type of food an animal consumes, animals can be classified as - primary consumers, secondary consumers, top consumers, and mixed consumers.
1) **Primary consumers:** These consumers are directly dependent on the producers(autotrophs). Herbivores are termed primary consumers.
E.g. Goat, elephant, squirrel, etc.

2) **Secondary consumers:** Animals feeding on other herbivores for their food source are known to be secondary consumers. Carnivores are termed secondary consumers.
E.g.Owl, frog, snake, etc.

3)**Top consumers:** These consumers feed on both carnivores as well as herbivores for their food source. These carnivores are also termed to be the apex consumers as they are not consumed by any other organism and reside on top of the food chain.
E.g.Lion, tiger, etc.

4)**Mixed consumers (Omnivorous):** These consumers are known to have a diverse type of nutrition as they feed on both carnivores and herbivores. They can obtain energy from both plant and animal matter.
E.g.Humans, bears, etc.

**Food chain**
• The interactions between the producers, consumers, and decomposers that go on continuously are called the food chain.
• It is a linear sequence of interactions.
• Each food chain consists of four, five, or more links.

[Figure 1]
**Food web**
• The food web is formed by the interconnections between the various food chains at different levels.
• It is an intricate network and looks like a web.
• The food web is found everywhere in nature.

title: food chain and food web
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Food chain and food web › food chain and food web — Revision note (part 1/3)

**Food chain:**
• It is a sequential transfer of energy from one organism to another through a series of repetitive eating and being eaten.
• Different steps in the food chain are called a trophic levels.
• There are three different types of the food chain:

**Grazing or predator food chain:**
• It is the most common food chain.
• It is called the predator food chain as predation occurs at every trophic level.
• It consists of producers, consumers, and decomposers (fungi and bacteria).
• The consumers are of 3-5 types first-order (primary), second-order (secondary, third-order (tertiary), and fourth-order (quaternary) consumers.
1. Producers:
• These include the producers i.e. plants that make food with the help of sunlight. They constitute the first trophic level in the food chain.
• They store the food in the form of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.
2. Primary consumers or Herbivores:
• These feed on the plants. For e.g. Grasshoppers, Insects, Deers, Fishes, Rabbits, and even Man.
• As the herbivores transfer plant matter into the animal matter they are called the **key industrial animals.**
3. Secondary consumers or Primary carnivores:
• They ingest or prey on herbivores. For e.g. Frog, Wild cats, Foxes, jackals, etc.
4. Tertiary consumers or Secondary carnivores:
• These are larger carnivores that prey on the primary carnivores. For e.g. Wolf and Snake.
5. Top carnivores:
• These are the last order of carnivores which themselves are not been preyed upon by other animals. For e.g. Shark, tigers, peacocks, and crocodiles. etc.

title: food chain and food web
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Food chain and food web › food chain and food web — Revision note (part 2/3)

**Detritus food chain:**
• It is also known as the saprotrophic food chain.
• It involves the transfer of energy from dead organic matter of decaying plants and animals to microorganisms.
• There are three types of detritus feeders.
1. Scavengers:
• They form the first trophic level of the detritus food chain and feed on dead animals and leave large fragments of their bodies.
• For e.g. Crow, Kite, Vulture, and Hyena.
2. Detritivores:
• These are small organisms feeding on the leftover food of the scavengers.
• For e.g. Millipedes, Termites, Earthworms, Beetles, etc. They break larger fragments into fine particles.
3. Decomposers:
• These solubilize organic matter by secreting enzymes.
• For e.g. Bacteria, actinomycetes, and fungi.
• During this step; mineralization and humus formation takes place. Small organisms feed upon the decomposers which are in turn preyed by large animals.

**Parasitic food chain:**
• It starts with larger animals and food energy passes to smaller organisms.
• The larger animals are hosts, and the small animals which fulfill their own nutritional requirements from the host are called parasites.

**Ecological principles derived from food chains:**
1. Complete food chain: A food chain must begin with photosynthesis and end with decay. The food chain must get energy from the outside to keep going.
2. Size of the food chain: Shorter the food chain, the more efficient it is. More steps would lead to a loss of energy.
3. Size of population: Population usually decreases with the rise in trophic level.
4. Size of organisms: The members which are larger in size are fewer in number.
5. Operation at different trophic levels: An organism cannot be assigned to any one trophic level.

title: food chain and food web
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Food chain and food web › food chain and food web — Revision note (part 3/3)

**Food web:**
• The interconnection of several food chains forms a food web.
• It provides an alternate pathway for food availability.
• It helps in the stability and development of an ecosystem.
• It is also referred to as the consumer-resource system

**Characters of a food web:**
• No food chain is independent.
• It is formed by interlinking various food chains.
• It provides alternative pathways for food availability. More the number of food chains more stable the ecosystem is.
• It helps to check the overpopulation of highly fecund species of plants and animals.
• It operates according to the food preferences of the organisms at each trophic level.

**Importance of food web:**
• It increases the stability of the ecosystem by providing alternate sources of food.
• This allows the endangered species to increase in number.

[Figure 1]

• It increases the competitiveness and adaptability of the same and other species.

title: The energy pyramid
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Energy pyramids and trophic levels › the energy pyramid — Revision note (part 1/3)

**Energy pyramid:**

The energy pyramid is a graphical representation of energy transferred from one organism to the next in the food chain.

Or

It is the pattern of energy exchange in an ecosystem.

**Trophic levels:**

1. Each level present in the food chain is called a trophic level.
2. A trophic level is a step at which the organism obtains its food in the chain.
3. The amount of matter and energy gradually decreases from producers at the lowest levels to the top consumers present at the highest level.
4. **1942**- **Lindeman**studied the food chain and energy flow through it.
5. **1927**- **Charles Elton**, a British scientist first proposed the concept of the Ecological Pyramid after his study of the Tundra Ecosystem of the Beer islands in England.
6. Hence, the energy pyramid is also called the **Eltonian**Pyramid.
7. It generally comprises four primary levels, starting at the base with producers that obtain energy from the sun, and moving upward to primary, secondary, and tertiary consumers.
The initial quantity of energy goes on decreasing at every level of energy exchange
8. As there is a flow of energy at each trophic level, after the death of the apex consumer, this energy is available to the decomposers.
9. The energy is transferred from producers to apex consumers and energy is lost at each trophic level.
10. Similarly, the number of organisms also decreases from the lowest level to the highest level.

[Figure 1]

title: The energy pyramid
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Energy pyramids and trophic levels › the energy pyramid — Revision note (part 2/3)

1. According to the 10% law of Lindeman, only 10% of energy transfers to the next trophic level from the previous one. For example, if producers have 100% energy, then 10%, 1%, 0.1%, and so on transfer to the primary, secondary, tertiary consumers, and so on, respectively.
2. The energy in the apex consumer will be used for its life processes while it's alive and the leftover energy after its death will be transferred to the decomposers, detritivores, parasites, etc.
3. If energy remains trapped in the body of Apex consumers then energy will not be available for decomposers and they will not survive thus disturbing the balance of the ecosystem.
4. Decomposers and fungi act like decomposers which degrade the dead remains of plants and animals and convert them into simple carbon compounds, thus returning the nutrients back to earth and completing the food chain. These simpler compounds will be taken up by plants and the cycle continues. These substances easily mix with air, water, and soil from where they are again absorbed by plants and incorporated into the food chain.

**Decomposers and their significance:**

1. Decomposers are organisms that obtain food by feeding on dead and decaying matter. They break complex substances into simple carbon compounds.
E.g., Fungi and other micro-organisms.
2. These broken-down simple carbon compounds then easily mix with air, water, and soil and get absorbed by the plants where they get incorporated into the food chain again.
3. If there were no decomposers, decomposition will not happen and the nutrients will be trapped in the bodies of plants and animals which will disturb the food chain, food web, and the equilibrium in the ecosystem.

title: The energy pyramid
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Energy pyramids and trophic levels › the energy pyramid — Revision note (part 3/3)

The pyramid of energy is always a true pyramid because the energy level decreases from going to the top from the bottom level.
The pyramid of energy in aquatic and forest ecosystems is always upright.

The food web formed by the various modes of nutrition circulates energy and various nutrients continuously in the ecosystem.

**Energy flows through an ecosystem is a one-way transport:**

1. Energy flows through an ecosystem is termed to be a one-way transport because when the energy enters the green plants (from the sun) during photosynthesis, it is then transferred through a food chain from one organism to another.
2. Decomposers dissipate some amount of energy in the form of heat.
3. This transferred energy is not returned to the source again. Thus, the energy flow is unidirectional in an ecosystem.

**The apex carnivores population is always less than other consumers:**

1. The number of tertiary consumers depends on secondary consumers for their food and secondary consumers feed on primary consumers, and they depend on it for its food.
2. The tertiary consumers always have less than those other consumers because of this inefficiency, only a few top-level consumers have enough food.

title: Biogeochemical cycle
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Biogeochemical cycle › biogeochemical cycle — Revision note (part 1/2)

The cyclical flow of nutrients within an ecosystem is called the bio-geo-chemical cycle.

Biogeochemical cycles are pathways by which substances mainly circulate through biotic (biosphere) and abiotic (lithosphere, atmosphere, and hydrosphere) parts of Earth.

The flow of energy in the ecosystem is one way while the flow of nutrients is cyclic.
Nutrients required for the growth of organisms are always transferred from abiotic to biotic factors and biotic to abiotic factors within an ecosystem.

This cycle operates continuously through the medium of the biosphere formed by the lithosphere, atmosphere and hydrosphere. The recycling of biological, geological and chemical sources of nutrients in this process is a complex process and depends upon the level of energy transfer in the ecosystem.

Biogeochemical cycles are mainly of two types:

**i) Gaseous cycle:**
The transfer of abiotic gaseous nutrients to different biotic or abiotic factors in the earth's atmosphere is known as the gaseous cycle.An accumulation of the main abiotic gaseous nutrient materials is found in the earth’s atmosphere.
It includes the Water cycle, Nitrogen cycle, Carbon cycle, and Oxygen cycle.

**ii) Sedimentary cycle:**
An accumulation of the main abiotic nutrient materials found in soil, sedimentary rocks, etc. of the earth.
The gaseous cycles are faster than the sedimentary cycle.
It involves the phosphorus, calcium, iron cycle, etc.

Climatic changes and human activities seriously affect the speed, intensity, and equilibrium of these cycles.

The gaseous and sedimentary cycles are dependent on each other.

**Examples:**

Nitrogen is present in the form of a gas in the atmosphere (gaseous cycle) and in the form of compounds like nitrogen oxide in the soil and sediments (sedimentary cycle).

text:

Carbon occurs in abiotic form mainly in coal, granite, diamond, limestone, etc. in the earth's crust (sedimentary cycle) and in the form of carbon dioxide gas in the atmosphere (gaseous cycle).

Generally, carbon is present in plants and animals for a much shorter duration than it is in coal.

title: Carbon cycle
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Biogeochemical cycle › carbon cycle — Revision note (part 1/2)

● Carbon dioxide makes up 0.039 % of our atmosphere and 49.5% of the dry weight of organisms.
● Fossil fuel is also a reservoir of carbon
● It occurs as diamonds and graphite on Earth.
● It is essential for protein synthesis, carbohydrates, fats, nucleic acids, and vitamins in living organisms.

The carbon cycle is one of the important biogeochemical cycles.

**Carbon dioxide Fixation:**

Plants convert carbon dioxide to glucose through photosynthesis. They are known as producers. The glucose molecules are converted into other biologically important molecules. Marine animals use carbonates dissolved in seawater to make shells, and exoskeletons. Green plants and algae are the most important agents of carbon dioxide fixation. Carbon fixation is an important process as it removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

**Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere:**

Carbon dioxide is added to the atmosphere by the process of combustion. It is also added in considerable amount by respiratory activities of consumers. The process of respiration involves uptake of oxygen by animals and the exhalation of carbon dioxide. The exhaled carbon dioxide is used by plants for the process of photosynthesis. Decomposers also contribute to the carbon dioxide pool. The atmosphere serves as an exchange pool for the carbon cycle. As carbon exists in two forms such as carbon dioxide and methane. Carbon dioxide is absorbed by plants through the process of photosynthesis and is removed from the atmosphere.

The flow of energy in the carbon cycle is linear. Carbon dioxide is used by plants in the process of photosynthesis which is exhaled by animals and humans during the process of respiration.

**The Greenhouse Effect:**

title: Carbon cycle
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Biogeochemical cycle › carbon cycle — Revision note (part 2/2)

The percentage of carbon dioxide is doubled since the industrial revolution. Human beings burn fossil fuels on a very large scale causing more heat to be retained by the atmosphere which leads to Global Warming. It is called the Greenhouse Effect.

Following are the major steps involved in the process of the carbon cycle:

1. Carbon present in the atmosphere is absorbed by plants for photosynthesis.
2. These plants are then consumed by animals, and carbon gets bioaccumulated into their bodies.
3. These animals and plants eventually die, and upon decomposing, carbon is released back into the atmosphere.
4. Some of the carbon that is not released back into the atmosphere eventually become fossil fuels.
5. These fossil fuels are then used for man-made activities, which pump more carbon back into the atmosphere.

**Importance of Carbon Cycle:**
Even though carbon dioxide is found in small traces in the atmosphere, it plays a vital role in balancing the energy and traps the long-wave radiations from the sun. Therefore, it acts like a blanket over the planet. If the carbon cycle is disturbed it will result in serious consequences such as climatic changes and global warming.

Carbon is an integral component of every life form on earth. From proteins and lipids to even our DNA. Furthermore, all known life on earth is based on carbon. Hence, the carbon cycle, along with the nitrogen cycle and oxygen cycle, plays a vital role in the existence of life on earth.

title: Oxygen cycle
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Biogeochemical cycle › oxygen cycle — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Oxygen cycle** is a biogeochemical cycle involving the circulation and recycling of oxygen within the atmosphere, ecosystem, biosphere, and lithosphere. Like other biochemical cycles, this cycle also includes biotic and abiotic components.

Oxygen is continuously produced as well as used up in the atmosphere.

Oxygen forms 21% of the amosphere.

**Oxygen production:**

1. Photosynthesis is the major process leading to production of oxygen on earth.
2. Phytoplanktons are the major producers of oxygen. Scientists estimate that at least 50 percent of the oxygen in our atmosphere has been produced by phytoplankton. At the same time, they are responsible for drawing down significant portions of the carbon dioxide from the air.
3. Green plants possessing chlorophyll pigment undergo the process of photosynthesis using sunlight, water, carbon dioxide, and other nutrients from soil to create their food and liberate oxygen as a by product.
4. Oxygen is also produced in the atmosphere due to sunlight. When sunlight reacts with water vapour, oxygen is produced.
5. When an ozone molecule absorbs even low-energy ultraviolet radiation, it splits into an ordinary oxygen molecule and a free oxygen atom. Usually this free oxygen atom quickly re-joins with an oxygen molecule to form another ozone molecule.
6. A significant amount of oxygen is also stored in the earth's crust in the form of oxides but this is unavailable for the respiration process to organisms as it is not in free state.

**Oxygen usage:**

Oxygen is used in breathing, combustion, decomposition,Rusting.

title: Oxygen cycle
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Biogeochemical cycle › oxygen cycle — Revision note (part 2/2)

Breathing: It is a process by which aerobic organisms including plant, animals inhale oxygen rich air from the environment and exhale carbon dioxide rich air bag into the atmosphere. This oxygen is used for respiration purposes at cellular level and helps in functioning of the organism.

Aerobic organisms require oxygen for life processes. Some microorganisms are anaerobic meaning they don't require oxygen for their life processes.

Oxygen is important for the synthesis of proteins, carbohydrates, and fats. It is also used in various chemical reactions. Ozone (O3 ) is produced from oxygen through various atmospheric processes.

Decomposition: all the organisms in a food chain eventually dies and are degraded by the action of decomposers microorganisms. They convert the dead remains of organisms into simpler compounds that can be taken up again by plant and enter the food chain. This process of decomposition requires oxygen and it also releases carbon dioxide.

Combustion: oxygen is must for the combustion process where is fossil fuels, plastic, wood, and other materials in the presence of oxygen release carbon dioxide.

Rusting: Rusting is a process in which hydrated iron oxide is formed on iron containing items. This brown coloured Rust is formed in the presence of oxygen and moisture.

Oxygen is highly reactive and it readily reacts with other elements and compounds. Hence oxygen is found in many compounds like water, carbon dioxide, oxides of other elements and it is also found in the molecular form i.e O2. The oxygen cycle undergoing in biosphere is extremely complex.

title: Nitrogen cycle
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Biogeochemical cycle › nitrogen cycle — Revision note (part 1/2)

Nitrogen cycle:
Nitrogen accounts for 78% of our atmosphere.
Nitrogen is an essential element present in proteins, nucleic acids (DNA and RNA), vitamins, and certain secondary metabolites like alkaloids and urea also.
The simple atmospheric molecular nitrogen is converted into more complex molecules in living beings. This nitrogen comes back again to the atmosphere

The circulation and recycling of nitrogen gas into the form of different compounds through various biotic and abiotic processes in nature is called the nitrogen cycle.

All organisms participate in the nitrogen cycle.

Nitrogen is inactive and does not easily combine with other elements. Most organisms cannot use the free form of nitrogen.

**Nitrogen fixation:**

1. The free nitrogen present in the atmosphere can not be directly taken by the plants thus, it needs to be converted into nitrate and nitrate which are usable forms of nitrogen.
2. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert molecular nitrogen into nitrite and nitrate with the help of the enzyme nitrogenase.
3. These are commonly present in the root nodules of leguminous plants.
4. The nitrite and nitrate forms taken up by the plants are used for the formation of proteins.
5. This fixed form of nitrogen is then made available through plants to other organisms of different trophic levels.
6. Microorganisms undergoing nitrogen fixation can be free-living or symbiotic.
7. Free-living organisms: Azotobacter, Beijernickia, Rhodospirillum, cyanobacteria, etc.
8. Symbiotic organisms: Rhizobium (in the root nodules of legumes) and Frankia (in the root nodules of non-leguminous plants), etc.

Other natural processes such as lighting, temperature, and pressure also convert nitrogen into oxides of nitrogen.

Important processes of nitrogen cycle:

**Ammonification:**

Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Biogeochemical cycle › nitrogen cycle — Revision note (part 2/2)

Organisms excreta i.e urine contains nitrogenous wastesWhen an organism, the nitrogen in its tissues is in the form of organic nitrogen, for example, amino acids and DNA.

Various fungi and prokaryotes then decompose the tissue and release inorganic nitrogen back into the ecosystem as ammonia in the process known as ammonification.

**Nitrification**:

Nitrification is a microbial process carried out by microorganisms like _Nitrosomonas_. Nitrification is defined as the aerobic oxidation of ammonia to nitrite followed by the aerobic oxidation of nitrite to nitrate.

**Denitrification**:

Denitrification is the microbial process of reducing nitrogen compounds like nitrate and nitrite to gaseous forms of nitrogen, principally nitrous oxide (${N}_{2}O$) and nitrogen (${N}_{2}$). Denitrification reduces the amount of fixed nitrogen present in the soil.

title: Main processes in carbon cycle
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Carbon cycle › main processes in carbon cycle — Revision note (part 2/3)

1. Transportation
2. Electricity production
3. Factories
4. Commercial and Residential: arise primarily from fossil fuels burned for heat, the use of certain products that contain greenhouse gases, and the handling of waste.
5. Agriculture
6. Land Use and Forestry
7. Forest fires
8. Volcanoes: When volcanoes erupt, they vent the gas containing carbon dioxide to the atmosphere and cover the land with fresh silicate rock
9. Ocean:
The movement of carbon from the atmosphere to the lithosphere (rocks) begins with rain. Atmospheric carbon combines with water to form a weak acid—carbonic acid—that falls to the surface in rain. The acid dissolves rocks—a process called chemical weathering—and releases calcium, magnesium, potassium, or sodium ions. Rivers carry the ions to the ocean.
In oceans when organisms with calcium carbonate shells die, their body decomposes, leaving behind their hard shells. These accumulate on the seafloor and are eventually broken down by the waves and compacted under enormous pressure, forming limestone.
When these limestone rocks are exposed to air, they get weathered and the carbon is released back into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.

**Carbon movement among ecosystem:**

$Producers\rightarrowConsumers\rightarrowSecondaryconsumers\rightarrowApexconsumers\rightarrowDecomposers\rightarrowEnvironment\rightarrowagainplants.$

In this way, biotic carbon is transported from plants to herbivores, from herbivores to carnivores, and from carnivores to apex consumers.

The carbon cycle is more effective in temperate zones:

Temperate zones are the mild temperature areas located between the subtropical and the polar regions.

title: Main processes in carbon cycle
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Carbon cycle › main processes in carbon cycle — Revision note (part 3/3)

The temperate zone is most suitable zone for most of the biological and biochemical processes, hence the carbon cycle is more effective in the temperate zone than any other zone.

Carbon itself is not responsible for the rise in temperature. Carbon when gets burnt and combines with atmospheric oxygen forming carbon dioxide which is majorly responsible for the rise in temperature. Hence, even though the carbon content on Earth is constant, there is a rise in temperature due to carbon dioxide.

Without carbon dioxide, Earth's natural greenhouse effect would be weak to keep the average global surface temperature above freezing. By adding more carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, people are enhancing the natural greenhouse effect, causing global temperatures to rise.

title: Food chain and food Webs
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Exploring Food Chains and Food Webs › Exploring Food Chains and Food Webs — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Food Chain**

- A food chain shows how energy and matter pass from one organism to another through feeding relationships.
- Each step in a food chain is called a trophic level.
- Energy flows from one trophic level to the next.

**Trophic Levels**

- Producers - Green plants that make their own food through photosynthesis.
- Primary Consumers (Herbivores) - Animals that eat plants.
- Secondary Consumers (Carnivores) - Animals that eat herbivores.
- Tertiary Consumers - Top carnivores that eat other carnivores.
- Decomposers - Organisms that break down dead plants and animals at all trophic levels.

**Forest Food Chain**

$Greenplantsandtrees\rightarrowDeer\rightarrowTiger$

- Plants are producers.
- Deer is a primary consumer.
- Tigers are the top carnivores.
- This is a grazing food chain because it starts with green plants.

**Grassland Food Chain**

$Grass\rightarrowGrasshopper\rightarrowFrog\rightarrowSnake\rightarrowEagle$

**Pond Food Chain**

$Aquaticplants\rightarrowSmallaquaticorganisms/insects\rightarrowFish\rightarrowHeron$

**Energy Flow in a Food Chain**

- Energy moves from producers to consumers.
- Energy flow is unidirectional.
- Energy is not recycled through the food chain.

**Food Web**

- In nature, organisms often have multiple food sources.
- Different food chains become interconnected.
- This interconnected network is called a food web.

**Examples of a Food Web**

- Frogs, birds, or lizards may eat grasshoppers.
- Snakes may feed on frogs and small rodents.
- Multiple feeding relationships connect different food chains.

**Importance of a Food Web**

title: Food chain and food Webs
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Exploring Food Chains and Food Webs › Exploring Food Chains and Food Webs — Revision note (part 2/2)

- Provides stability to the ecosystem.
- Organisms can switch to alternative food sources if one becomes scarce.
- Ensures continuous energy flow.
- Increases survival during changing environmental conditions.

**10% Law of Energy Transfer**

- Proposed by Raymond Lindeman.
- Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next level.
- About 90% of the energy is lost through:
- Heat
- Movement
- Respiration
- Digestion
- Other life processes

**Example of the 10% Law**

- Producers: 10,000 J
- Primary consumers: 1,000 J
- Secondary consumers: 100 J
- Tertiary consumers: 10 J

**Consequences of the 10% Law**

- Ecosystems cannot support many trophic levels.
- Most food chains contain only 3–4 trophic levels.
- Top carnivores are usually fewer in number than organisms at lower trophic levels.

title: introduction to microbes
text:
Useful and Harmful Microbes › Introduction to microbes › introduction to microbes — Revision note (part 1/1)

1) Microbes are small microscopic organisms that may be unicellular or multicellular. Micro-organisms are extremely simple life forms with minimal nutrient requirements. They were first discovered by Antonie Van Leeuwenhoek in 1674.
2) Microbes are divided into seven types: bacteria, archaea, protozoa, algae, fungi, viruses and multicellular animal parasites.

[Figure 1]

3) They are found all around us i.e. soil, air and water. Our human body is also a home of many microbes. Some of the micro-organisms are useful for the maintenance of human health.

4) The most common microbes are bacteria, viruses, and fungi. The microbes belonging to the group of protozoa are responsible for diseases such as cholera, tuberculosis, food poisoning etc.

5) The microbes are not visible to the naked eye and can only be seen with the help of a microscope.

[Figure 2]

6) Some micro-organisms help in the preparation of certain foods as they carry out **fermentation.** The fermentation takes place in the absence of oxygen.
Some help plants in providing nitrogen. Many secondary metabolites extracted from microbes are important in the pharmaceutical industry.

title: lactobacilli
text:
Useful and Harmful Microbes › Useful microbes › lactobacilli — Revision note (part 1/1)

1) _Lactobacilli_ are lactic acid bacteria, that produce lactic acid as a part of their metabolism.

2) They are rod-shaped, gram-positive, motile organisms that perform anaerobic respiration i.e. they produce energy in the absence of oxygen.

[Figure 1]

3) _Lactobacilli_ use the lactose present in milk and convert it into lactic acid through a process called **fermentation.** As acid formation increases, the pH of the milk decreases. This leads to coagulation in milk. The low pH destroys the harmful microbes present in the milk.

[Figure 2]

4)During **coagulation**, milk proteins are separated from other constituents of the milk. This process takes place when milk changes to yoghurt. Yoghurt has a distinctly sour taste that is developed due to lactic acid.

[Figure 3]

**Uses of**_**Lactobacilli**_

• _Lactobacilli_ are used on a large scale for the production of yoghurt, buttermilk, ghee, cheese etc.

title: Antibiotics
text:

• Antibiotics are carbon compounds obtained from some bacteria and fungi that are developed to destroy or prevent the growth of harmful microorganisms.
• The discovery of antibiotics in the 20th20th century brought a revolution in the field of medicine.
• Most antibiotics are used against bacterial diseases, while some antibiotics can be used to destroy diseases caused due to protozoa.
• Antibiotics such as penicillin, cephalosporins, monobactam, bacitracin, erythromycin, gentamycin, neomycin, streptomycin, tetracycline, vancomycin, etc. are used against various strains of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.
• Rifamycin is used against tuberculosis.

**Broad-spectrum antibiotics:**
• Useful against a wide variety of bacteria.
• These antibiotics are used when the symptoms of the disease are visible, but the causative pathogen is not identified.
• Examples are ampicillin, amoxicillin, tetracycline, etc.

**Narrow-spectrum antibiotics:**
• Useful when pathogenic microorganism of the disease is known.
• Examples are penicillin, gentamycin, erythromycin, etc.

**Alexander Fleming:**

Alexander Fleming was a professor of microbiology at St Mary’s Hospital.

On 3 September 1928, while observing staphylococci cultures, he
made an interesting observation in one Petri dish. In that Petri dish, fungal colonies had grown but the area around
those colonies was clean and clear. i.e. bacteria had actually been destroyed.

After further studies, he confirmed that the fungus growing there was Penicillium and its secretion destroyed the bacterial colonies.
Thus, the first antibiotic - penicillin had been discovered accidentally and this formed the basis for attempts to find cures for incurable diseases.

**Fungi:**

Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophic organisms that include microorganisms such as yeasts, molds, and mushrooms. These reproduce by asexual reproduction including sporulation, budding, etc.

**Instances of fungal infection in day-to-day life:**

1. In the rainy season, we can notice whitish-green cotton-like growth or black powder or white discs on leather articles and gunny (jute) bags during the rainy season as these articles are infected by fungus.
2. Microscopic spores of fungi are present in the air.
3. If there is sufficient moisture, spores germinate on cotton fabric, gunny bags, leather, wooden items, etc. The fungal hyphae (fibers of the fungus) penetrate deep into the material to obtain nutrition and reproduce.
This causes the materials to wear and become weak.
4. These articles get spoilt because of fungal infections and can no longer be used since the properties are changed.
5. As a result, gunny bags, leather items like shoes, purses, belts, etc. on which fungi have grown do not last long. Wooden items also get spoilt.
6. This spoilage doesn't occur in the summer or winter season as the moisture content is lesser in the atmosphere as compared to that in rainy season and spores don't have favourable conditions to germinate and cause infection.
7. A black powder or white disc floats on the pickle or murabba when a jar is opened after a long time. This is an infection caused by mold and yeast or fungus.

**Fungi spoils the food:**

They use the nutrients in these food items for growth and reproduction. Fungi deteriorate the food product and hence it is not good to consume such foods. Fungi release mycotoxins, certain poisonous chemicals, into the food, and thus food becomes poisonous. Hence, the food on which fungi have grown cannot be eaten.

The tradition of forecasting the monsoon season in India is older than 100 years.

**History:**

1. After the serious countrywide drought and famine in 1877, the Government of India’s anxiety for the earliest possible information about the progress of the monsoon grew and Sir H.F. Blanford, the first Chief Reporter of India Meteorological Department (IMD), was called upon to make attempts for estimating the prospective rains.
2. Blanford issued tentative forecasts from 1882 to 1885 utilizing the indications provided by the snowfall in the Himalayas. In 1885, it was decided that a monsoon forecast should thenceforward be issued annually as a matter of routine.
3. In the 1930's the then director of IMD, Sir Gilbert Walker had underlined the relationship between various worldwide climatic factors and the Indian monsoon, and, based on available observations and previous recordings related to this relationship he put forth a hypothesis regarding the nature of the monsoon.
4. Walker discovered three important large-scale see saw variations in global pressure patterns. These are Southern Oscillation, North Atlantic Oscillation, and North Pacific Oscillation.
5. With the initiative of Dr. Vasantrao Govarikar in the decade of the 1990's a monsoon model based on 16 worldwide climatic parameters was developed. This model was in use from 1990 to 2002.

**Monsoon models:**

**1. Statistical model:**

1. It is a traditional model to predict monsoons.
2. It equates relationships of physical parameters for example sea surface temperatures, snowfall, the temperature of landmass, etc. With the actually observed rainfall in the past.
3. In this model, current climatic observations in a region are compared with earlier parameters such as oceanic temperature, atmospheric pressure, and the nature of the monsoon rainfall of several years.
4. This data is comparatively analyzed by statistical methods and predictions are made about the monsoon in the present conditions.

**Mathematical model:**

1. It is also called the Monsoon Mission Coupled Forecast System or Dynamic model.
2. By estimating the existing weather-associated events and ongoing physical interactions between them, predictions are made.
3. Param supercomputer is used to study present parameters of climate.
4. By using supercomputer technology many mathematical models are made utilizing the geographical events daily.

**Holistic model:**

1. Predictions are done on the basis of parameters used in other models which have the greatest effect on the monsoon.
2. It is called the Holistic model because the declared predictions are the result of many models.

Any meteorological model depends upon the inter-relationship between parameters used in that model and the results expected from it.

However, as these inter-relationships with reference to the ocean and atmosphere are never constant, meteorological models need to be changed continually.

Meteorological models should be changed regularly because these models are based on inter-relationships with different parameters like the ocean and atmosphere which never remain the same.

title: Introduction to spherical mirrors
text:
Reflection Of Light › Spherical mirrors and terms related to spherical mirrors › introduction to spherical mirrors — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Spherical Mirrors**

The mirror whose reflecting surface is not flat like that of the plane mirror, and it can be thought as the part of the hollow sphere. Such mirror is called as the spherical mirror.

[Figure 1]

The reflecting surface of the spherical mirror can be either the outside or the inside of the curved surface.

The mirror whose reflecting surface is on the inside of the curved surface is called a concave mirror.

The mirror whose reflecting surface is on the outside of the curved surface is called a convex mirror.

**Terms used for describing the spherical mirrors:**

The centre of the mirror is called its pole, and is denoted by P.

The centre of the sphere of which the mirror forms a part is called the centre of curvature (C).

The radius of the sphere of which the mirror is a part is called the radius of curvature (r).

The line passing through the centre of curvature of the mirror and the pole is called the principal axis of the mirror. This line is perpendicular to the mirror at the pole.

All the above terms for the convex and the concave mirrors are shown in the figure below-

IMAGE

[Figure 2]

In case of the concave mirror, the rays converge after reflection. The point at which all the rays parallel to the principal axis meet or converge after reflection is called the principal focus of the concave mirror.

[Figure 3]

In case of the convex mirror, the rays parallel to the principal axis diverge after reflection. If these reflected rays are extended backwards, they appear to meet at the point. Thus the point at which the reflected rays from the convex mirror meet after they are extended backwards is called the principal focus of the convex mirror.

[Figure 4]

The principal focus can simply be called as focus and is denoted by F.

When the object is kept at principal focus, the image will be formed at infinity in front of a concave mirror. The image formed will be inverted, real and enlarged.

3.The object between the centre of curvature and focus:

title: How will you find out if a mirror is concave or convex?
text:
Reflection Of Light › Image formed by the convex mirror › how will you find out if a mirror is concave or convex? — Revision note (part 1/1)

Concavity and convexity are terms depicting curvature of a surface from a reference point / direction. For spherical surfaces or a section of a spherical surface, the view of the surface from the centre of the sphere along a radius is concave- while the same surface when viewed from outside ( i.e. the side away from the centre) is a convex surface.

So in the case of mirrors, if the reflecting surface is on the outside and viewing is done from any point towards the centre it is a concave mirror. If the inside is the reflecting surface and viewing is from outside the sphere it is a convex mirror.

Mirror formula:

$\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{u}$

where, f = focal length of mirror,

v= image distance

u= object distance.

In convex mirror v and f are always positive.

For a concave mirror, u and f are always negative.

Magnification:

M = $\frac{Heightoftheimage}{Heightoftheobject}$

= $\frac{{h}_{1}}{{h}_{2}}$

= $-\frac{v}{u}$

The negative sign in the above equation indicates that all real images are inverted. If the image is virtual, the image distance will be negative, and the magnification will be positive for the erect image.

title: Propagation of Sound
text:
Study Of Sound › Propagation of Sound › Propagation of Sound — Revision note (part 1/2)

Study Notes: Propagation of Sound

1. How Sound is Created & Travels
• Sound is created by vibrations.

• Sound needs a medium (material) to travel through — it cannot travel in a vacuum.

• Sound can travel through solids, liquids, and gases.

2. Sound Travelling Through Solids
• Experiment: Scratch a desk surface — audible through air.

• Placing your ear directly on the wood makes the sound clearer and louder.

• Conclusion: Sound travels efficiently through solids.

3. Sound Travelling Through Liquids
• Experiment: Tap two spoons together while submerged in water.

• Vibrating spoons push water molecules, creating a path for sound.

• Conclusion: Liquids can act as a medium for sound, just like solids.

4. What is a Medium?
• A medium is any material that carries sound (e.g., air, water, wood).

• Sound needs molecules to pass vibrations from one point to another.

• Without a medium, sound cannot travel.

5. Sound and Vacuum — Bell Jar Experiment
• Setup: A ringing bell is placed inside a sealed jar; a pump removes the air.

• As air is removed, the sound becomes fainter.

• In a complete vacuum, the sound vanishes entirely — even though the bell is still ringing.

• Key takeaway: No molecules = no sound propagation.

6. Why Space is Silent
• Outer space is a vacuum — there are no air molecules.

• Astronauts cannot talk to each other through air in space.

• Even clashing metal objects produce no audible sound in space.

• Astronauts use electronic devices that convert voices into radio waves.

• Radio waves do not need a medium to travel (unlike sound).

Key Terms to Remember
• Vibration: The back-and-forth motion that creates sound.

• Medium: Any material through which sound can travel.

concept_name: Introduction to sound as a wave
title: nature of sound waves
text:
Study Of Sound › Introduction to sound as a wave › nature of sound waves — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Nature of sound waves**

Sound is one kind of longitudinal wave, in which the particles of the medium vibrate to and fro in the same direction of wave propagation.

Sound waves cannot be transmitted through a vacuum. The transmission of sound requires a medium, which can be solid, liquid, or gas.

As the pressure decreases, the change seen in the case of sound waves is called a rarefaction. As the pressure increases, the change seen in the case of sound waves is called compression. i.e. Compressions are high-pressure zones and rarefaction are low-pressure zones in the sound wave.

Sound waves have low frequency and large wavelengths. The value of amplitude determines the strength of the sound. The value of frequency determines the pitch of the sound. The intensity of the sound wave is directly proportional to the square of the amplitude.

**Echo and reverberation are the characteristics of sound waves**

Echo is the repetition of sound because of reflection from some rigid surface at a distance from the source of the sound. This reflected sound arrives at the listener with a delay after the original sound.

Reverberation is multiple reflections of the sound waves.

Higher frequency sounds are emitted by the small speaker called a tweeter. Lower frequency sounds are emitted by the large speakers called woofers.

For the sound waves having a wavelength $\lambda$, velocity $\nu$ and frequency n the relation is given as: $n=\frac{v}{\lambda}$

The speed of sound can be given as :

$v=nλorv=\frac{\lambda}{T}$

where,

$v-velocityofsound\ n-frequencyofsoundwave\ \lambda-wavelengthofsoundwave\ T-Timeperiod$

When we see the lightning bolt we hear the sound a short while after it. This means that the sound does not reach us instantaneously but travels in a medium with a finite speed.

Thus, it takes some time to reach us from the place where it is produced.

The speed of sound in the air is approximately $330m/s$

The frequency of sound depends on the source and it does not change when the wave travels from one medium to another medium.

title: range of hearing
text:

**Range of hearing:**

Human beings can hear sound whose frequency range liesbetween 20 Hz to 20000 Hz**.**

The different ranges of hearing are given below.

**1.)** **Audible range:** The range of audible frequency lies between 20 Hz to 20000 Hz which is heard by human beings and some animals.

**2.)** **Infrasonic Sound:** The sound waves which have a frequency of fewer than 20 Hz are called infrasonic sound, these are produced by vibrations of the pendulum, earthquakes produce low frequency before main shock waves.

**3.)** Ultrasonic Sound: The sound waves which have a frequency of more than 20000 Hz are called ultrasonic sounds, these are produced by animals such as dolphins, bats, etc.

An ultrasound can travel along a well-defined straight path because it does not bend appreciably at the edges of an obstacle because of its small wavelength

In the air, the speed of all the sound waves is 330 m/s. As the frequency increases the wavelength of the sound decreases but the speed of sound in a particular medium always remains constant.

title: applications of ultrasound
text:
Study Of Sound › Uses of ultrasonic sound › applications of ultrasound — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Applications of Ultrasound :**

Ultrasound frequencies are higher frequencies capable of travelling along well-defined paths even in the presence of an obstacle.

**1.)** Ultrasound is useful to clean parts located in hard-to-find places. Due to high frequencies, the particles dust, grease, etc gets detached and removed.

**2.)** Ultrasounds are used in finding flaws in metal blocks that are used in the construction of buildings, bridges. Ultrasound is made to pass through the structure and is reflected back at the defective part.

**3.)** Ultrasounds are used in echocardiography where ultrasonic waves are made to reflect from parts of the heart and form the image of the heart.

**4.)** Ultrasound scanner which uses ultrasound waves to detect abnormalities in organs wherein waves travel through tissue density and reflects back when it encounters a change in density.

**5.)** Ultrasound is used to break small stones formed in the kidneys.

subconcept_name: reflection of sound, good and bad reflectors
title: Reflection of sound, good and bad reflectors
text:
Study Of Sound › Reflection of sound › reflection of sound, good and bad reflectors — Revision note (part 1/1)

Reflection of sound:

Sound can bounce off a solid or a liquid. Some materials like metals and walls are called Good Reflectors of Sound as they do not absorb the sound while others like clothes and sponge are called Bad Reflectors of Sound as they absorb the sound easily.

Laws of reflection

There are two basic laws of reflection of sound:

(i) Angle of incidence is equal the angle of reflection.

(ii) The incident wave, the reflected wave and the normal all lie in the same plane.

Stethoscope is a medical instrument used for listening to sounds produced within the body, mainly in the heart or lungs. In stethoscopes the sound of the patient’s heartbeat reaches the doctor’s ears by multiple reflection of sound
Generally the ceilings of concert halls, conference halls and cinema halls are curved so that sound after reflection reaches all corners of the hall, Sometimes a curved soundboard may be placed behind the stage so that the sound, after reflecting from the sound board, spreads evenly across the width of the hall. These are some of the applications of reflection of sound.

Good and bad reflectors of sound:

Hard surfaces such as glass, solid wood, walls will readily reflect sound. The smoother such surfaces are the better the reflection.

Soft materials such as soft furnishings (settees, heavy drapes, thick carpet) tend to absorb sound waves, particularly the upper register, creating a muffling effect. Apparently early recording studios preferred to clad their walls with soft sound-deadening materials to prevent ‘reflections’ - short-term echoes.

title: Sonography
text:
Study Of Sound › Sonography › sonography — Revision note (part 1/1)

### Sonography:

Medical ultrasound is a diagnostic imaging technique based on it. It is used for the imaging of internal body structures such as muscles, joints, and internal organs. Ultrasonic images are known as sonograms. In this process, pulses of ultrasound are sent to the tissue using a probe. The sound echoes off the tissue, where different tissues reflect sound varying in degrees. These echoes are recorded and displayed in an image.

[Figure 1]

This technique makes use of a probe and a gel. The gel is used to make proper contact between the skin and the probe so that the full capacity of the ultrasound can be utilized. The gel is applied to the skin outside the internal organ to be studied. High-frequency ultrasound is transmitted inside the body with the help of a probe. The sound reflected from the internal organ is again collected by the probe and fed to a computer that generates the image of the internal organ. As this method is painless, it is increasingly used in medical practice for diagnosis.

text:

**Velocity:**

1. $v=\frac{\lambda}{T}$, where $\lambda$ = wavelength and T = time period of the wave

2. $v=f\times\lambda$, where f is the frequency.

Frequency : $\text{f=}\frac{1}{T}$, where T = timeperiod.

Velocity is directly proportional to the square root of absolute temperature i.e. $v\alpha\sqrt{T}$

Velocity is inversely proportional to the square root of the density of the medium i.e. $v\alpha\frac{1}{\sqrt{\rho}}$

Velocity is inversely proportional to the square root of the molecular weight of the gas i.e. $v\alpha\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}$

**Echo :**

$1.$ Distance travelled by sound $=$Speed $x$ Time

$2.$ For an echo, $2d=vxt$

**Example :**

If the person standing between the two cliffs or two parallel reflecting surfaces hears the first echo after $x\sec$ and second echo after$yseconds$. And if the velocity of sound in air is v m/s, then solve the problem by following below steps :

$a)$ Calculate the distance of the person from one end of the cliff by the equation of echo :

$2{d}_{1}=vxt$ (i.e. the time at which the first echo is heard i.e. here $x\sec$)

$b)$ Calculate the distance of the person from second end of the cliff by the equation of echo :

$2{d}_{2}=vxt$ (i.e. the time at which the second echo is heard i.e. here y sec )

so the total distance between the walls of the cliff is $d={d}_{1}+{d}_{2}$

• For the generation of electricity in the thermal power plants.

**2. Coke**
• It contains 98% carbon and is formed by the destructive distillation of coal along with coal tar, coal gas, and ammoniacal solution.

• Coke is an amorphous allotrope of carbon and burns without smoke. It is black, porous, a good reducing agent and a bad conductor of heat and electricity.

$Coal{\rightarrow}_{distillation}^{destructive}Coke+Coaltar+Coalgas+Ammoniacalsolution$

**Uses**
• As a smokeless domestic and industrial fuel.
• As a reducing agent for extraction of metals from their ores and to prepare metallic carbides.
• In the production of water gas $(CO+{H}_{2})$ and producer gas $(CO+{N}_{2})$ and artificial graphite.

**3. Charcoal:**

• A solid organic substance on destructive distillation results in the formation of a black porous solid called charcoal.
• It is made from animals bones, horns, etc. or by combustion of wood in an insufficient supply of air.

text:
Carbon: An Important Element › Hydrocarbons › basics of hydrocarbons, solubility and reactions of carbon — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Hydrocarbons: Basic organic compounds:**

• The compounds which are formed only from carbon and hydrogen are called basic organic compounds.
• They are also called hydrocarbons. The electronic configuration of carbon is 2, 4. If four electrons are added to the second orbit of carbon, its octet becomes complete and its electronic configuration becomes stable like that of the nearest inert gas neon (2, 8).
• Therefore, the valency of carbon is 4.
• However, this occurs by sharing of an electron rather than donating or accepting electrons.
• In other words, a carbon atom can form four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms or atoms of different elements.
• When a carbon atom shares one electron each with four hydrogen atoms and forms four C-H bonds, a methane ${CH}_{4}$ molecule gets formed.

1. Covalent compounds have low melting and boiling points.
2. Generally, they are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.

**•** **Saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons:**
Carbon can form a chain of carbon atoms by forming covalent bonds with other carbon atoms.
The hydrocarbons having only single bonds between carbon atoms are called saturated hydrocarbons.
Example: Ethane $\left({C}_{2}{H}_{6}\right)$ which is $\left({CH}_{3}-{CH}_{3}\right)$, propane $\left({CH}_{3}-{CH}_{2}-{CH}_{3}\right)$, etc.
Some hydrocarbons have multiple bonds between two carbon atoms.
A multiple bond can be a double bond or a triple bond. Hydrocarbons having at least one multiple bond is called unsaturated hydrocarbons.
Example: Ethene $({H}_{2}C={CH}_{2})$, ethyne ($HC≡CH$), propene $({CH}_{3}-CH={CH}_{2})$, propyne $\left({CH}_{3}-C≡CH\right)$.
**•** **The solubility of carbon:** Carbon is insoluble in water but soluble in organic compounds.
**•** **Reactions of carbon with oxygen:**Lime water reacts with carbon dioxide to form calcium carbonate and water.
