title: Reaction of carbon with oxygen
text:
Carbon: An Important Element › Hydrocarbons › reaction of carbon with oxygen — Revision note (part 1/2)

Aim: To demonstrate the reaction of carbon with oxygen

Materials Required: Coal, match box, moist litmus paper, bunsen burner, pair of tongs

Hello dear students. During the winter season, that is during the cold months of the year, you might have observed that people take warmth by burning a coal fire. But it is always advised that one should not sleep in closed room with a coal fire burning. Why is this so? Let’s understand the reason behind this by carrying out a simple activity.

As you can see here I have a piece of coal. With the help of tongs, I am holding this piece of coal. Now I am going to heat this piece of coal on the flame of the bunsen burner. Can you notice that while igniting coal there is some gas which is being released? Which is this gas? Let’s find it out.

Now I am going to take a moist blue litmus paper and hold it over the gas that is being liberated while igniting the coal. What do you observe? Look the moist blue litmus paper turns red. What does this indicate? Yes. That the gas being released has acidic nature. But how? What is the substance formed? Well! Coal is made up of the element carbon. On ignition the carbon in the coal reacts with oxygen in the atmosphere to form carbon dioxide gas.

When we ignite coal, a gas is liberated that is the carbon dioxide gas. This carbon dioxide gas reacts with water (moisture) present in the moist blue litmus paper resulting in the formation of carbonic acid. Because of this carbonic acid formed, the moist blue litmus paper turns red.

title: Reaction of carbon with oxygen
text:
Carbon: An Important Element › Hydrocarbons › reaction of carbon with oxygen — Revision note (part 2/2)

But when you burn coal in a closed room, the available oxygen in the room gets depleted which then results in incomplete burning of coal. This incomplete combustion of coal results in the liberation of carbon monoxide gas which is a poisonous gas. Carbon monoxide gas mixes with the haemoglobin present in our blood forming carboxyhaemoglobin that thereby reduces the capacity of blood to carry oxygen in our body. As a result, it may lead to suffocation and may even lead to death of the person. Hence , it is dangerous to sleep in a closed room with buring coal.

title: Lime water turns milky
text:
Carbon: An Important Element › Hydrocarbons › lime water turns milky — Revision note (part 1/2)

Aim: To study the effect of carbon dioxide gas on lime water

Materials Required:lime water, lemon juice, bent tube, cork, test tube, baking soda

Hello dear students. Look what I have here today. Lime water. Yes! You guessed it alright. Today we will be performing a very simple experiment using this lime water. For this, here I have taken a test tube. Let us add some lime water in this test tube. Now I am going to take another test tube containing small amount of lemon juice.

I have a bent tube and a rubber cork. Let us fit this bent tube in this rubber cork like this. Make sure that you keep the bent tube and the rubber cork handy. Now with the help of this spatula I am going to add some baking soda in this test tube containing lime water. As soon as I add baking soda, I need to immediately fix the bent tube over the test tube. We will insert the other end of the bent tube in the test tube containing lime water. What do you observe? What happens?

title: Lime water turns milky
text:
Carbon: An Important Element › Hydrocarbons › lime water turns milky — Revision note (part 2/2)

We can observe that as soon as baking soda is added to lemon juice, bubbles or effervescence is seen. This effervescence indicates the release of some gas. This gas released passes through the bent tube into the test tube containing lime water. As soon as the lime water comes in contact with the gas released, lime water turns milky. What does this indicate? Which is the gas being liberated? The gas liberated is carbon dioxide gas. When carbon dioxide gas is passed through lime water, lime water turns milky. This confirms that the gas being released is carbon dioxide. But from where does this carbon dioxide come? This carbon dioxide is liberated as a result of the reaction between lemon juice and baking soda. Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate which reacts with lemon juice (acidic) thereby resulting in liberation of carbon dioxide gas.This indicates that when a carbonate or a bicarbonate is reacted with an acid, it results in the formation of salt, water and carbon dioxide gas. This liberated carbon dioxide gas reacts with lime water to form a precipitate of calcium carbonate which is white in colour. Hence, lime water turns milky on the passage of carbon dioxide gas. But what if we pass excess carbon dioxide gas into this milky lime water? As you can see the white precipitate formed dissolves. But how did this happen? When excess of carbon dioxide gas is passed through milky lime water, the carbon dioxide gas reacts with the insoluble calcium carbonate resulting in the formation of calcium hydrogen carbonate that is water soluble. You can also try out this experiment at home by simply blowing air into the lime water with the help of a straw.

• **Carbon-dioxide (${CO}_{2}$)**:
The molecular formula of carbon dioxide is ${CO}_{2}$.
Its molecular mass is 44 and melting point is - $56.6^{\circ}C$.
• **Occurrence:** Carbon dioxide occurs in the air in the free state and its percentage is about 0.03%.
The air which is exhaled contains about 4% of ${CO}_{2}$. ${CO}_{2}$ is present as salt in chalk and Shahabad tiles/ marble/ limestone.
${CO}_{2}$ is produced during the combustion of wood and fossil fuel coal.
• **Physical and chemical properties of carbon dioxide $\left({CO}_{2}\right)$**: Carbon dioxide is colourless. The gas is odourless at low concentrations.
When carbon dioxide is passed through an aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide, the product formed is sodium carbonate (washing soda).$2NaOH+{CO}_{2}\rightarrow{Na}_{2}{CO}_{3}+{H}_{2}O$
And, when carbon dioxide is passed through an aqueous solution of sodium carbonate, the product formed is sodium bicarbonate $\left({NaHCO}_{3}\right)$.
${Na}_{2}{CO}_{3}+{CO}_{2}+{H}_{2}O\rightarrow2{NaHCO}_{3}$
• **Uses**:
• It is used to make aerated drinks.
• In cold storage, solid carbon dioxide is used. Its role is to keep milk, milk products and frozen substances cool during transportations.
• It is also used to create special effects of a mist in movies.
• Liquified carbon dioxide is used to remove caffeine from coffee.
• Plants utilise the carbon dioxide present in the air for photosynthesis.
• In modern eco-friendly dry cleaning, liquid carbon dioxide is used as a solvent.
• ${CO}_{2}$ obtained by chemical reaction or kept under pressure is utilised in fire extinguishers.

text:

• **Methane**
[Figure 1]
• **Occurrence:**Methane gas was discovered by the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta between 1776 and 1778**.**Methane is the only hydrocarbon with one carbon atom. It is the first member of the homologous series of alkanes. Methane is present in biogas.
Methane is also called as Marsh gas as it is found bubbling out in the marshland.
It also occurs in coal and mines and in natural gas over petroleum.
It constitutes 35% of coal gas too.
Decomposition of organic matter in the absence of air produces methane.
Fractional distillation of natural gas gives methane in its pure form.
On heating, a mixture of hydrogen and carbon monoxide at $300^{\circ}C$ in the presence of nickel, methane gas is formed.
Methane occurs in natural gas upto 87%.

**Preparation:**

**A) Laboratory method of preparation:**
1. In the laboratory, it is prepared by heating sodium acetate with soda lime

${CH}_{3}COONa+NaOH\rightarrow{CH}_{4}+{Na}_{2}{CO}_{3}$
[Figure 2]

2. By the reduction of methyl iodide with zinc in $dil.{H}_{2}{SO}_{4}$ or zinc-copper couple
${CH}_{3}I+2H\rightarrow{CH}_{4}+HI$

3. By the action of water on aluminium carbide.
${Al}_{4}{C}_{3}+12{H}_{2}O\rightarrow4Al{(OH)}_{3}+3{CH}_{4}$

${\left({C}_{6}{H}_{10}{O}_{5}\right)}_{n}+{\text{nH}}_{2}O\rightarrow3{nCO}_{2}+3{nCH}_{4}.$

B) **Industrial method:**On a large scale, it is prepared by the direct synthesis in an electric arc.
$C+2{H}_{2}\overset{{1200}^{^{\circ}}C}{\rightarrow}{CH}_{4}$

By direct synthesis in an electric arc.

**Physical properties:**
1) It is colourless, odourless and neutral to litmus paper.
2) Methane is highly soluble in organic solvents like gasoline, ether and alcohol. But is sparingly soluble in water
3) It is half as dense as air (Specific gravity = 0.55).
4) It freezes at -184$^{\circ}$C and liquefies at 0$^{\circ}$C and 150$^{\circ}$C atmosphere pressure or at -161.4$^{\circ}$C and normal pressure.
5) Melting point of methane is -182.5$^{\circ}$C.
6) Methane is in gaseous state at room temperature.

**Chemical properties:**

**1. Halogenation:**
Direct ignition or sunlight gives an explosive reaction.
${CH}_{4}+2{Cl}_{2}\rightarrowC+4HCl$

2. Heating gives less violent action.

${CH}_{4}+4{Cl}_{2}\rightarrow{CCl}_{4}+4HCl$

2. **Oxidation**
a. Burns in the air with pale blue non-luminous flame. Here in this reaction, 213 kcal/mol$213kcal/mol$ of heat is given out.

${CH}_{4}+2{O}_{2}\rightarrow{CO}_{2}+2{H}_{2}O+Heat$
b. With ozone, or by incomplete combustion at ${350}^{0}C-{500}^{0}C$ we get formaldehyde.

${CH}_{4}+2O\rightarrowHCHO+{H}_{2}O$
c. With nickel catalyst and high pressure, it forms methanal.

${CH}_{4}+O\rightarrow{CH}_{3}OH$

3. **Pyrolysis:**
Heated to ${1000}^{0}C$ in the absence of ${O}_{2}$, carbon and ${H}_{2}$ are formed.

${CH}_{4}\rightarrow\underset{Carbonblack}{C}+2{H}_{2}$

4. **The action of steam:**
With steam in the presence of Nickel at ${1000}^{0}C$ it gives $CO$ and ${H}_{2}$.

${CH}_{4}+{H}_{2}O{\rightarrow}_{Nickel}^{{1000}^{0}C}CO+3{H}_{2}$

5.**Conversion to HCN:**

$2{CH}_{4}+{N}_{2}\underset{Electricarc}{\rightarrow}2HCN+3{H}_{2}$

text:

6. **Combustion:**
The combustion reaction of methane is expressed as,

${CH}_{4}+2{O}_{2}\rightarrow{CO}_{2}+2{H}_{2}O+heat$
Methane is highly inflammable. It burns by reacting with oxygen to give a bluish flame. In the above reaction, 213 $kcal/mol$ of heat is given out. Methane burns completely.

7.**Chlorination:**

Methane and chlorine gas react with each other at the temperature of 250$^{\circ}C$ 400$^{\circ}C$ in the presence of ultraviolet light and form mainly methyl chloride (chloromethane) and hydrogen chloride.

**Salts:**
Salts are formed by the reaction between acids and bases. Such reactions are called a neutralization reaction.
The salts which are formed from neutralisation reactions are not always neutral. A neutral salt is formed by the neutralization of a strong acid by a strong base.
The pH value of salts of a strong acid and a strong base is 7, therefore they are neutral.
On the contrary, salts of a strong acid and weak base are acidic as their pH value is below 7 and salts of a strong base and weak acid are basic in nature, with pH value more than 7.

**Sodium chloride $\left(NaCl\right)$****:**
The most used of all salts present is **Table salt or common salt**. It is liable for giving a salty taste to food.
Its chemical name is sodium chloride.
It is formed by carrying a neutralization reaction between sodium hydroxide **$\left(NaOH\right)$** and hydrochloric acid $\left(HCl\right)$.

concept_name: Substances in common use - Important salts

text:

**Properties and uses of sodium chloride:**
**Table salt**is a colourless, salty in taste and crystalline ionic compound. No water of crystallization is present in its structure.
It is a neutral salt, as it formed by the reaction between a strong acid and a strong base.
It is used for the production of salts such as ${Na}_{2}{CO}_{3}$, ${NaHCO}_{3}$.
When electricity is allowed to pass through a saturated solution of sodium chloride (brine), it is electrolysed and hydrogen gas is liberated at the cathode while chlorine gas is liberated at the anode.
In this method, a basic compound known as sodium hydroxide is formed in the electrolytic cell.
$2NaCl+2{H}_{2}O\rightarrow2NaOH+{Cl}_{2}↑+{H}_{2}↑$
When salts are subjected to heating at a high temperature (about $800^{\circ}C$), it melts. This is termed as the fused state of the salt.
Chlorine gas is released at the anode and liquid sodium metal at the cathode when the fused state of salt is electrolysed.
Salt is also obtained from a certain type of rock. This salt is called **Rock salt**. Examples: mineral halite, Himalayan rock salt.
The 25% aqueous solution of salt is called **Saturated brine**.

**Sodium bicarbonate (****${NaHCO}_{3}$)****:**
Baking soda is a white non-crystalline powder.
Sodium hydrogen carbonate or sodium bicarbonate is the chemical name of it.
Its molecular formula is **${NaHCO}_{3}$.**

**Properties and uses of sodium bicarbonate:**
When **${NaHCO}_{3}$**reacts with moist litmus paper, it turns blue indicating that it is basic in nature.
It is used to make bread, dhokla, cake.
Being alkaline in nature, it is used to diminish the acidity in the stomach.
${NaHCO}_{3}$ is used to make the active substance carbon dioxide in the fire extinguisher.
It is also used to clean an oven.

When oil or animal fat is subjected to boiling with an aqueous solution of sodium or potassium hydroxide, the compound formed is sodium or potassium salts of carboxylic acids (fatty acids). These salts are known as soap.

title: Nature and characteristics of radioactive radiation
text:
Substances in Common Use › Substances in common use- Radioactive substances › nature and characteristics of radioactive radiation — Revision note (part 1/2)

• **Radioactive substances****:**

• Elements with a high atomic number exhibit a property of spontaneously emitting invisible, highly penetrating and high energy radiation.
• Such elements include uranium, thorium, radium, etc.
• This property is termed as radioactivity. Substance those exhibit these properties are generally called a radioactive substance.
• The nucleus of such radioactive elements is unstable and radiation occurs from such an unstable nucleus.
• The type of radiation that is emitted out by these substances is divided into three categories: alpha, beta and gamma rays.

• **Nature of radioactive radiation:**

concept_name: Substances in common use- Radioactive substances
subconcept_name: nature and characteristics of radioactive radiation
title: Nature and characteristics of radioactive radiation
text:
Substances in Common Use › Substances in common use- Radioactive substances › nature and characteristics of radioactive radiation — Revision note (part 2/2)

• In the year 1889, Rutherford discovered that the radiations emitted by radium were of two types namely alpha and beta radiation. Later on, Willard discovered the third type namely gamma radiation.
• When these rays are made to travel through two oppositely charged plates, they get separated. This method was suggested by Rutherford in 1902.
• Rutherford and Willard studied the radiation given out by radioactive substances. For this purpose, the rays were made to travel through an electrical field and a photographic plate was held in their path.
• It was observed that the radiation was divided into three types. One of them, deviated slightly towards the negatively charged plate, while the second type of radiation deviated substantially towards the positively charged plate.
• However, the third type of radiation did not deviate at all in the electrical field.
• The rays which deviated slightly toward negatively charged plate are known as alpha $\left(\alpha\right)$ rays, those which deviate substantially towards the positively charged plate are known as beta $\left(\beta\right)$rays and those which do not deviate at all are known as gamma $\left(\gamma\right)$ rays.

title: Uses of Radioactive isotopes
text:
Substances in Common Use › Substances in common use- Radioactive substances › uses of radioactive isotopes — Revision note (part 1/4)

• **Uses of radioactive isotopes:** Radioactive isotopes are utilized in various fields such as scientific research, agriculture, medicine, industry, etc.
These substances can be used in two ways: 1. By using the radiation alone. 2. By using the radioactive element itself.

1. **Industrial field Radiography:** Internal cracks and voids in cast iron articles and iron solder can be detected with the help of gamma rays. For this purpose, isotopes like cobalt-60, iridium-192 are used in the radiography camera. This technique is used for detecting flaws in metal work.

• **Measurement of thickness, density and level**: It is necessary to maintain the thickness which is required during the production of aluminium, plastic, iron sheets of differing thicknesses. In the manufacturing process, a radioactive substance is placed on one side and an instrument to measure radiation on the other. The radiation read by the measuring instrument varies with the thickness of the sheet.

• **Luminescent paint and radioluminescence:** The radioactive substances such as radium, promethium, tritium with some phosphor are used to make certain objects visible in the dark.
Example: the hands of a clock.
Krypton-85 is used in HID (High-Intensity Discharge) lamps while promethium-147 is used in portable X-ray units as the source of beta rays.

concept_name: Substances in common use- Radioactive substances
title: Uses of Radioactive isotopes
text:
Substances in Common Use › Substances in common use- Radioactive substances › uses of radioactive isotopes — Revision note (part 2/4)

• **Use in Ceramic articles:** To decorate ceramic tiles, utensils, plates, etc. luminous colours are used.
Earlier uranium oxide was used in these paints.
• **Field of agriculture:**
1. The genes and chromosomes that impart the properties like fast growth, higher productivity, etc. to the seed can be modified by means of radiation.
2. The radioactive isotope cobalt-60 is used for the purpose of food preservation.
3. Onions, potatoes are irradiated with gamma rays from cobalt-60 to prevent their sprouting.
4. Strontium-90 is used as a tracer in the research on various crops.

concept_name: Substances in common use- Radioactive substances
title: Uses of Radioactive isotopes
text:
Substances in Common Use › Substances in common use- Radioactive substances › uses of radioactive isotopes — Revision note (part 3/4)

• **Medical science:**
1. **Polycythemia:** Polycythemia is the condition in which the red blood cell count increases. Phosphorus- 32 is used in its treatment.
2. **Bone cancer:** In the treatment of bone cancer, strontium-89, strontium-90, samarium-153 and radium-223 are used.
3. **Hyperthyroidism**: The symptoms of hyperthyroidism include enlargement of the thyroid gland, weight loss in spite of appetite, insomnia, etc.
It happens due to the overproduction of hormones by the thyroid gland. Iodine-123 is used in the treatment of hyperthyroidism.
4. **Tumour detection**: Boron-10, iodine-131, cobalt-60 are used in the treatment of brain tumour whereas arsenic-74 is used in the detection of small tumours in the body.
• **Natural radioactivity:** Generally, those elements which have the atomic numbers in between 82 to 92 are found to be radioactive in nature.
• **Artificial radioactive elements:** The couple Fredric Joliot Curie and Irene Joliot Curie were the first ones to induce radioactivity. The radioactive elements formed in the nuclear fission processes carried out in the laboratory by the bombardment of particles are known as artificial radioactive elements. In 1935, they were awarded the Nobel prize for this discovery.

• **Hazards of radioactive substances and radiation:**

concept_name: Substances in common use- Radioactive substances
title: Uses of Radioactive isotopes
text:
Substances in Common Use › Substances in common use- Radioactive substances › uses of radioactive isotopes — Revision note (part 4/4)

• 1. Radioactivity affects the central nervous system.
• 2. Hereditary defects are produced by the bombardment of radiation on $D.N.A$ in the body.
• 3. Radiation can penetrate through the skin and can cause diseases like skin cancer, leukemia.
• 4. The radioactive pollutants created due to explosions enter the body through the air and it is difficult to control them.
• 5. The radioactive pollutants dumped in the seawater enter the bodies of fishes and through them enter the human body.
• 6. The radioactive isotopes strontium-90 can enter the body through plants, fruits, flowers, cereals, milk, etc. and cause diseases like bone cancer, leukemia.

• **Chernobyl disaster:** On 26th April 1986 the graphite reactor in the Chernobyl atomic power plant exploded, the explosion allowed the radioactive isotopes and radiation to come out. Due to this, radioactive isotopes entered the human body through water and land and caused many genetic disorders.
• These got carried further into the next generation. Due to this, thyroid disorders increased in children as well as adults. As a result, the incidence of throat diseases is greater there than in other places.

text:
Substances in Common Use › Chemical substances in day to day life › artificial colour, dye and deoderants and their harmful effects — Revision note (part 1/3)

• **Some chemical substances in day to day life:**The food that we consume daily, objects like clothes and utensils, watches, medicines, and other objects are prepared by using different kinds of matter. All these substances that we use, affect our health directly or indirectly.
Amongst them, few of the important categories are as follows:
• **Food colours and essences:**Food colours are added in most soft drinks and foodstuffs available in the market for consumption.
These food colours are available in various forms which include powders, gels and pastes.
Food colours are used in domestic as well as commercial products.
Certain colours and essences are added to ice cream, ice candies, sauce, fruit juices, cold drinks, jams and jelly, etc.
• **Harmful effects of artificial food colours:**
1. Food colours which are added to pickles, jam and sauce contain small quantities of lead and mercury.
2. Due to the excessive consumption of foods with added food colours, disease like ADHD(Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder) can occur in children.
• **Sources of food colour:**Food colours are natural as well as artificial. The food colours which are prepared from naturally occurring substance such as beetroot, flowers and fruit concentrate are natural. tetrazene and sunset yellow are artificial food colours which are used extensively.
However, the over-consumption of artificial food colours can be detrimental to health.

text:
Substances in Common Use › Chemical substances in day to day life › artificial colour, dye and deoderants and their harmful effects — Revision note (part 2/3)

• **Dye:**A dye is defined as the coloured substance which on applying to an article, will impart a colour to the article.
Generally, a dye is soluble in water and insoluble in oil.
It has been observed that a mordant has to be used to fix the colour after dyeing a cloth.
For preparing natural dyes, plants are the main source of colour. Roots, leaves, flowers, bark, fruits, seeds, fungus and pistil are used for preparing dyes.
In Kashmir, an excellent dye is made from saffron, which is used to dye fibres from which saris, shawls and dresses are made. These are expensive.
The use of henna leaves to colour hair is safe for health. In 1856, William Henry Perkin invented an artificial dye. Artificial dyes are classified into many categories depending upon the chemical properties and solubility. Petroleum products and minerals are used in these dyes.

**Uses:** They are used for colouring cloth and hair. Dyes are used to polish, leather shoes, purses and chappals. Fluorescent colours are used to make street boards that are visible at night.

**Adverse effects:** Dyeing hair can cause hair fall, damage to the texture of hair, burning of the skin, adverse effects on eyes.
Lipstick contains a dye named carmine. It does not affect lips but can cause stomach disorders.
Excessive use of plants for making natural dyes results in the deterioration of the natural environment.

title: Artificial colour, Dye and Deoderants and their harmful effects
text:
Substances in Common Use › Chemical substances in day to day life › artificial colour, dye and deoderants and their harmful effects — Revision note (part 3/3)

**• Artificial colour:**Artificial colours are regularly being used by all of us on Rang Panchami. We also utilise those colours for decorating the house by painting.
The red colour use on Rang Panchami is menacing. It contains a high proportion of mercury in it.
This poses risks like blindness, skin cancer, asthma, itching of the skin, permanent blocking of sweat pores, etc.
Therefore, it is necessary that artificial colours are used the utmost care.

**• Deodorant:** The bacterial breakdown of sweat causes body odour. Deodorant is used to prevent this odour. Everybody likes a fragrant deodorant to remain fresh the whole day. School children use deo on a large scale. This large scale use of deo in adolescent is a result of the advertisements shown on television.
Deodorants contain parabens (methyl, ethyl, propyl, benzyl and butyl) and also alcohol in large proportions.
The deodorants are classified into the following categories:
**1. Ordinary deo:** It contains a smaller amount of aluminium. It decreases the odour of the sweat.

**2.** **Antiperspirant deo:**This decreases the extent of sweating. It has about 15% of aluminium chlorohydrate. It clogs the sweat pores on the skin.

**3. Clinical deo:** Some people sweat heavily and it has harmful effects on the skin. Clinical deo is designed for such people. It contain 20 to 25% aluminium. It is used during the night.

• **Harmful effects:**
1. Aluminium – Zirconium compounds are the most harmful chemicals in the deodorant. Disorders like headache, asthma, respiratory disorders, heart disease are likely to occur without our knowledge.
2. There is a possibility of various skin disorders and also skin cancer due to the presence of aluminium chlorohydrates.

title: Teflon, Powder coating, anodizing and ceramics
text:
Substances in Common Use › Chemical substances in day to day life › teflon, powder coating, anodizing and ceramics — Revision note (part 1/3)

• **Teflon:**Teflon is used for coating cooking utensils and industrial equipment to make them non-stick. It is the polymer of tetrafluoroethylene.
In 1938 Roy J. Plunkett discovered it. Its chemical name is polytetrafluoroethylene ${\left({C}_{2}{F}_{4}\right)}_{n}$ **.**

• **Properties:** The atmosphere and chemical substances produce no effect on Teflon.
2. Neither water nor oil will stick to the articles which are coated with Teflon.
3. High temperatures do not affect Teflon because its melting point is $327^{\circ}C$.
4. Teflon coated articles are cleaned with ease.

**Uses of Teflon:**Teflon is a bad conductor of electricity. Hence, Teflon cladded wires and parts are used in high technology electronics instruments.
2. It is used for making non-stick kitchen utensils.
3. The coloured metal sheets of automobiles are given a Teflon coating to protect them from damage due to high temperature and rain.

• **Powder coating:** It is used to prevent rusting of iron.
In this method, a polymer resin, a pigment and some other substances are melt mixed, cooled and ground into a uniform powder. With the help of electrostatic spray deposition (ESD), this powder is sprayed on the polished metal surface. In this method, the particles of the powder are provided with an electrostatic charge which results in the formation of a uniform layer of the powder sticks to the metal surface. Then the object is subjected to heat. A chemical reaction occurs in the layer which results in the formation of long cross-linked polymeric chains. This powder coating is highly durable, hard and attractive. In day to day use, powder coating can be done on plastic and medium density fibre $\left(MFD\right)$.

text:

• **Anodizing:**When aluminium metal reacts with oxygen in the air, a protective layer is formed naturally on the surface of aluminium metal. By using the anodizing process, this layer can be made of the desired thickness. Anodizing is done by electrolysis. Dilute acid is taken in the electrolytic cell and the aluminium article is dipped in it as the anode. When an electric current is passed, hydrogen gas is released at the cathode and oxygen gas at the anode.
Oxygen reacts and a layer of hydrated aluminium oxide is formed on the anode, i.e. the iron article. To make the layer look attractive, colours can be added to the electrolytic cell. We use anodized cooking utensils like griddles and cookers.

• **Ceramic:** Ceramic is a heat resistant substance formed by kneading an inorganic substance in water and then shaping it and hardening it by heating. Pots made by a potter, construction bricks, terracotta articles are some examples of common ceramic articles.

When the clay is kneaded in water, shaped and then fired in a kiln at a temperature of $1000to1150^{\circ}C$, a porous ceramic gets formed.
To remove the porosity, the fired object is covered with finely ground glass powder suspended in water (glaze) and is then fired again. As a result, the surface of the ceramic becomes shiny and its porosity disappears.

• **Porcelain:**Hard, translucent and white coloured ceramic used in the laboratory as it is highly resistant to heat.

**• Bone china:** Bone china is prepared by adding some ash of animal bones in the mixture of china clay, feldspar and fine silica while making porcelain.
This ceramic is harder than porcelain.

This ceramic requires a temperature of $1600to1800^{\circ}C$ and an oxygen-free atmosphere for firing. This process is termed as sintering.

title: introduction to coordination and the process in plants
text:
Life Processes in Living Organisms › Coordination in plants › introduction to coordination and the process in plants — Revision note (part 1/2)

Living organisms respond to stimuli like heat, light, cold, touch, pressure, etc. This is known as responsiveness to stimuli. This characteristic is shown by living organisms.

Example: Withdrawal of the hand touching a hot object.
Proper coordination is necessary to maintain a state of equilibrium called homeostasis, which is necessary for the optimal efficiency of the body.
**Coordination in plants**: Plants respond to the stimulus by coordination.
**Trophic Movement:** Growth or movement of plants in response to external stimulus.
**Phototrophic Movement:** Growth or movement of the plant towards the light source.
**Gravitropic Movement:** Root system of plant responses to stimuli like water or gravitation.
**Chemotrophic Movement:** Movement of the plant in response to certain chemicals. E.g. Pollen tube growing towards the ovule.

[Figure 1]

**Pollen tube growing towards the ovule**

All the above movements are called **growth-relevant movements**.

**Growth irrelevant movement:**

There are certain responses of the plants called **growth irrelevant movement** that does not lead to the plant's growth.
Plants use electrochemical impulses to transfer information from one part to the other.

Plant cells change their shape by increasing or decreasing their water content and thereby bringing about the movements of plants.

title: Coordination in human being- Introduction
text:
Life Processes in Living Organisms › Coordination in human beings › coordination in human being- introduction — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Some instances of control and coordination in action:**

Playing cricket involves catching the ball, batting, fielding, running, thinking, etc.

Playing badminton involves holding the racket, judging the direction of incoming cork, hitting the cork, running

Playing chess involves critical thinking, and the movement of body parts like eyes, hands, etc.

**Control & Coordination:**

Different processes go on simultaneously in the human body.

All these processes need to be efficiently and effectively controlled and coordinated.

The brain and spinal cord comprises the central nervous system which has connection to nerves that carry control all other systems, carry messages, and controls the sense organs too.

**Nervous System**

The nervous system consists of a well-organized network of nerves that can conduct information in the form of electrical impulses from one part of the body to another.

Humans can respond to changes in their surroundings due to nervous control.

Impulses are generated in the human body, in accordance with changes in the surroundings.

Nervous control plays the important role of empowering the body cells with the ability to respond to these impulses.

This ability depends upon the complexity of the organization in the organism’s body structure.

Unicellular animals like the amoeba do not have a nervous system that produces such impulses and responses.

However, multicellular animals like humans, have a nervous system to respond to stimuli.

Control and coordination are brought about with the help of a special type of cells called nerve cells or neurons.

Brain is an important organ protected in skull.

It has walnut-like appearance

Functions: Stores information and creates a memory.

**Main parts of the Brain:**

Cerebrum

Brain stem

Life Processes in Living Organisms › Coordination in human beings › coordination in human being- introduction — Revision note (part 2/2)

**Cerebrum:**

Thinking part, responsible for speech, thoughts, learning, intelligence, and memory

It lies along the central axis of the body.

It includes the brain and spinal cord.

It lies along the periphery of the body.

The PNS comprises all the nerves of the body associated with the CNS.

It comprises the Somatic nervous system and Autonomic Nervous System.

**Chemical Control**

Control and coordination in our body are also brought about with the help of certain chemical substances called hormones.

**Reflex Action:** An immediate and involuntary response given to a stimulus from the environment is called a reflex action.

The spinal cord acts instead of the brain to prevent any damage.

**Sense Organ - Eyes**

Controls eyesight and processes images with the help of brain.

Optic nerve sends the information of image seen to the brain

Eyelids protect eyes from bright light and dust

The inner ear changes the vibrations into the message and send it to the brain

If we close our noses, no smell is detected.

The nerves on the tongue (taste buds) surface detect the taste and send a message to the brain.

**Sense Organ - Skin**

Many nerve endings present on the skin

Due to these nerves, our skin feels and responds.

title: Neurons and transmission of impulses
text:
Life Processes in Living Organisms › Coordination in human beings › neurons and transmission of impulses — Revision note (part 1/2)

All images

Neurons (Nerve cells) : Special types of cells which conduct impulses from one place to another in the body are called neurons. Neurons are the structural and functional units of the nervous system. Nerve cells, the largest cells in the human the body, may measure up to a few metres in length. Nerve cells have the ability to generate and conduct electro[1]chemical impulses. The cells that support the nerve cells and help in their functioning are called neuroglia. Nerve cells and neuroglial cells together form the nerves. All the information about our surroundings is collected by the ends or dendrites of the neuron. The chemical process begins at those ends and electric impulses are generated which are conducted from the dendrites to the cell body, from the cell body to the axon and from the axon to its terminal. These impulses are then to be transferred from this nerve cell to the next. Now the impulse that reaches the terminal of an axon, stimulates the nerve cell to secrete certain chemicals. These chemicals pass through a minute space, called the synapse, between two adjacent neurons and generate the impulse in the dendrites of next neuron. In this way, impulses are conducted in the body and these impulses are finally conveyed by nerve cells to muscle cells or glands.

title: Neurons and transmission of impulses
text:
Life Processes in Living Organisms › Coordination in human beings › neurons and transmission of impulses — Revision note (part 2/2)

When an action or movement is to be brought about in the body, the work of the muscular tissue comes last in the sequence. Movement of muscle cells is essential to bring about any activity. When cells contract to change their shape, movement occurs at cellular level. Muscle cells have the ability to change their shape due to a special type of protein. Besides, due to these same proteins, cells become able to respond to electrical impulses of nerves. Thus, we can say that the nervous system consists of a well-organized network of nerves that can conduct information in the form of electrical impulses from one part of the body to other.

subconcept_name: types of neurons and introduction to CNS
title: Types of neurons and introduction to CNS
text:
Life Processes in Living Organisms › Coordination in human beings › types of neurons and introduction to CNS — Revision note (part 1/2)

The nervous system is very complex, there are only two main types of cells in nerve tissue.

1. The neuron which is the conducting cell that transmits impulses and is the structural unit of the nervous system.
2. The other type of cell is the neuroglia, or glial, cell. They provide developmental, physiological, and metabolic support for neurons.

According to their function, nerve cells are classified into three types:

**Sensory neurons:**

1. Sensory neurons conduct impulses from sensory organs to the brain and the spinal cord.
2. The inputs that activate sensory neurons can be physical or chemical, corresponding to all five of our senses.
3. Thus, a physical input can be things like sound, touch, heat, or light. A chemical input comes from taste or smell, which neurons then send to the brain.
4. Most sensory neurons are pseudounipolar meaning they only have one axon which is split into two branches.

**Motor neurons:**

1. Motor neurons of the spinal cord are part of the central nervous system (CNS).
2. Motor neurons conduct impulses from the brain or spinal cord to effector organs like muscles or glands.
3. Motor neurons are multipolar, each with one axon and several dendrites.

**Association neurons:**

1. These are also called interneurons. Association neurons perform the function of integration in the nervous system. They connect spinal motor and sensory neurons.
2. Interneurons can also communicate with each other, forming circuits of various complexity.

**Central Nervous System or CNS:**

subconcept_name: types of neurons and introduction to CNS
title: Types of neurons and introduction to CNS
text:
Life Processes in Living Organisms › Coordination in human beings › types of neurons and introduction to CNS — Revision note (part 2/2)

1. The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord.
2. The organization of the brain is extremely delicate and highly evolved.
3. The brain is the main controlling part of the nervous system and it is safely located in the cranial cavity.
4. The brain is protected in a bony skull.
5. The spinal cord is protected by the vertebral column.
6. In the space between the delicate central nervous system and its bony covering are the protective layers called the meninges.
7. Three layers of membranes are called meninges to protect the brain and spinal cord.
8. The delicate inner layer is the pia mater.
9. The middle layer is the arachnoid, a web-like structure filled with fluid that cushions the brain.
10. The tough outer layer is called the dura mater.
11. Cavities present in various parts of the brain are called ‘ventricles’ whereas the long tubular cavity of the spinal cord is called the ‘central canal’.
12. The functions of the ventricles are the production and circulation of cerebrospinal fluid.
13. The ventricles, central canal, and spaces between the meninges are filled with cerebrospinal fluid.
14. This fluid supplies nutrients to the central nervous system and protects it from shock.

subconcept_name: structure of brain- cerebrum, cerebellum, and medula oblongata
title: Structure of brain- Cerebrum, cerebellum, and medula oblongata
text:
Life Processes in Living Organisms › Coordination in human beings › structure of brain- cerebrum, cerebellum, and medula oblongata — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Structure of Brain:**

1. The brain of an adult human weighs about 1300 – 1400 grams.
2. Consists of approximately 100 billion neurons.
3. Human brain is about 75% water.
4. Left side of brain- controls the right side of our body.
5. Right side of brain- controls left side of the body.
6. Left side of the brain - controls our speech and conversation, writing, logical thinking, etc.
7. Right side - controls artistic abilities.

**Cerebrum:**

1. Largest part of our brain.
2. Makes up 85% of the brain’s weight.
3. Consists of two cerebral hemispheres.
4. Hemispheres are joined with each other - tough fibers and nerve tracts.
5. Occupies two-thirds of the brain.
6. Hence, also called the large brain.
7. Surface- deep, irregular ridges and grooves called convolutions present.
8. Convolution increases the surface area of the cerebrum which allows the accommodation of a large number of nerve cells.
9. Thinking part of the brain.
10. Controls voluntary muscles.

**What if the cerebrum is damaged?**

Personality disorders, loss of senses, difficulty in thinking and learning.

**Cerebellum:**

1. Smaller part of the brain
2. Situated below the cerebrum at the back of the cranial cavity
3. Surface shows shallow grooves instead of deep convolutions.

**Functions of cerebellum:**

1. Balance
2. Movements
3. Muscle control
4. Language processing
5. Memory

**What would be the effect if the cerebellum is injured?**

Movement coordination would be affected which might lead to staggering while walking, inability to take rapid actions, difficulty in judging distance, etc.

**Medulla Oblongata:**

1. Hind-most part of brain.
2. Two triangular swollen structures called pyramids - upper side of medulla oblongata.
3. The medulla oblongata continues downwards as the spinal cord.

title: Functions- Brain & Spinal Cord
text:
Life Processes in Living Organisms › Coordination in human beings › functions- brain and spinal cord — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Spinal Cord:**

**Hormones:**

Hormones are chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands. They help coordinate various body functions, including growth, development, metabolism, and responses to changes in the environment.

1. Endocrine glands: These are ductless glands that release hormones directly into the bloodstream. The blood transports hormones to their target organs or tissues.

2. Coordination: The endocrine system and the nervous system work together to coordinate and regulate the activities of the body.

3. Rate and duration of action: Hormonal responses are generally slower to develop but may last longer than nervous responses, which are usually rapid and short-lived.

4. Regulation of secretion: Hormone secretion is regulated according to the body's requirements, often through feedback mechanisms. For example, insulin secretion increases when blood glucose levels rise.

Seven Essential Life Processes
Life processes are the basic activities performed by living organisms to maintain life. The seven essential life processes are movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, and nutrition.

1. Movement
Movement is the change in position of the whole organism or a part of its body. Animals move from one place to another, while plants show movements in response to stimuli.

Example: A sunflower shoot bends towards light.

2. Respiration
Respiration is the process by which cells break down food to release energy required for various life activities.

Aerobic respiration: Takes place in the presence of oxygen.
Anaerobic respiration: Takes place in the absence of oxygen.
3. Sensitivity (Response to Stimuli)
Sensitivity is the ability of living organisms to detect and respond to changes in their surroundings. These changes are called stimuli.

Example: A touch-me-not plant folds its leaves when touched.

4. Growth
Growth is a permanent increase in the size, mass, or number of cells of an organism.

Example: A seed develops into a seedling and eventually into a mature plant.

5. Reproduction
Reproduction is the biological process by which organisms produce offspring of their own kind. It ensures the continuity of a species.

Sexual reproduction: Involves the fusion of male and female gametes.
Asexual reproduction: Occurs without the fusion of gametes.
Example: Humans reproduce sexually, while Amoeba reproduces by binary fission.

6. Excretion
Excretion is the process of removing metabolic waste products from the body.

Example: Human kidneys remove urea, excess water, and salts from the blood to form urine.

7. Nutrition
Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain food and utilise it for energy, growth, repair, and maintenance.

Autotrophic nutrition: Organisms prepare their own food, as green plants do through photosynthesis.
Heterotrophic nutrition: Organisms obtain food from other organisms, as animals do.
Example: Green plants prepare food through photosynthesis, whereas humans obtain food by eating plants and other animals.

The functional unit of the kidney

Performs the basic function of filtration.

Working of dialysis unit:

About 500 ml of blood is sent at one time through this machine. Purified blood is reinfused into the body of the patient.

It is a process of separating small solutes from macromolecular colloids with the help of a selectively permeable membrane.

Mechanism:

The patient's blood is slowly pumped from the patient's radial artery into the dialyzer, where waste products and extra fluids are removed; the purified blood is then returned into a vein in the same arm. Blood from the artery is mixed with heparin and cooled at zero degrees Celsius and passed through a cellophane tube which acts as a semi-permeable membrane. Heparin is an anticoagulant and thus prevents blood from clotting.

text:

Every eukaryotic species has a characteristic number of chromosomes (chromosome number).

In organisms reproducing asexually, the chromosome number is the same in all organisms' cells.

Among sexually reproducing organisms, the number of chromosomes in the body (somatic) cells is diploid (2n; a pair of each chromosome), twice the haploid (1n) number found in the sex cells, or gametes.

The haploid number is produced during meiosis.

During fertilization, two gametes combine to produce a zygote, a single cell with a diploid set of chromosomes.

Generally, in somatic cells chromosomes are in pairs.

If the pair consists of similar chromosomes by shape and organization, they are called ‘homologous chromosomes’ and if they are not similar they are called ‘heterologous chromosomes’.

In organisms that reproduce sexually one of the chromosomal pairs is different from all others. Chromosomes of this different pair are called ‘sex chromosomes’ or allosomes and all other chromosomes are called ‘autosomes’.

Types of chromosomes can be easily identified during cell division.

The structure of chromosomes is best studied when they are completely condensed i.e at the Metaphase stage.

Each chromosome is divided into two sections (arms) based on the location of a narrowing (constriction) called the centromere. By convention, the shorter arm is called p, and the longer arm is called q.

**Structure of DNA:**
• **James Watson and Francis Crick** in 1953 based on an X-ray diffraction study deduced the molecular structure of DNA
• The silent features of the double-helix model are:
1) According to the double-helix model, a DNA molecule consists of two long strands coiled around a central, imaginary axis.

2) **Structure of each strand:**
• It is made up of a number of nucleotides and each nucleotide is made up of a Nitrogenous base, a phosphate group, and deoxyribose sugar.
• The adjacent nucleotides of the same strand are linked through 3’-5’ phosphodiester linkage.
• The phosphate group is attached to the 5^(th)carbon.
• Hydroxyl attached to 3^(rd) carbon.

3) **Complementary base pairing:**
• Purines base with a pyrimidine.
• Cytosine pairs with guanine, due to the chemical structure. Adenine and Thymine form two hydrogen bonds between them. Guanine and Cytosine form three hydrogen bonds between them.
• Adenine and Thymine A=T (Double bond) Guanine and Cytosine G≡C (Triple bond).

4) **Purine Pyrimidine Ratio:**
• The ratio of purine to pyrimidine is 1.
• A+G = T+C called Chargaff's rule.
• It is expressed as$\frac{A+G}{T+C}=1$.

5) **Polarity****of strand:**
• Two chains have antiparallel polarity.
• One of the strands runs in ${5}^{'}-{3}^{'}$ one direction while the other in ${3}^{'}-{5}^{'}$ direction.

6) **Major and minor grooves:**
• Two chains coiled in a right-handed manner.
• Deep grooves (major groove) and shallow (minor groove) grooves in an alternate manner.

7) **Dimensions:**
• The diameter of the DNA molecule is 2 nm.
• The angle between two successive steps is${36}^{^{\circ}}$.
• 10 base pairs are present in one complete turn.
• It makes one complete ${360}^{^{\circ}}$ after covering a distance of 3.4 nm.

**The function of genes:**

• Genes store information about protein synthesis.
• They transmit the hereditary characteristics from parents to offspring, hence called the functional unit of hereditary.
• This is the reason behind similarities between parent and their offspring.

**DNA fingerprinting:**

It is a method of identifying the DNA of different people by locating the differences in the arrangement of nucleotides in the DNA sequence that are repeated several times.

**Principle:**

About 99.9% of the base sequence among all humans is the same. Thus only 0.1% of the total base pairs show the difference in the arrangements that make every human being unique.
• The differences in the arrangement occur in both functional and non-functional (repetitive) DNA.
• DNA fingerprinting involves identifying these differences in the repetitive DNA sequence.

**Applications of DNA fingerprinting:**

text:
Heredity and Variations › Gene › gene and DNA fingerprinting — Revision note (part 2/2)

1. The sequence of the genes in the DNA of a person i.e. the genome of the person is identified.
2. DNA fingerprinting is used in forensic tests to identify criminals because it is unique to every person and in paternity tests.
3. Sex of an individual: Badly damaged bodies of victims can be identified.
4. Fingerprinting can be used to trace evolutionary change.
5. Kinship analysis: Infer the blood relationship amongst the members of the same family.

**Celera Genomics Corporation** (a private industry in the USA) sequenced the human genome at a fraction of the cost of the publicly-funded Human Genome Project (HGP), using about $300 million of private funding.

title: Human Genome Project
text:
Heredity and Variations › Discovery & use of DNA › human genome project — Revision note (part 1/1)

• Genome is a haploid set of chromosomes in a gamete or organism, or in any cell of a multicellular organism.
• The human genome project sequenced only euchromatic regions of the genome, which was 99% of the entire human genome with an accuracy of 99.99%.
• The aim of the Human genome project was to map the entire human genome by determining the sequence of nucleotides in the DNA of each 22 pairs autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes.
• The human genome project was a 13-year project funded by the National Institute of Health (NIH) and the US Department of Energy.
• In 1990, the **‘Human Genome Project’** was together undertaken by all the geneticists of the world.
• The Human Genome Project (HGP) was announced to be completed in April 2003.
• A preliminary rough draft of the human genome was made available in June 2000 and a working version was completed and published by February 2001, followed by full sequencing of the human genome on 14 April 2003.
• The scientists confirmed that the number of genes in the human genome is about 20,000 to 30,000.
• Due to research in genomics, disease-causing genes can be identified, and genetic disorders can be diagnosed and properly treated.
• In addition to studying the human genome, the HGP involved in mapping and sequencing genomes from number model organisms like _E.coli_, _Arabidopsis thaliana_, _S.cerevisiae_.

title: Introduction to RNA and its types
text:
Heredity and Variations › RNA › introduction to RNA and it's types — Revision note (part 1/3)

### RNA -

1. It is a polymer of nucleotides similar to DNA with a few differences in structure and function.

2. It is made up of -

**a. Pentose sugar - Ribose ${C}_{5}{H}_{10}{O}_{5}$.**

**b. Nucleic base/Nitrogen base - Purine (Adenine and Guanine) & Pyrimidine (Cytosine and Uracil).**

**c. Phosphate group - ${H}_{3}{PO}_{4}$.**

3. Thymine is replaced by uracil in RNA.

4. RNA is usually single stranded while DNA is double-stranded in nature.

### Functions -

1. Serves as a genetic material in some viruses such as the Tobacco Mosaic Virus, Human Immunodeficiency Virus, Reovirus etc.

2. It can perform catalytic activity like an enzyme they are known as ribozyme.

3. It mediates the transfer of information from DNA to ribosomes for protein synthesis by forming an intermediate coded polymer of mRNA.

4. It has the ability to carry amino acids for protein synthesis through tRNA.

5. It forms major components of Ribosome which is the organelle of protein synthesis.

### **Composition of Ribonucleic acid (RNA):**

It consists of ribose sugar, phosphate molecules, and four types of nitrogenous bases: Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine, and Uracil and hence form four types of nucleotides.

| **Pentose sugar** | **Nucleic base** | **Nucleoside** | **Phosphate group** | **Nucleotide** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ribose | Adenine | Adenosine | Phosphoric acid | Adenosine monophosphate / Adenylic acid |
| Ribose | Guanine | Guanosine | Phosphoric acid | Guanosine monophosphate / Guanylic acid |
| Ribose | Cytosine | Cytidine | Phosphoric acid | Cytidine monophosphate / Cytidylic acid |
| Ribose | Uracil | Uridine | Phosphoric acid | Uridine monophosphate / Uridylic acid |

text:
Heredity and Variations › RNA › introduction to RNA and it's types — Revision note (part 2/3)

RNA can be classified into two types based on their function as a genetic/non-genetic material:

### 1) **Genetic RNA:**

1. In-plant viruses and some animal viruses genetic material is RNA, unlike DNA.

2. Example - In the Tobacco Mosaic Virus, it is the genetic material.

### 2) **Non-Genetic RNA:**

1. They are of three types: mRNA, rRNA and tRNA.

[Figure 2][Figure 3]

### 1. **Ribosomal RNA (rRNA):**

1. rRNA form 50-60% part of ribosomes which form the catalytic zone within the ribosome.
2. It accounts for 80-90% of the cellular RNA present within the cytoplasm and nucleus.
3. It is synthesized in nucleus and forms a coiled structure by intrachain complementary base pairing.
4. rRNA was discovered by **Charles Gabriel Kurland**in 1960.

### 2.**Messenger RNA (mRNA):**

1. mRNA carries codons which are translated by ribosomes in the cytosol.
2. It is a linear polynucleotide which accounts for 3% of cellular RNA.
3. Its molecular weight is several million.
4. mRNA molecule carrying information to form a complete polypeptide chain is called cistron.
5. Size of mRNA is highly variable dependent on the number of codons.
6. Synthesis of mRNA begins at 5’ end of DNA strand and terminates at 3’ end.

### 3. **Transfer RNA (tRNA):**

title: monohybrid cross
text:
Heredity and Variations › Monohybrid cross › monohybrid cross — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Monohybrid cross:**
- In monohybrid, mono means one and hybrid refers to two individuals of different species.
- A cross between two pure homozygous parents having a single contrasting character.
• In a monohybrid cross, Mendel started with a pair of pea plants with two contrasting traits, one tall and one dwarf called parental generation.
• The cross-pollination of tall and dwarf plants resulted in tall plants, and none were dwarf.
• He called such suppressed traits as recessive traits and expressed traits as dominant traits.
• The resulting offsprings named as ${F}_{1}$ hybrid or ${F}_{1}$ generation (First filial generation).
• A self cross between ${F}_{1}$ individuals resulted in ${F}_{2}$ generation.
• Mendel observed that traits that were absent in ${F}_{1}$ generation had reappeared in the null generation. Surprisingly, dwarf character which was not expressed in ${F}_{1}$ generation was present in ${F}_{2}$ generation.
• Mendel allowed self-pollination in ${F}_{1}$ generation, These seeds were collected sown to obtain plants that belonged to second filial generation (${F}_{2}$ generation).
• He found that plants of ${F}_{2}$ generation were both dwarf and tall plants were three times more numerous than the dwarf ones.
• In ${F}_{2}$ generation, tall and dwarf plant appeared in the ratio of 3:1. He called it a phenotypic ratio. **Phenotypes** are physical characteristics. • When **ratios** are used to describe **phenotypes** it's called a **phenoty****pic ratio**. **Phenotypic ratio** is the number of one **phenotype** compared to another **phenotype**.
•The genotypic ratio of a ${F}_{2}$ of monohybrid cross is 1 : 2 : 1.
• When ${F}_{2}$ tall and dwarf plants were allowed for self-pollination to obtain ${F}_{3}$ generation.

[Figure 1]

title: mendel's laws of inheritance
text:
Heredity and Variations › Laws of mendel › mendel's laws of inheritance — Revision note (part 1/1)

1) **Law of dominance:**
• The law of dominance states that when two alternative forms of trait or character (genes) are present in an organism, only one factor is expressed in the ${F}_{1}$ progeny and is considered dominant, while the other that remains masked is called recessive.
• The recessive character can be expressed only when the pair consists of both (homozygous recessive).
• E.g. Allele for tallness is dominant over the allele for dwarfism

- The law of dominance was not universally applicable.

2) **Law of segregation of genes:**
• This law states that the alleles do not show any blending (mixing) and both the characters are restored as such in the ${F}_{2}$ generation, though one of these is not seen in the ${F}_{1}$ generation.
• The gametes combine together by fusion at the time of zygote formation.

3) **Law of independent assortment:**
• This law states that when two pairs of traits are present in a hybrid, the segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair of characters at the time of gametogenesis.
• Mendel proposed the law on the basis of the results of dihybrid crosses, where the inheritance of two traits was considered at the same time.

title: genetic disorders: Introduction and disorders due to chromosomal abnormalities
text:
Heredity and Variations › Genetic disorders › genetic disorders: introduction and disorders due to chromosomal abnormalities — Revision note (part 1/1)

• Grouped into two categories- **Mendelian disorders** and **chromosomal disorders**.
• **Mendelian disorders**- based on alteration or mutation in the single gene.
• The most common of these are haemophilia, cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell anaemia, colour blindness, phenylketonuria, thalassemia, etc.
• It can be dominant or recessive.
• The trait can also be linked to a sex chromosome, such as haemophilia and colour blindness.
• Sickle cell disease is caused due to mutation in the haemoglobin protein- a beta gene located on chromosome 11.
• Phenylketonuria is caused by a defect in chromosome 12.
• Cystic fibrosis is caused due to mutations in a gene on chromosome 7.
• Huntington's disease is caused by a genetic defect on chromosome 4.
• Colour blindness is located on the X chromosome.

**Chromosomal disorders:**
• The entire set of chromosomes in a species or in an individual organism is known as a karyotype, i.e. 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of allosome.
• The chromosomal disorder can be caused due to absence, excess or abnormal arrangement of one or more chromosomes.
• Improper segregation of chromatids during the cell division cycle results in the gain or loss of a chromosome(s), is called **aneuploidy**.
• Aneuploidy is an abnormal number of chromosomes in a cell and it can be caused by missing a chromosome in a pair or more number of chromosomes than the normal.
For example,
**Down’s syndrome** results in the gain of an extra copy of chromosome 21.
**Turner’s syndrome** results due to the loss of the X chromosome in human females.
Absence of cytokinesis after telophase stage of cell division - increase in a whole set of chromosomes in an organism and phenomenon is known as **polyploidy**.

title: klinefelter's syndrome
text:
Heredity and Variations › Genetic disorders › klinefelter's syndrome — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Klinefelter's syndrome:**
• This genetic disorder is caused by the presence of an extra X chromosome in males.
• It results in a chromosome count of 47(44 + XXY) instead of 46.
**Symptoms:**
• Such an individual has a masculine physique but has feminine development such as breast development i.e., gynecomastia.
Klinefelter syndrome males may have: small, firm testes, a small penis, sparse pubic, armpit and facial hair, enlarged breasts (called gynecomastia), tall stature, and abnormal body proportions (long legs, short trunk).
• Such individuals are sterile, i.e. they cannot reproduce.
• Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and Luteinizing hormone (LH) levels are higher and testosterone levels are lower in Klinefelter's sufferer. The two X chromosome causes an increase in female sex hormones and less male sex hormones

**Diagnosis:**The standard diagnostic method of Klinefelter's syndrome after birth is the analysis of the chromosomes karyotype on lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are easily available and nucleated and can be cultured for three days which makes it a good source to study human karyotype.

**Treatment:**Behavioural therapy, hormone therapy, and testosterone intake are considered as the treatment options for Klinefelter syndrome.

title: sickle cell anemia
text:
Heredity and Variations › Mutation of single gene (monogenetic) › sickle cell anemia — Revision note (part 1/2)

• Sickel cell anaemia is an autosomal linked recessive trait.
• It is controlled by a single pair of allele, i.e. ${Hb}^{A}$${Hb}^{S}$.
• Normal haemoglobin has glutamic acid as the 6th amino acid in the molecular structure.
• However, if it is replaced by valine, the structure and shape of the haemoglobin molecule changes.
• The mutation in sickle cell anemia is a single nucleotide substitution (A to T) in the codon for amino acid 6. This change converts a glutamic acid codon (GAG) to a valine codon (GTG).
• Due to this, the RBC's which are normally biconcave become sickle-shaped. This condition is known as 'sickle cell anaemia'.
• The oxygen carrying capacity of haemoglobin in such individuals is very low.
• In this condition, clumping and thereby the destruction of red blood cells occur most often. As a result of this blood vessels are obstructed and the circulatory system, kidneys, brain, etc. are damaged.
• In sickle cell anaemia homozygous individuals of sickle cell anemia show ${Hb}^{s}{Hb}^{s}$.
• The heterozygous individual is unaffected having ${Hb}^{A}$ ${Hb}^{S}$.

**Symptoms of sickle-cell anaemia:**
• Swelling of arms and legs, Periodic pain in joints, general body aches, frequent colds and cough, constant low-grade fever, pale face and low haemoglobin content.
• Red blood cells have a life span of 120 days before they need to be replaced. But sickle cells usually die in 10 to 20 days, leaving a shortage of red blood cells causing anaemia.
• The person with sickle cell anaemia is resistant to the parasite that causes malaria. A small genetic change in the haemoglobin; both causes sickle cell anaemia and protects against malaria.
**Diagnosis of sickle-cell anaemia:**
• Electrophoresis is a confirmatory diagnostic test performed for sickle-cell anaemia.

title: Introduction to cell biology
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Introduction to biotechnology › introduction to cell biology — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Cells** are the minute components that constitute the body of a living organism and their number varies in different living organisms.

The organizational levels in living organisms are cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, and organisms.

**Tissue**: A group of cells combine to form a tissue that performs a specific function. They have the same origin, structure, and function.

Millions of cells are divided into different groups that perform different functions.

Plant tissue culture is a Modern technique of farming & gardening.

Tissue culture is the ‘Ex vivo growth of cells or tissues in an aseptic and nutrient-rich medium’.

•With the help of tissue culture, a complete organism is developed from just a single cell or even from the tissue.
•Nutrient & energy supply: a liquid, solid, gel-like medium is prepared from agar.

Cytology/ Cell Biology: Study of structure, types & organelles of the cell, and study of cell division.

Cytology has contributed to human health.

Research Institutes: Research on cells and these are established at Pune and Bengaluru.

Pune: NCCS, Bengaluru: Instem.

Stem cells are special cells in multicellular organisms that can give rise to other types of cells. These have an important role in wound healing.

Fusion of male & female gamete: Zygote formation

At earliest stage of development, organism is in the form of mass of almost alike cells called stem cells.

Stem cells are cells with the potential to develop into many different types of cells in the body. They serve as a repair system for the body.

Differentiation of stem cells: Different types of cells > Different types of tissues > Different functions.

title: Epithelial tissue
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Types of animal tissues › epithelial tissue — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Epithelial Tissue:**

1. Protective covering on the body of the animal.
2. The cells that make up the tissue are closely packed together thereby forming a continuous layer.
3. When a foreign material enters our body, it is first encountered by the epithelial tissue.
4. A fibrous membrane separates the cells of the epithelial tissue from the underlying tissue.
5. Examples: Skin, Mucous layer of the mouth cavity, Inner surface of blood vessels, and Walls of the alveoli.

**Squamous epithelium:**

1. Located in the Inner surface of the mouth, esophagus, blood vessels, & alveoli.
2. It is a semipermeable membrane made up of thin, small, and flat cells.
3. Its main function is the selective transportation of substances.

**Stratified epithelium:**

1. It is located on the outer layer of the skin.
2. It is made up of many layers of cells.
3. Its main function is to prevent the wear & tear of organs and protect the organs.

**Glandular epithelium:**

1. It is located in the inner layer of the skin.
2. It is made up of cells that are packed with secretory material.
3. Its main function is to secrete sweat, oil (sebum), and mucus.

**Columnar epithelium:**

1. It is located on the Inner surface which is the mucosa of the intestine, and alimentary canal.
2. It is made up of tall column-like cells.
3. The upper free surface consists of folds that are made of these cells at places of absorption.
4. Its main function is to secrete digestive juices & absorb nutrients.

**Ciliated epithelium:**

The Inner surface of the respiratory tract is made up of ciliated epithelium.

The upper free surface consists of minute hair-like structures.

Its main function is to push air as well as mucous forward so as to keep the air passage free.

**Cuboidal epithelium:**

title: Muscular Tissue
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Types of animal tissues › muscular tissue — Revision note (part 1/2)

- Muscular tissues are made up of specialised cells that have unique properties of contractility and electric excitability.
- Contractility is due to myosin and actin filaments. The action of muscles is necessary for movement.
- Electrical excitability is due to the potential difference across the plasma membrane.
- It develops from the embryonic mesoderm.
- Iris muscles, muscles of the salivary gland, sweat gland, mammary glands are made from embryonic ectoderm.
- Muscles are bundles of fibres that can contract and relax.
- The muscles are attached to the bones via tendons.
- There are more than 600 muscles in the human body. It contributes almost 40% of the total weight of a healthy adult human body.
- There are almost 30 muscles in the human face. The human expressions like fear, sadness, happiness are expressed by the movements of facial muscles.

**1. Striated muscles/skeletal muscles/voluntary muscles:**
**Structure:**Cylindrical, unbranched, and multinucleated. They have primary and secondary bundles wherein muscle fibres lie parallel in the connective tissue.
**Location:** Limbs, body wall, tongue, pharynx and beginning of oesophagus.
Myofibrils: Contractile apparatus; has transverse striations of alternate dark and light bands
**Functions:**

- Skeletal or striated muscles are voluntary and contract rapidly but get fatigued very soon.
- They bring the movement of bones as bones attach them. They are controlled by the central nervous system.

title: Muscular Tissue
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Types of animal tissues › muscular tissue — Revision note (part 2/2)

**2. Unstriated muscles /smooth muscles/involuntary muscles:
Structure:** Elongated and spindle-shaped, myofibrils lie parallel to the long axis.
Functionally they are of two types:
**Single unit Smooth muscle:**All the muscle in the sheet contract simultaneously.
**Multi-unit Smooth muscle:**Fibres contract more or less independently.
**Functions:**

- Bring about opening and closing of apertures.
- Carry out peristalsis.
- Stomach muscles churn the food. Also present in urinary bladder and help in expulsion of urine.
- These muscles do not get fatigued easily. They are controlled by the autonomic nervous system.

**3. Cardiac muscles:
Structure:**Cylindrical, branched. Cells are connected by intercalated discs. Show striations. They are uninucleate.
**Functions:**

- They make up the walls of the heart. Their contraction and relaxation help to pump the blood throughout the human body. They are striated but involuntary.
- These muscles are immune to fatigue. They are controlled by the autonomic nervous system.

title: nervous tissue
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Types of animal tissues › nervous tissue — Revision note (part 1/2)

For Identifying the singer, listening to music, and Identifying the food, nervous tissue plays an important role.

**Nervous Tissue:**

1. Stimulates muscle contractions and creates an awareness of the environment, emotions, memory, and reasoning.
2. Responds to stimuli – touch, sound, colour, odour
3. For all of its functions, communication between cells is a must.
4. Communication occurs using electrical nerve impulses
5. Cells of the nervous tissue become excited
6. Conduction of excitation from one part of the body to different parts of the body.

**Nerve cell:**

1. The cell body, comprising the cytoplasm & the nucleus, forms the main part of the nerve cell.
2. Three principal parts: **the dendrites, the cell body, and one axon.**
3. Cell body: Also known as the soma. It contains genetic information in the nucleus, maintains the structure of the neuron, and provides energy for the functioning of neurons.
4. Dendrites: Numerous, branched, small fibres arise from the cell body.
5. Extensions, or processes, of the cytoplasm that carry impulses to the cell body.
6. Axon: Extremely long fibre
7. An extension or process called an axon carries impulses away from the cell body.
8. Length of the nerve cell: can be up to 1 meter
9. A nerve is formed when many nerve cells are combined together via connective tissue.

- Nervous tissue = neurons (cells transmitting impulses) + glial cells (cells supporting the activities of neurons)
- Nervous tissue: Present in the brain, spinal cord & nerves that are spread throughout the body.
- Some glial cells bind neurons together and insulate them while others have phagocytic functions, providing defence against invading pathogens.
- Some of the glial cells provide nutrients by binding blood vessels to neurons.

title: connective tissue
text:

Connective Tissue: Different parts of the body are joined together by tissues called connective tissues.

The cells that make up the tissue are loosely packed together thereby forming free spaces in between.
The cells are packed with a ground substance. (solid/liquid/jelly-like)

Blood, Lymph, Areolar Tissue, Adipose Tissue, Cartilage, Bones, Tendons & Ligaments.

Blood:

Located in a closed circulatory system.
Comprises of leucocytes, platelets, and erythrocytes in liquid plasma
Its main function is to transport nutrients, waste, hormones & oxygen.

Lymph

Located in all the cells in the body.
The fluid oozes out from the blood capillaries comprised of leucocytes as well as liquid ground substance.
Its main function is to protect the body from infections.

Areolar Tissue

Located in the space between the skin and muscles.
Located around blood vessels.
It is made up of cells that are loosely packed.
The cells are supported by a ground substance (jelly-like) and elastic fibers.
Its main function is to support the internal organs in the body.

Adipose Tissue

Located around the internal organs as well as below the skin.
It is made up of cells that are filled with fat droplets.
The cells are supported by a ground substance (jelly-like).
Its main function is to store fats, supplying energy & insulation.

Cartilage

Located in ear, trachea, nose, and larynx.
The cells are supported by a ground substance (jelly-like, fibrous & flexible).
Its main function is to lubricate bone surfaces and to provide support & shape to the organs.

Bones

Forms the skeleton framework of the body.
Comprises of osteocytes that are embedded in ground substance which is made up of calcium phosphate.
Its main function is to enable movement and to provide support and protection to the organs.
