title: Nervous Tissue
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Types of animal tissues › understanding nervous tissue — Revision note (part 1/2)

What is Nervous Tissue?

- Nervous tissue is a specialised tissue that forms the nervous system.
- It controls communication and coordination within the body.
- It helps the body respond quickly to internal and external stimuli.

Nervous System

- The nervous system is the body's communication network.
- It connects different parts of the body and coordinates their activities.
- Main components:
- Brain
- Spinal cord
- Nerves

Role of the Brain

- The brain acts as the control centre of the nervous system.
- Functions of the brain:
- Thinking
- Memory
- LearningDecision-making
- Coordination of body activities

Example of Coordination

- During exercise, muscles require more oxygen.
- The brain detects this need.
- It sends signals to the heart.
- The heart beats faster and supplies more oxygen-rich blood to the body.

Neurons (Nerve Cells)

- Nervous tissue is made up of specialised cells called neurons.
- Neurons receive, process, and transmit messages.
- Messages are transmitted as nerve impulses.

Structure of a Neuron

- Cell Body
- The main part of the neuron.
- Contains the nucleus.
- Controls the activities of the neuron.
- Keeps the neuron alive and functional.
- Dendrites
- Short, branched extensions arising from the cell body.
- Receive signals from:
- Sensory receptors
- Carry signals toward the cell body.
- Axon
- Long, fibre-like extension of the neuron.
- Carries nerve impulses away from the cell body.
- Transmits signals to another neuron, muscle, or gland.
- Axon Terminals
- Branched endings present at the end of the axon.
- Transfer messages to the next neuron or target cell.

Synapse

- A small junction between two neurons.
- Messages pass from one neuron to another through synapses.

Nerve Impulses

title: Nervous Tissue
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Types of animal tissues › understanding nervous tissue — Revision note (part 2/2)

- Nerve impulses are electrical signals.
- They travel very rapidly through neurons.
- This allows the body to respond almost instantly to stimuli.

Example

- Touching a hot object causes an immediate withdrawal of the hand.
- This rapid response is possible because of fast nerve impulse transmission.

Functions of Nervous Tissue

- Controls body coordination.
- Enables communication between different body parts.
- Receives and processes information.
- Transmits nerve impulses.
- Helps the body respond quickly to stimuli.

title: Plant tissue: Meristematic tissue
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Plant tissue: Meristematic tissue › plant tissue: meristematic tissue — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Difference in Growth:**

| Plant Growth | Animal Growth |
| --- | --- |
| Indefinite or unlimited growth | Definite or limited growth |
| Increase in the number of parts | No increase in the number of parts |
| Growth occurs mainly at the shoot and root tips | Growth occurs by cell division in most tissues |
| Size increases often by an increase in cells upon absorbing water | Size increase is essentially by increasing cell number by cell division |
| Plant cells can differentiate into different cell types | Only stem cells can differentiate into different cell types. Other animal cells’ functions remain fixed. |

Activity:

1. Take two jars and label them as A and B.
2. Fill both jars A and B with water.
3. Now place an onion on each of the jars.
4. Make sure that the roots of the onion are dipped in water.
5. We will measure the length of the onion root of both onions for 3 days.
6. After 3 days, we will cut about 1 cm of the onion root only in flask B.
7. Now we will measure the length of the onion root of both onions for the following 5 days.
8. Note your observation.

| Length (cm) | Day 1 | Day 2 | Day 3 | Day 4 | Day 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Flask A | 0.25 | 0.6 | 1.2 | 1.7 | 2.0 |
| Flask B | 0.3 | 0.7 | 1.4 (after cutting = 0.4) | 0.45 | 0.6 |

**Observation:**

1. Flask A has longer onion roots.
2. This is mainly because of the meristematic tissue present at the tip of the onion root.
3. The meristematic tissue has dividing cells that continuously divide thereby the roots grow longer.
4. Flask B has shorter onion roots.
5. This is because the onion root tips were cut that is the meristematic tissue was cut off.

**Meristematic Tissue:**

title: Plant tissue: Meristematic tissue
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Plant tissue: Meristematic tissue › plant tissue: meristematic tissue — Revision note (part 2/2)

1. Located in specific parts of the plant
2. Meristematic tissue: Dividing cells (highly active)
3. Growth occurs in meristematic tissue only.
4. Comprised of cells with a cytoplasm (thick), conspicuous nucleus & cell wall (thin).
5. The cells are together compactly packed.
6. Absence of vacuoles (mostly)

**According to the location:**

1. Apical Meristem
2. Intercalary Meristem
3. Lateral Meristem

Apical Meristem:

1. Location: Root tip & stem
2. Function: Its main function is increasing the length of both the stem & root.
3. Root cap is produced by root apical meristem.
4. Stems, leaves, and reproductive structures are produced by shoot apical meristem.

Intercalary Meristem:

1. Location: Petiole base (leaves & branches)
2. Indeterminate growth in plants is due to intercalary meristem.
3. Promote the elongation of the stem and increase the height of the plant.

Lateral Meristem:

1. Location: Lateral side (stem & roots)
2. Function: Increases the diameter (stem & root)
3. Cylindrical meristem is found in roots and shoots resulting in secondary growth i.e. increasing the girth of root and shoot by producing vascular tissues.
4. Monocot stems don’t have lateral meristem.

title: simple tissue: Introduction and it's types- Epidermis, parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Simple tissues › simple tissue: introduction and it's types- epidermis, parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma — Revision note (part 1/2)

The permanent tissues are completely grown and have lost the ability of division. The division and differentiation of meristematic tissues form permanent tissues.

Permanent tissues are of two types- Simple permanent tissues and complex permanent tissues.

A simple permanent tissue is a homogenous tissue because it is formed of only one type of structurally and functionally similar mature cells that also have a common origin.

Simple permanent tissues are subdivided as:

**Guard cells and epidermal tissue:** The tissue aids in the protection and exchange of gases.

a) **Parenchyma:**

- The cells are thin-walled and oval or round in shape.
- They are loosely packed with large intracellular spaces. The cell wall is composed of hemicellulose or cellulose.
- The cells have vacuoles and very small nucleus and the protoplasm is living and dense.
- It is found in all parts of the plant and provides support to plants. It stores food and water.
- Parenchyma cells in between xylem and phloem bundles in the roots are called conjunctive tissue.

i) Parenchyma with chlorophyll performs photosynthesis is called chlorenchyma.

ii) The parenchyma cells with large air spaces to give buoyancy are called aerenchyma.

iii) An _idioblast_ is parenchymous cells that differ from neighbouring tissues.

**Functions:**They have various functions such as storage of reserves, excretory materials, pigments, and minerals. Vegetative propagation by cuttings, layering, etc is due to the meristematic potentialities of the parenchyma cells which divide and develop into buds and adventitious roots. Due to the turgid condition of parenchyma they give rigidity to the plant body.

[Figure 1] [Figure 2]

b) **Collenchyma:**

text:

- Cells are long and thick-walled while cell wall is composed of cellulose and pectin.
- It is found in the epidermis and the vascular bundle of dicot leaf.
- The cells have no or very few intercellular spaces. Presence of very few chloroplasts in the cells.

**Functions:**It provides flexible mechanical support and tensile strength to the plant organs. It allows growth and elongation of organs and prevents tearing of leaves. Allows easy bending of various parts of plants without breaking.

[Figure 3] [Figure 4]

c) **Sclerenchyma:**

- These are dead tissues, very hard and rigid in texture and commonly seen in the husk of the coconut. This term was coined by Georg Heinrich Mettenius in 1805.
- Cells are thick-walled with various size and shapes. Makes the plant hard and stiff, thickened due to lignin and no intercellular space. Safranin stains lignified elements of the tissue.
- Sclerenchyma is of two types, fibres and sclereids. Fibres usually develop from meristematic cells while sclereids form from parenchyma cells.
- The sclerenchyma tissue cells are also known as stone cells because the lignin deposition is so thick that the cell walls become strong, rigid, and impermeable to water.

**Functions:** It provides mechanical strength and rigidity to the plant body.

**Activity: Visualize Epidermis**

Structure like interconnected tubes conducts water and minerals only in upward direction.

title: biotechnology and tissue culture
text:

Biotechnology is a technique used for producing plants & animals possessing new characteristics along with their natural characteristics.

Biotechnology is a technique that focuses on improvement in living organisms by bringing about genetic changes & hybridization mainly for the welfare of human beings.

**What does biotechnology include?**

1. Techniques of genetic engineering
2. Techniques of tissue culture

**Uses of biotechnology:**

1. Cash crop production
2. Increasing the ability of crops to withstand environmental stress
3. Improvement in the variety of cash crop
4. Production of the vaccine
5. Organ transplant
6. Cancer research, diagnosis of congenital diseases
7. Production of artificial skin, cartilage, etc. in laboratories.

**Tissue Culture:**

1. ‘Ex vivo growth of cells or tissues in an aseptic and nutrient-rich medium’
2. The modern technique of farming & gardening
3. To grow and cultivate plants at home or in the garden, we must cultivate seedlings of different plants, and those seedlings must be watered regularly and nurtured properly. Fertilizers should be introduced whenever necessary.
4. Pruning is also important.
5. Measures should be taken if pest manifestation occurs.
6. With the help of tissue culture, a complete organism is developed from just a single cell or even from the tissue.
7. Nutrient & energy supply: a liquid, solid, gel-like medium that is prepared from agar.
8. A British botanist named Frederick Campion Steward showed that tissues as well as cells can be grown in ex vivo.
9. He proved this by isolating the carrot root cells and culturing the root cells in a nutrient medium that showed each cell’s ability to produce a new plant.

**Applications of biotechnology in agriculture:**
Biotechnology has allowed many changes in the agricultural management system.
1) Using biotechnology, production of new plants and animals that have new characteristics in addition to their natural ones can be done.
2) It is used in the production of cash crops, make plants withstand environmental stress and to fortify with specific vitamins.
3) Genetically engineered crops are produced by inserting new genes. These genes can have ability to pests, pathogens and chemical weedicides.
4) A better quality of crops is being produced all over the world that has increased the nutritive value.
5) High Yielding Varieties of many crops has been made like banana, maize, cotton, apple.
6) Pest-resistance has been introduced in crops like**Potato: Amflora, Tomato: Vaishali, Cotton: BT cotton.**
7)The BT cotton is resistant to bollworms.
8) The " green revolution" is achieved by the application of plant tissue culture to meet the food demands of people.
9) Golden rice is rich in vitamin A which is given to kids in Africa who have a deficiency of vitamin A in their diet.
10) Agricultural biotechnology provides a solution for plants by genetically modifying the plant's genes for cold and heat tolerance, virus resistance, herbicide tolerance etc.

**Life Cycle of Silk Moth**

[Figure 1]

•Four main stages: egg, larva, pupa & adult moth.
•Artificial incubation of eggs deposited by female moths shortens the incubation period.
•Eggs hatch out to give larvae that are released on the mulberry leaves.
•The larvae feed on the mulberry leaves for nutrition for about 3-4 days and then move towards the branches.

Larvae spins a cocoon (spherical shape) around itself which is made up of long threads.

title: telescopes
text:
Observing Space: Telescopes › Telescopes › telescopes — Revision note (part 1/3)

To see distant objects clearly in their magnified form telescope is used. The telescopes which are used to observe astronomical sources like the stars and the planets are called astronomical telescopes. Telescopes are of two types.

1. Refracting telescope – This telescope uses lenses.
2. Reflecting telescope – This uses lenses as well as mirrors.

**Refracting telescope (Optical Telescope)**

People have been making and using lenses for magnification for thousands of years. However, the first true telescopes were made in Europe in the late 16th century. These telescopes used a combination of two lenses to make distant objects appear both nearer and larger. The term _telescope was_ coined by the Italian scientist and mathematician Galileo Galilei (1564–1642). Galileo built his first telescope in 1608 and subsequently made many improvements to telescope design.

Telescopes that rely on the refraction, or bending, of light by lenses are called **refracting telescopes**, or simply _refractors_. The earliest telescopes, including Galileo’s, were all refractors. Many of the small telescopes used by amateur astronomers today are refractors. Refractors are particularly good for viewing details within our solar system, such as the surface of Earth’s moon or the rings around Saturn

**[Figure 1]**

Even though such a telescope is useful for space observations, it presents certain difficulties.

title: telescopes
text:
Observing Space: Telescopes › Telescopes › telescopes — Revision note (part 2/3)

- As we saw above, if we wish to obtain a bright image of a source by collecting the maximum possible light from it, the objective lens must be made as large as possible. However, it is very difficult to make very large lenses. Also, large lenses are very heavy and tend to get distorted.
- As the objective and eyepiece are placed at the opposite ends of the telescope, the length of the telescope also increases with an increase in the size of the lenses and the telescope becomes difficult to manage.
- The images formed by lenses have errors of colors. This is called chromatic aberration.

**Reflecting telescope:**As light rays get reflected by mirrors in these telescopes, they are called reflecting telescopes

The reflecting telescopes are mainly of two types:

- **Newtonian telescope:**light rays coming from space are reflected by the concave mirror. Before these reflected rays converge at the focus, they are deflected again by a small plane mirror. As a result, they get focused at a point lying perpendicular to the axis of the telescope’s cylinder. They pass through the eyepiece and we get a magnified image of the source.

[Figure 2]

- **Cassegrain telescope:**The Cassegrain telescope also uses a concave mirror. However, here light rays, after reflection from the concave mirror, are reflected back towards it by a small convex mirror. They pass through a hole at the centre of the concave mirror and then through the eyepiece situated at the back of the mirror. The eyepiece gives us a
magnified image of the source.

[Figure 3]

**Radio telescope:**Many heavenly objects emit radio waves in addition to visible radiation. We cannot see this radiation with our eyes. Hence, a special type of telescope is used to receive these rays. It is called a radio telescope. The radio telescope is made out of one or more dishes of a particular parabolic shape. As in optical telescopes, these dishes reflect the incident radio waves. These waves are then converged at the focus. A radio receiver is then positioned at the focal point. The information gathered by this receiver is passed on to a computer that analyses it and generates an image of the source.

[Figure 4]

GMRT has enabled scientists to study Solar System, Solar winds, Pulsar, Supernova and interstellar hydrogen clouds.

Hello, students. Today, we are going to learn a very interesting topic, that is Newton's third law of motion. Simply, we have to understand what is Newton's third law of motion. Consider a ball falls on the table. Students, in this case, ball is applying some force on the table. Also, the table is applying some force on the object, on the ball. Now, this downward force applied by the ball is known as action force, to which the force on the object is called reaction force. Thus, Newton's third law of motion comes into picture, that every action has equal and opposite reaction. That means when two objects interact, you will get force on each object. Students, here, there are some important points to remember. First, the action force and reaction force are present at the given instant. That is, only action force cannot exist. If action force is there, reaction force will be there. Also, if you notice, the action force is from the ball on the table, and reaction force is from the table on the ball, and thus, both the forces are not acting on the same object. Let's understand this with some example. The first one over here, a person is swimming in the river. The river is giving some action force, but the person is applying some reaction force. Also, a person getting off the boat. In this case, when the person is getting off the boat, the person is applying some action force, but the boat will get a reaction force. This was all about the Newton's third law of motion, but there are some important points to remember. First, action and reaction always occur in pairs.

Hello students. Today we will learn about Newton's third law of motion. Have you ever noticed that when you kick a ball, your foot feels a pushback? Newton's third law explains this perfectly. Whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object simultaneously exerts an equal and opposite force on the first. Think about pushing a heavy table while sitting on a chair with wheels. You push the table forward, but your chair moves backwards. Why? Because the table pushed you backwards with the same amount of force. If you pull the table backwards, your chair will move forward. Why? Because the table pulled you forward with the same amount of force. Motion is a conversation between two objects. To walk forward, you actually push the ground backwards. Friction is your friend here. It pushes you forward in response. The same happens in a canoe. You push the water back, and the water pushes you forward. Perhaps the most powerful example is a rocket. It doesn't push against the ground to fly. It expels gas downward at high speeds. The reaction to this downward force is an upward thrust that carries the rocket into space. If the forces are equal, why does the bullet fly so far while the gun only recoils slightly? It's all about mass. The same force acting on a tiny bullet creates huge acceleration, while on the heavy gun, the effect is much smaller. From the simplest step you take to the grandest rocket launch, Newton's third law is always in play. Every action has an equal and opposite reaction. The universe is always pushing back.

title: pH Scale and Indicators
text:
Acids, Bases and Salts › Acids, bases and salts - pH of a solution › pH Scale and indicators — Video lesson: pH Scale and Indicators (part 1/2)

Hello learners. In this video, we will learn about pH scale and indicators. How can we identify whether a substance is an acid or a base? For this, special substances called indicators are used. Indicators are substances that change color when added to acids or bases. This color change helps identify the nature of a solution. One commonly used indicator is litmus. Litmus is a natural indicator obtained from lichens. It shows different color changes in acids and bases. Blue litmus turns red in acids, while red litmus turns blue in bases. Using litmus, it is easy to determine whether a solution is acidic or basic. However, litmus has a limitation. It only tells us whether a substance is an acid or a base, but it does not indicate how strong or weak the acid or base is. To understand this, a universal indicator is used. A universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators. Instead of giving just one color change, it shows different colors for solutions of different acidic or basic strengths. Each color corresponds to a value on the pH scale. The pH scale shows how acidic or basic a solution is. The scale generally ranges from zero to 14. A pH value of seven represents a neutral solution, such as pure water. pH values less than seven represents acidic solutions. pH values greater than seven represent basic or alkaline solutions. As the pH value decreases below seven, the acidic strength increases. As the pH increases above seven, the basic strength increases. Universal indicator paper is often used to measure pH. When the paper is dipped into a solution, it changes color.

When the paper is dipped into a solution, it changes color. This color is compared with a pH color chart to estimate the pH value. The strength of acids and bases depends on the number of ions produced in an aqueous solution. Acids produce hydrogen ions, H+, in aqueous solutions, whereas bases produce hydroxyl ions, OH-. If an acid produces a large number of hydrogen ions, it is called a strong acid. If it produces fewer hydrogen ions, it is called a weak acid. For example, hydrochloric acid produces more hydrogen ions in water and is considered a strong acid, while acetic acid produces fewer hydrogen ions and is therefore a weak acid. Bases that produce a large number of hydroxide ions are called strong bases, while those producing fewer hydroxide ions are called weak bases. For example, potassium hydroxide produces more hydroxide ions in water and is considered a strong base, while ammonium hydroxide produces fewer hydroxyl ions and is therefore a weak base. They have a male and female part on the plant, and these two produce the male sporangia and female sporangia, which then combines to fertilize and produce a zygote. Cycas and Pinus are two monoecious gymnosperms. Now, dioecious gymnosperms. These plants bear male and female flowers on different sporophylls of different plants. Why is that so? Because they are flowering plant, they bear flower, and then they develop into fruit, which consist of the seed inside it. Flowers contain the reproductive organs. Now, as you can see that the flowers have the reproductive organs, anther and stigma. Now, anther has the pollen grains inside it. These pollen grains are nothing but male gametes. Angiosperm, since all the reproductive organ are present inside the flower, what happens, the pollen from anther, which is the male reproductive organ of the flower, produces pollen, which is received by the female reproductive organ in the stigma, which consist of an ovule sac or where the egg is present. This pollen passes through the pollen tube, fuses with the egg inside the ovarian sac, and there, the fertilization takes place, and all the male and female gamete, they combine to form a diploid zygote. This zygote develops into embryo, and this embryo is then enclosed inside a fruit. After the fruit is eaten or the fruit covering is degraded, the seed inside the soil germinates to form a new mature plant. Okay. That mature plant will again bear flowers, and that flower will consist of both male and female reproductive organs. So this is how the cycle goes on. Now, what is the difference between angiosperm and gymnosperm? So, in angiosperm, we can see that the male and female reproductive organs are present in a flower. So, there is anther that bears all the pollen inside it. There is stigma, style, and ovary which makes up the female reproductive organ.

We just understood that the sun gives us energy, and this energy is first utilized by the plants to make their own food. Now, this is the same energy which is going to be transferred from the plants to the different, different animals in the environment. These trophic levels, students, are represented by organisms which get their energy from a common source. Now, we can say that the common source or the ultimate source is the sun. From the sun, the energy is first utilized by the producers, meaning the green plants. So you will see they are right at the bottom, that is the lowest trophic level, or we can say the first trophic level. After producers, their energy, which is made by them by utilizing the energy coming from the sun, it is transferred to the herbivores, which can be called as the primary consumer. This is the second trophic level. The herbivores are eaten by carnivores, to be precise, primary carnivores, and we can call them the secondary consumer, and they are occupying the third trophic level. And finally, students, we have the secondary carnivore, or we can call it the tertiary consumer, occupying the fourth trophic level. concept_name: Exploring Food Chains and Food Webs
subconcept_name: Exploring Food Chains and Food Webs
title: Food chain and food Webs
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Exploring Food Chains and Food Webs › Exploring Food Chains and Food Webs — Video lesson: Food chain and food Webs (part 1/2)

Hello, students. In this session, we will learn about the food chain and the food web. In nature, organisms are connected through feeding relationships, forming a food chain. A food chain shows how energy flows from one organism to another. Each step in a food chain is called a trophic level. Food chains also represent the transfer of matter along with energy. Producers, like green plants, form the first trophic level. Herbivores or primary consumers form the second trophic level. Carnivores form the third and fourth trophic levels as secondary and tertiary consumers respectively. Decomposers act on all trophic levels by breaking down dead organisms. Let us understand this with the ecosystem examples. Food chain in a forest. Here, the green plants and trees act as producers. They are autotrophs, as they synthesize food. Producers are eaten by the primary consumers. For example, deer. Deer may be eaten by a tiger, a top carnivore. Now, look at the food chain in a pond. Aquatic plants are eaten by small insects or organisms. These are eaten by fish, which may be eaten by birds like herons. In all these examples, energy flows from producers to higher consumers. Energy flow in a food chain is unidirectional. That is, it moves only in one direction and is not recycled. However, in real ecosystems, one organism may be eaten by several different organisms. Similarly, a consumer may feed on more than one type of organism. For example, a grasshopper may be eaten by frogs, birds, or lizards. A snake may feed on frogs as well as small rodents.

concept_name: Exploring Food Chains and Food Webs
subconcept_name: Exploring Food Chains and Food Webs
title: Food chain and food Webs
text:
Energy Flow In an Ecosystem › Exploring Food Chains and Food Webs › Exploring Food Chains and Food Webs — Video lesson: Food chain and food Webs (part 2/2)

A snake may feed on frogs as well as small rodents. Because of such multiple feeding links, different food chains become interconnected. This interconnected network of food chains is called a food web. A food web is important because it provides stability to the ecosystem. If one food source decreases, organisms can switch to another food source. It ensures a continuous flow of energy in the ecosystem. It also increases the survival chances of organisms in changing conditions. An important point related to food chains and food webs is the 10% law of energy transfer. This law states that only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed to the next level. The rest of the energy is lost to the environment through heat, movement, digestion, respiration, and other life processes. Suppose green plants capture 10,000 joules of solar energy and convert it into food energy. When herbivores eat these plants, only about 10%, that is 1,000 joules, become part of the herbivore's body and is available for the next level. When secondary consumers feed on herbivores, again, only 10% of 1,000 joules, that is 100 joules, is transferred. At the next level, tertiary consumers receive only 10% of 100 joules, which is 10 joules. Because of this loss of usable energy, ecosystems cannot support many trophic levels. That is why most food chains are short and usually consist of only three or four steps. This also explains why top carnivores are fewer in number in an ecosystem. And that's all about this topic. Thank you for watching and keep learning.

Broad-spectrum antibiotics are used for pathogens which are unidentified. That is, when you talk about broad-spectrum antibiotics, these are given to patients in which the pathogen that is causing the infection is unidentified. So these antibiotics, they work on special proteins found on the pathogen, which are common to a number of pathogen, and hence can act on a variety of pathogen and hence they are called as broad-spectrum antibiotic, as their effect is on many pathogens. Now, some of the example of such broad-spectrum antibiotics include ampicillin, amoxicillin, tetracycline, and many more. After the broad-spectrum, here comes the narrow-spectrum antibiotics. Now, it is exactly opposite to the broad-spectrum. As the broad-spectrum antibiotic had effect on many pathogens, the narrow-spectrum antibiotics are very specific. They affect a particular pathogen, and this antibiotics are given to patients in which the pathogen causing the infection is identified. The antibiotics that come under narrow spectrum include penicillin, gentamicin, erythromycin, and many more. So, these are the two types of antibiotics. Now, this penicillin controls infection against Staphylococci, Clostridia, Streptococci, and many other bacteria. title: Propagation of Sound
text:
Study Of Sound › Propagation of Sound › Propagation of Sound — Video lesson: Propagation of Sound (part 1/1)

Hello students. Today, we will learn about the propagation of sound. We know sound is created by vibrations, but how does it reach us? Does it only travel through the air? Let's test the desk. When your friend scratches the surface, you can hear it through the air, but try placing your ear directly on the wood. The sound becomes clearer and louder. This proves that sound can travel efficiently through solids. What about liquids? If we submerge two spoons in a tub of water and tap them together, the sound still reaches our ears. The vibrating spoons push the water molecules, creating a path for the sound to travel. This confirms that liquids, just like solids, can act as a medium for sound. When it's air, water, or wood, sound needs a medium to travel through. We call any material that carries sound a medium. But what happens if there is no medium at all? What if you're in a vacuum? This is called the bell jar experiment. As the pump removes the air, the sound grows fainter. Once a vacuum is created, the sound vanishes entirely, even though the bell is still ringing. Without molecules to carry the vibration, sound is trapped. It cannot travel through a vacuum. That is why space is silent because outer space is a vacuum. Astronauts can't simply talk to each other in vacuum. Even if two metal objects clank together, there is no sound. They must use electronic devices to convert their voices into radio waves, which unlike sound, do not need a medium to travel. Thank you for watching and keep learning.

title: Hydrocarbons - saturated and unsaturated
text:
Carbon: An Important Element › Hydrocarbons › Saturated and Unsaturated Compounds — Video lesson: Hydrocarbons - saturated and unsaturated (part 1/2)

Hello, learners. In this video, we will learn about saturated and unsaturated carbon compounds. Carbon forms many compounds with hydrogen. Compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen are called hydrocarbons. Hydrocarbons are of two types, saturated and unsaturated. Let us first understand saturated carbon compounds. Consider ethane, which has the molecular formula C2H6. To draw its structure, the two carbon atoms are first linked by a single bond. Each carbon atom has four valencies. After forming the carbon-carbon bond, three valencies of each carbon atom remain. These remaining valencies are satisfied by bonding with hydrogen atoms. In ethane, all bonds between atoms are single bonds. The carbon compounds in which all valencies of carbon atoms are satisfied only by single bonds are called saturated compounds. These compounds are very stable and generally less reactive. Saturated hydrocarbons are also known as alkanes. Now let us look at unsaturated carbon compounds. Consider ethene with the molecular formula C2H4. Two carbon atoms are first linked together. Each carbon atom then forms bonds with two hydrogen atoms. After bonding with hydrogen, one valency on each carbon atom remains unsatisfied. These remaining valencies are satisfied by sharing another pair of electrons between the two carbon atoms, resulting in a double bond. The molecular formula of ethyne is C2H2. Here, two carbon atoms are joined together, and each carbon atom forms a bond with one hydrogen atom.

title: Hydrocarbons - saturated and unsaturated
text:
Carbon: An Important Element › Hydrocarbons › Saturated and Unsaturated Compounds — Video lesson: Hydrocarbons - saturated and unsaturated (part 2/2)

Here, two carbon atoms are joined together, and each carbon atom forms a bond with one hydrogen atom. The remaining valencies of the carbon atoms are satisfied by sharing additional pairs of electrons with each other. As a result, a triple bond is formed between the two carbon atoms. Compounds that contain double or triple bonds between carbon atoms are called unsaturated compounds. Unsaturated hydrocarbons containing double bonds are called alkenes, while those containing triple bonds are called alkynes. These compounds are usually more reactive than saturated compounds. That's all with this video. Thanks for watching and keep learning.

Like, in the purines and pyrimidines, cytosine always pairs with guanine due to its chemical structure, and adenine always pairs with thymine and forms two hydrogen bonds between them, whereas the cytosine and guanine form three hydrogen bonds. A monohybrid cross is a cross between two individuals having homozygous genotypes, which result in the formation of an opposite phenotype for a certain genetic trait. Also, this was put forth by Gregor Mendel. He is known as the father of genetics. Mendel worked on pea plants and observed the patterns of inheritance from one generation to other. So for this, he derived this method called as monohybrid cross. In this monohybrid cross, there was cross between two individuals with a single pair of contrasting characters were observed, that is height of the plant. So here, if you see, there are two alleles that is capital T, capital T, which stand for the tall plant, whereas the small t, small t, is representing the dwarf plant. Firstly, students, the very first law, that is the law of dominance. Let us see what this law states. It states that when two alternative forms of trait or character are present in an organism, only one factor is expressed in the F1 progeny, and this factor which was expressed is considered as dominant. While the other one, which remains masked, is called recessive. Now students, the recessive character can only express when the pair consists of both recessive characters. Then it will be called as a homozygous recessive. One example is the allele for tallness is dominant over the allele for dwarfism. Take a look at this image, students. Let us say the tall plant has the genotype big T, small t. Let us say the tall plant is homozygous dominant, meaning it has the genotype big T, big T. Whereas the dwarf plant can only have one genotype that is small t, small t. Now, if we cross these two plants in the F1 generation, all the plants will have the same genotype that is big T, small t. But I'm sure all of you must be knowing that even though their genotype is big T, small t, the phenotype is going to be tall. All the plants in the F1 generation were tall. This is because the big T, that is the trait or the allele for tallness, is dominant.

This is because the big T, that is the trait or the allele for tallness, is dominant. Therefore, it was the only one which got expressed in the F1 generation. This, students, is basically the law of dominance. And remember, students, this law was not universally applicable. Meaning what? There were some exceptions to this law. Moving on, now let us talk about the second law. That is the law of segregation of genes. This law states that the alleles do not show any blending or mixing, and both the characters are restored as such in the F2 generation, though one of these is not seen in the F1 generation. Students, the gametes combine together by fusion at the time of zygote formation, but the characters or the alleles do not mix or blend. Let us take an example of the flower color. Now students, as per Mendel's experiment, he had observed that the violet color flower was the dominant character, whereas white flower was recessive. So now students in the F1 generation, if the parents were having violet and white flowers, in the F1 generation, what Mendel expected was a flower which is neither violet nor white, something in between. That is, let us say, light violet color. But what he found out was that in the F1 generation, all the flowers were violet. So students, he did another cross that is the F2 generation. In the F2 generation, he found that three of the plants had violet-colored flowers, whereas there was one plant which had white-colored flowers. Now students, this basically proves the law of segregation of genes. It means that the white color flower was not lost.

But in the F2 generation, it again reappeared. So these alleles or the characters do not blend. Moving on students, this brings us to the last of Mendel's law, that is the law of independent assortment. Let us see what this law states. It states that when two pairs of traits are present in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of character is independent of the other pair of characters at the time of gametogenesis. Now students, Mendel proposed this law on the basis of the results of dihybrid cross, where the inheritance of two traits was considered at the same time. Take a look at the images. title: Muscular Tissue
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Types of animal tissues › muscular tissue — Video lesson: Muscular Tissue (part 1/10)

Hello, students, and welcome to another topic of biology, that is muscular tissue. So students, let us first go through what all we'll be learning in this particular topic. We will be studying about the introduction to the muscular system, and we will be also learning about the different types of muscles which are found in the human body. So let us begin. Students, muscular tissues are made up of specialized cells which have unique properties. These properties are contractility and electric excitability. Basically, students, when an electrical impulse reaches a muscle, the muscle can contract. Now students, this contractility is due to the presence of certain special protein filaments, which are myosin and actin. We will be discussing them in detail in a few moments. Now students, the action of muscles is very much necessary for movement. For example, any kind of movement which you are doing on your own. And other than that, all the different kinds of movement which is occurring inside a human body is all due to the muscles. Students, the electrical excitability of the muscles is due to the potential difference across the plasma membrane. Now students, remember one thing, that muscular tissue are mesodermal in origin, but there is an exception. There are a few muscles which are derived from the embryonic ectoderm. Let us see the examples. The iris muscles of the eye, then the muscles of the salivary gland, the muscles of the sweat gland, and the mammary glands are derived from the ectoderm. Rest, all of the muscles are mesodermal in origin.

title: Muscular Tissue
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Types of animal tissues › muscular tissue — Video lesson: Muscular Tissue (part 2/10)

Rest, all of the muscles are mesodermal in origin. Now students, let us talk a bit more about muscles. Muscles are basically bundles of fibers that can contract and relax. As you can see in the image, the same muscle bundle is shown in the contracted form and then it is shown in the relaxed form. Students, muscles are attached to bones via connections called as tendons. Remember this simple rule. A muscle will be connected to a bone by a tendon, whereas a bone will be connected to another bone by something called as ligaments. So remember, students, muscle to bone, tendons, bone to bone, ligaments. Moving on, there are more than 600 muscles which are present in the human body, and together they contribute almost 40% of the total body weight of a healthy human adult. Students, for example, there are as many as 30 muscles which are present just in our face, and these muscles help us give various expressions like fear, sadness, happiness, et cetera. Moving on, students. Now let us discuss the types of muscles. The first one are called as the striated muscles, which are also known as skeletal or voluntary muscles. Students, these muscles are cylindrical, unbranched, and multinucleated. You can see that there are so many nuclei present in a small space. Students, these have primary and secondary bundles wherein muscle fibers lie parallel in the connective tissue, as you can see very nicely in the image. Other than this, students, these muscles are under our voluntary control. That is, they are controlled by the central nervous system.

title: Muscular Tissue
text:

That is, they are controlled by the central nervous system. Basically, whatever I am doing right now, I am moving my lips, I am moving my head, all of these movements are controlled voluntarily by me, and these are being controlled by the striated muscles. Moving on students, these muscles are found in the limbs, body wall, tongue, pharynx, and also the beginning of the esophagus. I am only saying the beginning of the esophagus because swallowing the food is voluntary, but once you swallow the food, the further movement of the food down the esophagus is completely involuntary. Now students, the myofibrils which are present inside the muscles are the structures which contain the contractile apparatus, and these contain transverse striation of alternate dark and light bands. I'm sure the last two sentences have confused you. Students, don't fear, we are going to talk about this in detail in just a few moments. Now let us study the structure of skeletal muscles. Here you have a beautiful diagram showing you the actual structure of a muscle. Muscle consists of large number of fasciculi, which are wrapped by connective tissue sheath called as the epimysium or the fascia. Now students, each of the fasciculus is covered by perimysium and consists of many, many myofibers. Now students, let us see the flow of things. You have a muscle here Now, each muscle is itself made up of a bundle of muscle fibers called a fascicle. Now, each fascicle is made up of muscle fibers, which are basically the muscle cells.

title: Muscular Tissue
text:

Now, each fascicle is made up of muscle fibers, which are basically the muscle cells. And students, each muscle fiber is further made up of an even smaller unit called the myofibril. Students, inside these myofibrils is the contractile apparatus. Now, each muscle fiber is a syncytial fiber that contains several nuclei. I use the word syncytial because a syncytium is a multinucleated arrangement, which you can see very nicely in the given diagram. Students, cell membrane is called sarcolemma instead of plasmalemma, and it contains sarcoplasm instead of cytoplasm. Students, it is the same kind of structure, just the names are different in case of a muscle. Now, this contains a large number of myofibrils, which are arranged parallel to each other. I repeat again, students, the sarcoplasm contains a large number of myofibrils, which are arranged parallel to each other. And each myofibril is made up of repeated functional units, which you can see named in the diagram as sarcomere. Students, remember, a muscle is made up of muscle fiber or a muscle cell, but the functional unit of a muscle is not the muscle fiber. It is actually these units called sarcomeres. Moving on, students. Let us now focus on the structure of these functional units of muscles called sarcomeres. Take a look at the diagram. We have two parts of the diagram, part A and part B. Now, students, each sarcomere has a dark band called anisotropic or A band in the center. To look at that, just view the part B of the given image. You will see that there is a dark band called A.

You will see that there is a dark band called A. But do you notice at the center of the dark band, there is a light zone, which is called the H zone or the Henson's zone. Students, you can locate the same Henson's zone in the part A of the diagram. Do you see the two Z lines? Yes. Now, in between that lies one sarcomere. At the center of the sarcomere, do you see a light zone? Students, that is the H zone. And surrounding the H zone, the dark part is the anisotropic band or the A band. Moving on, in the center of the H zone, you will see there is a line that is called the M line. Moving on, students. The A bands are made up of two filaments. Now, look at the part A of the diagram. You will see that parallelly arranged, there are two filaments. One filament is thick and the other filament is thinner, and they are arranged one below the other. Students, the thicker filaments are the myosin filaments, whereas the thinner filaments are the actin filaments. Now, focus only on the A band. You will see that in this part, the actin filaments are overlapped. You will see that in this part, there are both actin and myosin filaments alternatively. Now, on either side of the A band, there is a light region, or it is the light band, also called the isotropic band or the I band. If you notice, in this part, there are only thin filaments, and thick myosin filaments are absent. This is the reason this part or this band appears to be light. Moving on, students. Myosin is thick and dark-colored, while actin filaments are thin and light-colored.

Myosin is thick and dark-colored, while actin filaments are thin and light-colored. Now, students, adjacent light bands are separated by another line called the Z line. And let me tell you, the part of the myofibril which lies between two Z lines is one sarcomere, which is the functional unit of a muscle. Moving on, students. Dark and light bands on neighboring myofibrils correspond with each other. Next, let us talk about the functions of striated muscles. Students, striated muscles are completely voluntary and contract rapidly, but they also get fatigued very soon. You must have noticed this when you play or run or do any kind of physical activity for a long time. Eventually, the muscles start to get fatigued or tired, and they even start to pain. Students, these striated muscles are responsible for bringing the movement of the bones. And let us now discuss the red and white muscles. This is another way of classifying the striated muscles. Red muscles contain very high amount of myoglobin. Students, white muscles, on the other hand, contain very low amount of myoglobin. Now, you must be thinking What exactly is myoglobin? Let me tell you, students, myoglobin is an iron-containing red-colored pigment, which is found only in muscles. Students, it consists of one heme and one polypeptide chain, and therefore, it can only carry one molecule of oxygen. Basically, what I'm saying is, muscles can obtain oxygen from two sources: the common source that is hemoglobin, and the special source that is myoglobin.

title: Muscular Tissue

Basically, what I'm saying is, muscles can obtain oxygen from two sources: the common source that is hemoglobin, and the special source that is myoglobin. And as mentioned before, red muscles contain high amount of myoglobin as compared to the white muscles. Moving on, students. Now let us discuss the second type of muscles, which are the unstriated or the smooth muscles, which are also called as involuntary muscles. Students, these are elongated and spindle-shaped. As you can see, the myofibrils lie parallel to an imaginary long axis, and these are not controlled by the central nervous system. Meaning, they are controlled by the autonomic nervous system, making them completely involuntary. That is, these muscles are not under our own control. Students, the fibers are unbranched and have single nucleus at the center. Also, sarcoplasm contains myofibrils, which contain contractile proteins like actin and myosin. But one point of difference between-- But students, in unstriated muscles, the number of myosin is less as compared to actin. Moving on, students. The striations, as you can see, are not at all present, and that is the reason these are called as smooth muscles or unstriated muscles. Also, these undergo slow and sustained involuntary contractions, and they are found in the walls of many visceral organs as well as the walls of the blood vessels. Students, these are the muscles which form longitudinal muscles or circular muscles of any organ. Moving on, students. Now, smooth muscles are themselves divided into two types.

title: Muscular Tissue
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Types of animal tissues › muscular tissue — Video lesson: Muscular Tissue (part 8/10)

Now, smooth muscles are themselves divided into two types. Single unit smooth muscle, in which case, all the muscles in sheet contract simultaneously as one. Whereas, the other type are multi-unit smooth muscles, in which fibers present in the muscle contract more or less independently. That is, the fibers in a particular muscle do not contract or relax at the same time. Some of them might contract, while at the same time, some of them might relax. That is basically what I mean when I say the fibers contract more or less independently. Now, this brings us to the functions of the unstriated muscles. Students, these are the muscles which bring about the opening and closing of the different apertures in the human body. Also, they carry out peristalsis, that is the movement of food down the elementary canal. Other than this, the stomach muscles are required for churning of the food. Also, students, there are smooth muscles present in the urinary bladder, which contract on their own, making sure that the urine is thrown out into the urethra and then outside. Other than this, these muscles, unlike striated muscles, do not get fatigued easily. Next, students, we learn about the last type of muscles of the human body, which are the cardiac muscles. The name itself tells us that these muscles are present in the heart. And students, they are cylindrical as well as branched. Students, these are striated, as you can see in the diagram, but they are not voluntary. So remember, students, striated muscles are voluntary. Unstriated muscles are involuntary.

title: Muscular Tissue

Unstriated muscles are involuntary. But cardiac muscles are striated, but still they are involuntary. Students, the cells of cardiac muscles are uninucleate, unlike the striated muscles. And these are also controlled by the autonomic nervous system. Moving on, students. Sarcolemma is not distinct, and adjacent muscle fibers join together to give branched appearance to the tissue. Students, one thing to remember here is that the points of adhesion between the muscle fibers are formed by transverse thickening of the sarcolemma, and this transverse thickening is called as intercalated disk. Basically, students, this makes sure that all the muscles contract simultaneously, which is of utmost importance in the heart. Moving on, students. The mammalian heart is myogenic. Meaning, the impulse for contraction of the heart originates in the heart itself. Students, there are some specialized muscle fibers in the heart which have the ability to generate their own impulse. Unlike this, there are cardiac muscles which need constant neural stimulus to initiate contraction. In such cases, the heart is called as a neurogenic heart, which is seen in insects like cockroach. Moving on, students. Let us study the functions of cardiac muscles. As you must have guessed already, it forms the myocardium of the heart wall and, students, the contraction and relaxation of the cardiac muscles helps us to pump blood throughout the human body. Also, these muscles are completely immune to fatigue. That is, as long as a human is alive, these muscles will never, ever get tired.

So plants show the growth which is indefinite or unlimited growth because they will be growing constantly throughout their life. Whereas animal growth is very much defined. For plant growth, the growth occurs majorly at the shoot and the two root tip region. But for the animal, the growth can occur by cell division in most of the time, all of the different types of tissues. Also, you would observe the size increases often by increase in the cells upon by absorbing water. Whereas, for animal growth, the size increase is there, but initially, which is increasing the cell number by cell division. Plant growth. Plant cells can differentiate into different types of cell types here after the division, whereas animal cells, only stem cells can show this kind of differentiation mechanism for different types of cell. Other animal cells are going to function remain as fixed. Activity.

Activity. So to understand this mechanism in detail, we are going to do an activity. We are going to take two jars and label them as A and B. And onto those jars, we are going to add some water, and now place onion onto each of the jar. So here we have to make sure that the roots of the onions are dipped in water. We will measure the length of the onion root of both the onions for three days. After three days, we will cut about one centimeter of the onion root only in the flask B. Now we will measure the length of the onion root of both the onions for the following five days. Then we are going to note down our observations. So what do we observe here is for the flask A, it was observed it has longer roots on to day one and on to day two. For flask A, on day one, the length of the roots was 0.25 centimeters, whereas for day two, it was 0.6. For day three, it was 1.3. For day three, it was 1.2. For day four, it was 1.7. And for day five, it was 2.0. Whereas for flask B, it was 0.3 for day one, 0.7 for day two. At day three, we have 1.4. After cutting, it was 0.4 left. Day four was 0.45, and day six was 0.6. So this is majorly because of a special type of tissue which is present over there, known as the meristematic tissue. It is majorly present under the tip of the onion roots. The meristematic tissue has a capacity of dividing this organism into any type of the cell, and thereby helps for the growth of the roots efficiently, and it helps to grow the roots at a faster rate. So flask B shows the shorter roots because there is no meristematic tissue left.

So flask B shows the shorter roots because there is no meristematic tissue left. This is because the onion tips were cut and that is why the meristematic tissue was also being cut off. So this would be allocated only into specific regions because the growth cannot happen at any part of the plant. It would be only into specific areas. So the meristematic tissues over here, they are highly active because they are dividing cells, constantly dividing, and the rate of cell division is very faster, so which helps for the growth of the plant also faster. So growth occurs in the meristematic tissue only, and they are present into various areas such as apical or intercalary. Depending upon the location, the cell division would be happening and the growth would be happening into the specific areas. It comprise of cells with cytoplasm, which is very thick, and it has a conspicuous nucleus and a cell wall. The cells are together compactly packed into this region. So if it is a meristematic tissue, then the vacuoles would be absent into this tissue. So we have different types of meristems such as depending upon the location, we have apical meristem that is present under the apex of the plant. Then we have intercalary meristem that is present in between two meristems. And we have lateral meristem, which is present onto the sides because not only the plant needs to grow with the length of the tree, but it has to also grow into the width that is into the surrounding region. So the apical meristem is located at the apex of the root and the shoot tip that is into the stem region.

title: Nervous Tissue
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Types of animal tissues › understanding nervous tissue — Video lesson: Nervous Tissue (part 1/2)

Hello everyone. In this video, we are going to understand nervous tissue. Now, think about this for a moment. How do you immediately pull your hand away after touching something hot, even before you consciously think about it? Well, this function is controlled by a specialized tissue called nervous tissue, which is a part of the nervous system. The nervous system forms the body's communication and coordination system. It helps different parts of the body stay connected and work together in a coordinated manner. At the center of the system is the brain, which acts as the control center. It helps in thinking, memory, learning, decision-making, and coordination. Along with the spinal cord and nerves, it ensures that messages travel rapidly throughout the body. For example, when you exercise, your muscles need more oxygen. The brain senses this, sends signals to the heart, causing it to beat faster. This helps deliver more oxygen to the body. Now let's understand the cells that make up nervous tissue. These cells are called neurons or nerve cells. Neurons are specialized cells that are designed to receive and transmit messages in the form of nerve impulses. If we look at the structure of the neuron, we will notice three main parts. First is the cell body. This is the main part of the neuron and contains the nucleus. The cell body controls the activities of the neuron and keeps the cell alive. Now notice the short branched extension arising from the cell body. They are called dendrites.

title: Nervous Tissue
text:
Introduction to Biotechnology › Types of animal tissues › understanding nervous tissue — Video lesson: Nervous Tissue (part 2/2)

They are called dendrites. The dendrites receive signals from other neurons or from sensory receptors and carry those signals towards the cell body. Now, observe this long fiber-like structure extending from the cell body. This is called the axon. The axon carries nerve impulses away from the cell body to another neuron, muscle, or gland. At the end of the axon, there are branched endings called axon terminals. These terminals pass the message to the next neuron through small junctions called synapses. Now, even though these signals are electrical in nature, neurons can transmit them extremely fast. That is why the body can respond almost instantly to stimuli. To summarize, nervous tissue controls coordination and communication in the body. Its specialized cells, called neurons, receive, process, and transmit signals. The cell body contains the nucleus of the neuron. Dendrites receive messages, and the axon carries them forward. And that's the complete picture of neurons. Thank you for watching and keep learning.

The displacement is obtained by finding the shortest distance between the inital and final positions. In this case it is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle.

Q: A ball is dropped vertically from a height d above the ground. It hits the ground and bounces up vertically to a height d/2. Neglecting subsequent motion and air resistance, its velocity varies with the height above the ground is (options not available)
Explanation: Let’s break the motion into two parts:

1. Falling from height d to the ground:

The ball starts from rest (initial velocity = 0).

As it falls under gravity, its speed increases.

When it reaches the ground, it has maximum speed.

The relationship between velocity (v) and height (h) is given by this equation from physics:
v = √[2g(d − h)]

This means: as h (height above the ground) decreases, v increases.

2. Bouncing back to height d/2:

After hitting the ground, it bounces up but not as high — only up to d/2.

While rising, the ball slows down due to gravity.

It starts with maximum speed and gradually comes to rest at the highest point (d/2).

Again, the relationship is:

$v=\sqrt{2g(d/2-h)}$

About the Graph (Option 1):

The x-axis shows height h above the ground.

The y-axis shows velocity v.

In the falling part (from height d to 0), the curve goes downward, showing increasing speed in the downward direction (often shown as negative velocity).

In the rising part (from ground to d/2), the curve goes upward, showing decreasing speed until it stops at height d/2.

The graph is shaped like a smooth curve (not a straight line), because the relation between v and h involves a square root. The left half of the curve represents falling (velocity increasing in the negative direction), and the right half represents rising (velocity decreasing in the positive direction).

Q: Which of the following causes acceleration? (options not available)
Explanation: Gravity, friction, and forces from other objects can all cause acceleration.

Gravity is a force that acts on all objects with mass. It pulls objects towards the center of mass of other objects. The acceleration due to gravity is approximately 9.81 m/s² on Earth.
Friction is a force that resists the motion of two surfaces in contact. It can cause objects to slow down or stop moving. However, friction can also cause acceleration if it is acting in the opposite direction of the object's motion. For example, when you step on the brakes in a car, friction between the brake pads and the rotors causes the car to accelerate in the negative direction, which means it slows down.
Forces from other objects can also cause acceleration. For example, if you push a book across a table, the force of your hand is causing the book to accelerate.

Q: The displacement - time graph for two particles A and B are straight lines inclined at angles of $30^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$ with the time axis. The ratio of velocities ${v}_{a}:{v}_{b}$ is (options not available)
Explanation: In a displacement-time graph, the slope of the line represents the velocity of the object. A straight line indicates constant velocity. The steeper the slope, the greater the magnitude of the velocity.
Relating Slope to Angles:
The slope of a line is mathematically defined as the tangent of the angle it makes with the horizontal axis (in this case, the time axis).
* For particle A, the angle with the time axis is $30^{\circ}$. Therefore, the velocity of A (${v}_{a}$) is proportional to $\tan(30^{\circ}).$
* For particle B, the angle with the time axis is $60^{\circ}.$ Therefore, the velocity of B (${v}_{b}$) is proportional to $\tan(60^{\circ}).$
Calculating the Ratio of Velocities (${v}_{a}:{v}_{b}$):
The ratio of their velocities will be the ratio of the tangents of their respective angles:
$\frac{{v}_{a}}{{v}_{b}}=\frac{\tan(30^{\circ})}{\tan(60^{\circ})}$
$weknow:\ \tan(30^{\circ})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}*\ \tan(60^{\circ})=\sqrt{3}$
Substitute these values into the ratio:
$\frac{{v}_{a}}{{v}_{b}}=\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{\sqrt{3}}$
To simplify this, we can multiply the numerator by the reciprocal of the denominator:
$\frac{{v}_{a}}{{v}_{b}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\times\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\ \frac{{v}_{a}}{{v}_{b}}=\frac{1}{3}$
Therefore, the ratio of the velocities${v}_{a}:{v}_{b}is1:3.$

Q: The speed of a body moving with uniform acceleration is $u$. This speed is doubled while covering a distance $S$. When it covers an additional distance $S$, its speed would become (options not available)
Explanation: As we know,

${v}^{2}={u}^{2}+2aS\ ⇒{\left(2u\right)}^{2}={u}^{2}+2aS\ ⇒2aS=3{u}^{2}$

Now, after covering an additional distance $'S'$, if velocity becomes $'v'$, then,

${v}^{2}={u}^{2}+2a\left(2S\right)\ ={u}^{2}+4as\ ={u}^{2}+6{u}^{2}\ =7{u}^{2}\ ∴v=\sqrt{7}u$

Q: A parachutist bails out from an aeroplane and after dropping through a distance of $20m$ opens the parachute and decelerates $1m/{s}^{2}$. If she reaches the ground with a speed of 1m/s, how long is she in the air? At what height did she bailout from the plane? (Take $g=10m/{s}^{2}$) (options not available)
Explanation: When the parachutist drops for the first 20m

Let the initial velocity be $u=0$

Distance, $S=20m$

Acceleration, $a=g=$$10m/{s}^{2}$

Time, $t={t}_{1}$

${v}^{2}={u}^{2}+2as\ =0+(2\times10\times20)\ =400\ v=20m/s$

$v=u+at\ 20=0+10\times{t}_{1}\ {t}_{1}=\frac{20}{10}=2s$

Now the final velocity after the drop at $20m$ is the initial velocity for the rest of the ball

Let the initial velocity be $u=20m/s$

Acceleration, $a=$ $-1m/{s}^{2}$

Let the final velocity, $v=1m/s$

$t={t}_{2}$

$v=u+at\ 1=20+(-1)\times{t}_{2}\ {t}_{2}=19s$

Total time the parachutist is in the air

$T={t}_{1}+{t}_{2}\ =2+19\ =21s$

Height through which the parachutist has fallen during the second half of the fall is given by

${v}^{2}-{u}^{2}=2as\ {1}^{2}-{20}^{2}=2\times-2\timess\ s=100m$

The height at which the parachutist bailed out = $20+100=120m$

Q: On a foggy day two cars are approaching each other on a straight road with speed $20m/s$ and $15m/s$. The drivers of the cars spot each other when they were $60m$apart. Both of them applied brakes retarding their cars at the rate of $6m/{s}^{2}$. At what distance they will avert collision under these conditions. (options not available)
Explanation: For the first car:

Let the initial velocity be $u=20m/s$

Let the final velocity be $v=0$

Acceleration, $a=-6m/{s}^{2}$

Distance, $S={S}_{1}$

${v}^{2}={u}^{2}+2aS\ 0={20}^{2}+2\times(-6)\times{S}_{1}\ {S}_{1}=\frac{400}{12}=33.33m$

For the second car:

Let the initial velocity be $u=15m/s$

Let the final velocity be $v=0$

Acceleration, $a=-6m/{s}^{2}$

Distance, $S={S}_{2}$

${v}^{2}={u}^{2}+2aS\ 0={15}^{2}+2\times(-6)\times{S}_{2}\ {S}_{2}=\frac{225}{12}=18.75m$

Total distance covered by two cars = $33.33+18.75=52.08m$

The collision will be averted at $52.08m$as this distance is less than the initial distance between two cars.

Q: Is centrifugal force a real force? (options not available)
Explanation: Centrifugal force is not a real force in the context of an inertial (non-accelerating) frame of reference. It is an apparent force that appears to act outward on an object moving in a circular path when observed from a rotating frame of reference. This apparent force arises due to the object's inertia, which tends to keep it moving in a straight line (as per Newton's first law of motion).

In reality, the force acting on the object is the centripetal force, which is directed inward toward the center of the circular path and is responsible for keeping the object in circular motion. Centrifugal force is simply a result of analyzing the motion from a rotating perspective.

Q: The normal reaction on a body due to surface always acts (options not available)

Explanation:

The normal reaction force is a contact force exerted by a surface on a body in contact with it. It acts perpendicular to the surface at the point of contact, irrespective of the orientation of the surface.

The incorrect options are explained as follows:

Vertically upwards: This is incorrect because the normal force is not always vertical. It depends on the orientation of the surface. For example, on an inclined plane, the normal force acts perpendicular to the plane, not vertically upward.

Opposite to the external forces: This is incorrect because the normal force only balances the component of the external force perpendicular to the surface. It does not oppose all external forces.

Horizontally opposite to the motion: This is incorrect because the normal force is unrelated to the direction of motion. It acts perpendicular to the surface regardless of the motion's direction.

Q: A bus moves with a uniform acceleration of $0.1{ms}^{-2}$ for two minutes after starting from rest. What will be the distance travelled by the bus? If it moves with a uniform acceleration of $4{ms}^{-2}$, how much time will it take to cover a distance of $128m$? (options not available)
Explanation: Given:

In the first case,

Acceleration, $a=0.1{ms}^{-2}$

Time, $t=2min=120s$

Initial velocity, $u=0{ms}^{-1}$

From the second equation of motion we have,

$\begin{matrix} s=ut+\frac{1}{2}{at}^{2} \\ =(0\times120s)+\frac{1}{2}\left(0.1{ms}^{-2}\right)\times(120s{)}^{2} \\ =720m \end{matrix}$

Distance travelled by bus is $720m$.

In second case, acceleration $a=4{ms}^{-2}$ ; distance, $s=128m$; initial velocity, $u=0{ms}^{-1}$

From the second equation of motion we have,

$\begin{matrix} s=ut+\frac{1}{2}{at}^{2} \\ 128m=(0\timest)+\frac{1}{2}\left(4{ms}^{-2}\right)\times(t{)}^{2} \\ 128=2{t}^{2} \\ \frac{128}{2}={t}^{2} \\ {t}^{2}=64 \\ t=\sqrt{64} \\ t=8s \end{matrix}$

Thus, the body takes $8s$ to cover a distance of $128m$.

Explanation: Newton's third law of motion states that when two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other. This means that if object A exerts a force on object B, object B simultaneously exerts a force of equal magnitude but in the opposite direction on object A. These forces are often referred to as "action-reaction pairs."

The incorrect options are explained as follows:

Newton's first law of motion: This law states that an object will remain at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force (inertia). It does not describe the action-reaction relationship.

Newton's second law of motion: This law relates the force applied to an object and its acceleration $(F=ma)$. It does not describe the equal and opposite reaction principle.

Q: In an Olympic skating event, a male skater of mass$65kg$pushes a female skater of mass$45kg$, which causes her to accelerate at a rate of $2.0{ms}^{-2}$. What will be the acceleration of the male skater? What is the direction of his acceleration? (options not available)
Explanation: [Figure 1]

Consider two free bodies of $65kg$ and $45kg$.

Given: ${F}_{mf}=$Force of the male exerted on a female.

${a}_{f}=2.0{ms}^{-2}$

where ${a}_{f}$ is the acceleration of female

${F}_{fm}=$Force of the female exerted on male.

${a}_{m}=$Acceleration of male.

According to Newton's third law of motion, for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. Hence the force exerted on a female is equal to the force exerted by a female on male.

${F}_{mf}={F}_{fm}$$=45(2)=90N$

As we know, ${F}_{mf}={F}_{fm}$

${F}_{mf}={m}_{m}{a}_{m}$

${a}_{m}=\frac{{F}_{mf}}{{m}_{m}}$

${a}_{m}=\frac{90}{65}$

${a}_{m}=1.4{ms}^{-2}$

Explanation: According to Newton's third law, when the body exerts a force on the table (action), the table exerts an equal and opposite force on the body (reaction). These forces are called action-reaction pairs.

The action force is the gravitational force exerted by the body on the table. This is the weight of the body, calculated as:

$=40\times980\ =39200dyne$

The reaction force is the normal force exerted by the table on the body. According to Newton's third law, this force is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the action force. Therefore:

$ReactionForce=39200dyne$.

Q: Assertion: The force that pushes you upward after you hit the trampoline comes from the elastic potential energy stored in the trampoline.
Reason: The trampoline deforms when you land, and as it returns to its original shape, it exerts an upward force on you. (options not available)
Explanation: When you jump on a trampoline and land on it, the trampoline surface stretches downward due to your weight and the force of your fall. This stretching is a form of deformation, during which the trampoline stores energy in the form of elastic potential energy. This is similar to what happens when you compress a spring.

As the trampoline returns to its original shape (bounces back), it releases this stored elastic potential energy. This released energy turns into kinetic energy, which pushes you upward with a force. This is the action-reaction pair: you push down, the trampoline pushes up. The reason directly explains how the trampoline behaves when deformed, and that behavior causes the upward force mentioned in the assertion.

The incorrect options are explained as follows:

Newton's 1st law of motion: This law deals with the inertia of an object, stating that an object will remain at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force. While it explains the tendency of a bird to remain in motion, it does not directly explain how a bird flies.

Newton's 2nd law of motion: This law relates force, mass, and acceleration (F = ma). While it applies to the bird's movement, it does not specifically explain how flight is achieved.

Newton's law of gravitation: This law describes the force of attraction between two masses, such as the Earth and the bird. While gravity affects the bird's flight, it does not explain the mechanism of flight itself. The bird stays airborne by pushing air downwards, which is explained by Newton's 3rd law.

title: newton’s third law of motion

Q: The force of action and reaction are equal and opposite but the motion of the body is not same because (options not available)
Explanation: According to Newton's third law of motion, when two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other. These forces are called action-reaction pairs. However, these forces do not act on the same object; they act on two different objects. This is why the motion of the two objects may not be the same.

The incorrect options are explained as follows:

Both action and reaction act on the same body in same direction: This is incorrect because action and reaction forces are never applied to the same body. They always act on two different bodies, which is a fundamental aspect of Newton's third law.

Both action and reaction act on the same body in opposite direction: This is also incorrect because the action and reaction forces do not act on the same body. They act on different objects, and therefore, the same body cannot experience both action and reaction forces.

title: newton’s third law of motion
text:
Laws of Motion › Newton’s third law of motion › newton’s third law of motion — Practice question

Q: A small boat of mass $200,\text{kg}$ is floating at rest in a lake. A person of mass $50,\text{kg}$ on the boat jumps horizontally off the back of the boat with an initial velocity of $4,\text{m/s}$relative to the water. Assuming there is negligible water resistance, what is the velocity of the boat immediately after the person jumps? Also, what is the total kinetic energy of the person-boat system after the jump? (options not available)
Explanation: Part 1: Velocity of the boat
Initially, the total momentum of the system (boat + person) is zero because both are at rest.
Initial momentum $({p}_{i})=({m}_{boat}+{m}_{person})\times0=0$
After the person jumps, let the velocity of the person relative to the water be ${v}_{p}=4\text{m/s}$ and the velocity of the boat relative to the water be${v}_{b}$. According to the conservation of momentum, the total momentum after the jump must also be zero.
Final momentum$({p}_{f})=({m}_{person}\times{v}_{p})+({m}_{boat}\times{v}_{b})$
Setting initial momentum equal to final momentum:
$0=(50\text{kg}\times4\text{m/s})+(200\text{kg}\times{v}_{b})\ 0=200\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}+200\text{kg}\times{v}_{b}\ -200\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}=200\text{kg}\times{v}_{b}\ {v}_{b}=\frac{-200\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}}{200\text{kg}}\ {v}_{b}=-1\text{m/s}$
The negative sign indicates that the velocity of the boat is in the opposite direction to the velocity of the person's jump.
Therefore, the velocity of the boat immediately after the person jumps is $1\text{m/s}$ in the opposite direction to the jump.
Correct Answer for boat's velocity: $1\text{m/s}$ in the opposite direction to the jump
Part 2: Total kinetic energy of the person-boat system
The kinetic energy (KE) of an object is given by the formula:
$KE=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}\ Kineticenergyoftheperson(K{E}_{p}):\ K{E}_{p}=\frac{1}{2}\times50\text{kg}\times(4\text{m/s}{)}^{2}⇒K{E}_{p}=\frac{1}{2}\times50\text{kg}\times16{\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2}\ K{E}_{p}=25\text{kg}\times16{\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2}\ K{E}_{p}=400\text{J}$
Kinetic energy of the boat ($K{E}_{b}$):
$K{E}_{b}=\frac{1}{2}\times200,\text{kg}\times(-1,\text{m/s}{)}^{2}⇒K{E}_{b}=\frac{1}{2}\times200,\text{kg}\times1,{\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2}\ K{E}_{b}=100\text{kg}\times1{\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2}\ K{E}_{b}=100\text{J}\ Totalkineticenergyofthesystem(K{E}_{total})=K{E}_{p}+K{E}_{b}\ K{E}_{total}=400\text{J}+100\text{J}\ K{E}_{total}=500\text{J}$

Q: Assertion: When you bounce on a trampoline, the trampoline's elastic energy is responsible for pushing you back up.
Reason: The elastic potential energy is stored in the trampoline as you land, which is then released to push you upwards. (options not available)
Explanation: This question is again based on the principle of energy transformation and elasticity. When you land on the trampoline, it stretches and stores the energy of your fall as elastic potential energy. The deeper the trampoline bends, the more energy it stores. When the trampoline recoils or moves back to its original shape, this energy is released and converted into kinetic energy.

This kinetic energy acts on your body and pushes you upward again, allowing you to keep bouncing. Therefore, the reason gives the exact mechanism that supports the assertion. The trampoline’s ability to store and then release elastic potential energy is central to why you keep bouncing.
