Q: What information can be directly determined from a velocity-time graph? (options not available)
Explanation: The information that can be directly determined from a velocity-time graph is initial velocity.

Initial velocity is the velocity of an object at the beginning of its motion. It can be determined from a velocity-time graph by drawing a tangent to the graph at the initial point and measuring its slope. The slope of the tangent gives the object's initial velocity.

Momentum is the product of an object's mass and velocity. It cannot be directly determined from a velocity-time graph because the mass of the object is not given.

Mass is the amount of matter in an object. It cannot be determined from a velocity-time graph because the mass of the object is not given.

Force is the push or pull on an object that causes it to accelerate. It cannot be determined from a velocity-time graph because the force acting on the object is not given.

Q: Calculate the work done by the force in the third second of its motion (in joules), when a $5N$ force acts on a $15kg$ body initially at rest. (options not available)
Explanation: Here, $u=0,m=15kg,F=5N$

Therefore, $F=ma$

or $5=15\timesa$

or $a=\frac{1}{3}{ms}^{-2}$

Distance travelled by the body in ${n}^{th}$second is,

${S}_{n}=u+\frac{a}{2}\left(2n-1\right)$

Hence, distance travelled by the body in ${3}^{rd}$ second is

${S}_{3}=0+\frac{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}{2}(2\times3-1)\ {S}_{3}=\frac{5}{6}m$

Therefore, work done by the force in ${3}^{rd}$ second is

$W=F\times{S}_{3}\ W=5\times\frac{5}{6}\ W=\frac{25}{6}J\ W=4.16J$

Q: What should be the range of $\theta$ for the work done to be negative, when the force and displacement are positive? (options not available)
Explanation: The work done ($W$) by a constant force ($\vec{F}$) causing a displacement ($\vec{S}$) is defined as the dot product of the force and displacement vectors:
$W=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{S}$
This can also be expressed in terms of the magnitudes of the vectors and the angle \theta between them:
$W=|\vec{F}||\vec{S}|\cos\theta$
The question states that the force ($|\vec{F}|$) and displacement ($|\vec{S}|$) are positive.
We want the work done ($W$) to be negative.
Since $|\vec{F}|and|\vec{S}|$ are positive, for $W$ to be negative, the \cos \theta term must be negative.
Now, let's consider the range of $\cos\theta:$
The cosine function is negative in the second and third quadrants of the unit circle.
For the angle $\theta$ between two vectors, it is conventionally taken to be in the range$0^{\circ}\le\theta\le180^{\circ}(or0\le\theta\le\piradians).$
In this range:
$*\cos\theta>0for0^{\circ}\le\theta<90^{\circ}\ *\cos\theta=0for\theta=90^{\circ}\ *\cos\theta<0for90^{\circ}<\theta\le180^{\circ}$
Therefore, for the work done to be negative when force and displacement are positive, the angle \theta between the force and displacement vectors must be greater than 90^\circ and less than or equal to $180^{\circ}.$
In radians, this range is $\frac{\pi}{2}<\theta\le\pi.$
The range of \theta for the work done to be negative, when the force and displacement are positive, is $90^{\circ}<\theta\le180^{\circ}.$

text:

Q: A man pulls a cart on a straight road of 2 m by applying a force of 200 N. Later the road gets inclined at an angle of 60 degrees with horizontal and the man starts pulling his cart from the base of the inclined road to the top. The length of an inclined portion of the road is 4 m.

(i) What will be the work done by the man to pull the cart on the horizontal road?

(ii) What will be the work done by the man to pull the cart along the inclined part of the road?

(iii) What will be the height of the inclined surface?

(iv) How much time will man consume to pull the cart along an inclined road if he applies a power of 2.5 horsepower? (options not available)
Explanation: Given:
* Force applied by the man, $F=200N$
* Distance on horizontal road, ${d}_{horizontal}=2m$
* Angle of inclination of the road, $\theta=60^{\circ}$
* Length of the inclined portion of the road, ${L}_{inclined}=4m$
* Power applied by the man$,P=2.5$ horsepower
Conversion for Power:
We need to convert horsepower to Watts.
$1horsepower(hp)=745.7Watts(W)\ P=2.5\text{hp}\times745.7\text{W/hp}=1864.25\text{W}$
On a horizontal road, the force applied by the man is in the same direction as the displacement.
$Workdone(W)=Force(F)\timesDistance(d)\ {W}_{horizontal}=F\times{d}_{horizontal}\ {W}_{horizontal}=200\text{N}\times2\text{m}\ {W}_{horizontal}=400\text{J}$
Along the inclined part, the force applied by the man is presumably parallel to the incline.
$Workdone(W)=Force(F)\timesDistance({L}_{inclined})\ {W}_{inclined}=F\times{L}_{inclined}\ {W}_{inclined}=200\text{N}\times4\text{m}\ {W}_{inclined}=800\text{J}$
The height (h) of the inclined surface can be found using trigonometry. We have a right-angled triangle formed by the incline, the horizontal ground, and the vertical height.
$\sin(\theta)=\frac{\text{Opposite}}{\text{Hypotenuse}}=\frac{h}{{L}_{inclined}}$
$h={L}_{inclined}\times\sin(\theta)\ h=4\text{m}\times\sin(60^{\circ})\ h=4\text{m}\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\ h=2\sqrt{3}\text{m}\ h≈2\times1.732\text{m}\ h≈3.464\text{m}$
We use the definition of power:$Power(P)=Workdone(W)/Time(t)$
We want to find the time (t), so $t=W/P.$
The work done along the inclined road is ${W}_{inclined}=800\text{J}(frompartii).$
The power applied is $P=1864.25\text{W}.$
$t=\frac{{W}_{inclined}}{P}\ t=\frac{800\text{J}}{1864.25\text{W}}\ t≈0.429\text{s}$

Q: The mass of the body gets doubled. What should the square of the final velocity be, to keep the value of kinetic energy the same? (options not available)
Explanation: Let ${m}_{1}$ be the initial mass and ${m}_{2}$ be the final mass. Let ${v}_{1}$ be the initial velocity and ${v}_{2}$ be the final velocity.

Let ${K}_{1}$ be the initial kinetic energy and ${K}_{2}$ be the final kinetic energy.

${K}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{m}_{1}{{v}_{1}}^{2}$ and ${K}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}{m}_{2}{{v}_{2}}^{2}$

Given ${K}_{1}={K}_{2}$ and ${m}_{2}=2{m}_{1}$

$∴\frac{1}{2}{m}_{2}{{v}_{2}}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}{m}_{1}{{v}_{1}}^{2}\ ∴2{m}_{1}{{v}_{2}}^{2}={m}_{1}{{v}_{1}}^{2}\ ∴2{{v}_{2}}^{2}={{v}_{1}}^{2}\ ∴{{v}_{2}}^{2}=\frac{{{v}_{1}}^{2}}{2}\$

Hence, to keep the kinetic energy of the body constant, the square of the final velocity should be halve of square of initial velocity if the mass of the body is doubled.

Q: The velocity of a car increases from 54 km/hr to 72 km/hr. How much is the work done if the mass of the car is 1500 kg? (options not available)
Explanation: Mass of the car $m=1500kg,$

The initial velocity of the car,$u=54km/h$

$=\frac{54\times1000m}{60\times60s}\ =15m/s$

Similarly, the final velocity of the car,

$v=72km/h\ =\frac{72\times1000m}{60\times60s}\ =20m/s$

Work done (W) = Final kinetic energy - Initial kinetic energy

$=\frac{1}{2}{mv}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{mu}^{2}\ =\frac{1}{2}m({v}^{2}-{u}^{2})\ =\frac{1}{2}\times1500\times({20}^{2}-{15}^{2})\ =\frac{1}{2}\times1500\times(400-225)\ =\frac{1}{2}\times1500\times175\ W=131250J$

The amount of work done is 131250J.

Q: If the energy of a ball falling from a height of $10$ metres is reduced by $40%$ when hit to the ground, how high will it rebound? (options not available)

Let ${P}_{2}$ be the reduced potential energy. Height (${h}_{2}$) be the rebound height.

Potential energy is given by, $P=mgh$.

The initial potential energy of the ball at the start of the fall ${P}_{1}$$=mg$${h}_{1}$ ..........(i)

The final potential energy of the ball after reaching maximum height after rebound ${P}_{2}$$=mg$${h}_{2}$.........(ii)

dividing equation (ii) with equation (i), we get,

$\frac{{P}_{2}}{{P}_{1}}=\frac{{mgh}_{2}}{{mgh}_{1}}\ \frac{60%of{P}_{1}}{{P}_{1}}=\frac{{h}_{2}}{10}\ \frac{60\times{P}_{1}}{100\times{P}_{1}}=\frac{{h}_{2}}{10}\ \frac{60}{100}=\frac{{h}_{2}}{10}\ {h}_{2}=\frac{60\times10}{100}\ {h}_{2}=6m$

Therefore, the ball will rebound $6m$ high

Q: (i) What is the value of $g$ on the earth ?

Explanation: Given:

Time, $t=\frac{1}{2}\sec$

Acceleration of the car, $a=+10m/s$

$=\frac{(0{ms}^{-1}+5{ms}^{-1})}{2}\ =2.5{ms}^{-1}$

(iii) Distance traveled, $s=\frac{1}{2}{at}^{2}$

$=\frac{1}{2}\times10{ms}^{-2}\times(0.5s{)}^{2}\ =\frac{1}{2}\times10{ms}^{-2}\times0.25{s}^{2}\ =1.25m$

Thus, the height of the ledge from the ground is $1.25m$.

Q: The direction of acceleration due to gravity of earth will be: (options not available)
Explanation: The acceleration due to gravity (g) always acts in the direction of the gravitational force, which points radially inward toward the center of the Earth. The incorrect options are explained as follows:

Away from the center of Earth: This is incorrect because gravity is an attractive force, not a repulsive one. The acceleration due to gravity pulls objects toward the Earth’s center, not away from it.

Tangential to the surface of Earth: A tangential direction would mean the force is parallel to the Earth's surface. However, gravity acts perpendicularly, pointing toward the center of the Earth, not along the surface.

Both B and C: This is incorrect because acceleration due to gravity cannot act simultaneously in both a radial (toward the center) and tangential direction. It only acts radially inward.

Q: A car of mass $m$ is moving with velocity $v$, and acceleration $a$ along a straight level road which is against a constant external resistive force $R$. Calculate the rate of work done by the car engine. (options not available)
Explanation: The rate of work done by the car engine is its power output.
* Identify forces: The engine applies a forward force (${F}_{\text{engine}}$). A resistive force ($R$) acts backward.
* Apply Newton's Second Law: The net force on the car causes its acceleration: ${F}_{\text{net}}=m\cdota.$
* Relate forces: The net force is the engine force minus the resistive force: ${F}_{\text{net}}={F}_{\text{engine}}-R.$
* Solve for engine force: Combining the above, ${F}_{\text{engine}}-R=m\cdota⇒{F}_{\text{engine}}=m\cdota+R.$
* Calculate power: Power (P) is the product of force and velocity: $P={F}_{\text{engine}}\cdotv.$
* Substitute: $P=(m\cdota+R)\cdotv.$
In short, the rate of work done (power) by the car engine is $(ma+R)v.$

Q: A constant power P is applied to particle of mass m. The distance travelled by the particle when its velocity increases from ${v}_{1}$ to ${v}_{2}$is : (Neglect friction) : (options not available)
Explanation: Power P is defined as the product of force F and velocity v:
$P=F\cdotv$
Since force F can also be expressed as
$F=m\cdota$ (where a is acceleration), we can rewrite the power equation as:
$P=m\cdota\cdotv$
Step 2: Express acceleration in terms of velocity and distance
Acceleration a can be expressed as:
$a=\frac{dv}{dt}$
Using the chain rule, we can express a in terms of velocity and distance:
$a=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{dv}{dx}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{dv}{dx}\cdotv$
Thus, we can rewrite the power equation as:
$P=m\cdot\left(\frac{dv}{dx}\cdotv\right)\cdotv=m\cdotv\cdot\frac{dv}{dx}\cdotv=m\cdot{v}^{2}\cdot\frac{dv}{dx}$

So,

$P=Fv\ P=mav\ P=m\left(\frac{vdv}{dx}\right)v\ ⇒P={mv}^{2}\frac{dv}{dx}\ ⇒dx=\frac{m}{P}{v}^{2}dv\ ⇒{∫}_{0}^{x}dx=\frac{m}{p}{∫}_{{v}_{1}}^{{v}_{1}}{v}^{2}dv\ x=\frac{m}{P}\frac{\left({v}_{2}^{3}-{v}_{1}^{3}\right)}{3}\ x=\frac{m}{3P}\left({v}_{2}^{3}-{v}_{1}^{3}\right)$

Q: Unit of potential difference is (options not available)
Explanation: Potential difference (voltage) is the work done per unit charge to move a charge between two points. Its unit, volt (V), is defined as 1 joule per coulomb (1 V = 1 J/C).

Why Not the Other Options?

Joule (J):

Joule is the unit of energy or work done, not potential difference.
While work done = charge × potential difference (W = QΔV), the unit of potential difference itself is volt (V = J/C).

Ohm (Ω):

Ohm is the unit of electrical resistance, not potential difference.
Resistance relates voltage and current (V = IR), but it is not a measure of voltage itself.

Coulomb (C):

Coulomb is the unit of electric charge, not potential difference.
Charge (Q) is related to current (I = Q/t) but is not a measure of voltage.

Q: The resistance of a wire is $RΩ$. If it is melted and stretched to '$n$' times its original length $l$, its new resistance will be - (options not available)
Explanation: The resistance of a wire of length '$l$' , area '$A$', and resistivity '$\rho$' is given by

$R=\frac{\rhol}{A}$

Given that the wire is melted and stretched to the new length ${l}^{'}=nl$.

As the wire is stretched, the length of the wire will increase but the area of cross-section will decrease, thus the volume of the wire will remain constant.

Thus, we have,

$A'l'=Al\ ⇒A'=\frac{Al}{l'}=\frac{Al}{nl}(∵l'=nl)\ ∴A'=\frac{A}{n}$

Therefore, the new resistance $R'$of the wire will be

$R'=\frac{\rhol'}{A'}=\frac{ρnl}{\frac{A}{n}}=\frac{{n}^{2}\rhol}{A}\ ∴R'={n}^{2}R$

Q: The electric resistance of a certain wire of iron is $R$. If its length and radius are both doubled, then what will be the resistance and specific resistance of the wire (options not available)
Explanation: The resistance is given by

$R=\frac{\rhol}{A}=\frac{\rhol}{{πr}^{2}}$

Where, $\rho$ is the resistivity or specific resistance, $l$ is the length and $A$ is the area of cross-section.

Given that the length and the radius of the wire is doubled, the new resistance $R'$ will be

${R}^{'}=\frac{\rho\times2l}{\pi(2r{)}^{2}}=\frac{\rho\timesl}{2{πr}^{2}}=\frac{R}{2}$

hence the resistance will be halved.

Specific resistance $\rho$ is independent of dimensions i.e., length and area of cross-section but depends on the nature of the material, thus the specific resistance or resistivity will remain the same.

Q: The potential drop across the $3\Omega$ resistor is

[Figure 1] (options not available)
Explanation: In the given circuit the $4\Omega$ resistance is connected in series with the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination of the resistances $3\Omega$ and $6\Omega$ .

$∴$The equivalent resistance of the circuit is

$R=4+\frac{3\times6}{3+6}=6\Omega$ and also the battery voltage is $E=3V$.

Therefore, the main current $i=\frac{E}{R}=\frac{3}{6}=0.5A$

The potential drop across $3\Omega$ can be calculated in two ways as shown bellow.

Method $1$. The potential difference across the parallel combination of $3$ $\Omega$ & $6$$\Omega$,

$V=iR=0.5\times\left(\frac{3\times6}{3+6}\right)=1Volt$

In the parallel combination, the voltage across each resistance remains constant. Thus the same potential difference also develops across $3$ $\Omega$ resistance, as the two resistance are connected in parallel.

Method $2$. Total voltage = voltage across $4\Omega$ + voltage across effective resistance of $3\Omegaand6\Omega$

Voltage across $4\Omega$=$4\Omega\times0.5A=2V$. Since total voltage is $3V$, voltage across effective resistance of $3\Omegaand6\Omega$ is $3V-2V=1V$.

In the parallel combination, the voltage across each resistance remains constant. So $1V$ is present across $3\Omega$.

Q: What is the difference between a live wire and a neutral wire in a domestic electric circuit? (options not available)
Explanation: - The difference between a live wire and a neutral wire in a domestic electric circuit is the voltage that they carry. A live wire is a wire that is carrying current, while a neutral wire is a wire that is not carrying current.The voltage on a live wire is typically 220 volts in India.
- This means that there is a potential difference of 220 volts between the live wire and the ground.
- The voltage on a neutral wire is typically 0 volts, which means that it is at the same potential as the ground.
- The current flowing through a circuit is equal to the voltage divided by the resistance. Therefore, the current flowing through a circuit will be higher if the voltage is higher. The higher voltage on the live wire means that it can carry more current than the neutral wire.
- Live wires are typically colored red or brown, while neutral wires are typically colored black or blue. It is important to be able to identify live and neutral wires when working with domestic electric circuits, as this is essential for safety.

- Use insulated tools and equipment. This will help to protect you from electric shock.
- Avoid working on the circuit when it is wet. Water is a good conductor of electricity and can increase the risk of electric shock.
- Be aware of the location of live and neutral wires. Live wires are typically colored red or brown, while neutral wires are typically colored black or blue.

Q: If two atoms have the same outermost orbit, which atom will be smaller? (options not available)
Explanation: The answer is **The atom with fewer electrons in the outermost orbit.**The outermost orbit of an atom is called the valence shell. The number of electrons in the valence shell determines the chemical properties of an atom. If two atoms have the same outermost orbit, but the atom with fewer electrons in the valence shell, the nucleus will have a stronger pull on the electrons. This means that the atom with fewer electrons in the valence shell will be smaller.

The atom with more electrons in the outermost orbit is incorrect because the atom with more electrons in the valence shell will have a weaker pull on the electrons, which makes the atom larger.

Both atoms will have the same size is incorrect because the atoms will not have the same size. The atom with fewer electrons in the valence shell will be smaller.

The number of protons in the nucleus does not affect the size of the atom as much as the number of electrons in the valence shell.

Bromine (Br) is in group 17, so it has 7 valence electrons, so it gains 1 electron to reach 8 (stable octet); therefore, its valency is 1

Magnesium (Mg) is in group 2, so it has 2 valence electrons, so it loses 2 electrons to achieve stable octet; therefore, its valency is 2

Calcium (Ca) is in group 2, so it has 2 valence electrons, so it loses 2 electrons to achieve stable octet; therefore, its valency is 2

= 0.3 moles / 3 M
= 0.1 liters

Q: What type of reaction occurs when an acid reacts with a base to produce a salt and water? (options not available)
Explanation: The answer is **Neutralization reaction.**A neutralization reaction is a chemical reaction that occurs when an acid and a base react to produce salt and water. Q: Which of the following is NOT a factor that determines the reaction of acids with metals? (options not available)
Explanation: The answer is **Color of the metal.**The reaction of acids with metals is determined by the strength of the acid, the concentration of the acid, and the reactivity of the metal. The color of the metal does not affect the reaction.For example, both copper and zinc are reactive metals, but they have different colors. Copper is a reddish-brown metal, while zinc is a silvery-gray metal. However, both metals will react with acids to form hydrogen gas.

Strength of the acid is correct because the strength of the acid determines how easily it can donate H+ ions. The stronger the acid, the more easily it can donate H+ ions, and the more reactive it will be with metals.

Concentration of the acid is correct because the concentration of the acid determines the number of H+ ions available to react with the metal. The higher the concentration of the acid, the more H+ ions will be available, and the more reactive the acid will be with metals.

Reactivity of the metal determines how easily it can lose electrons. The more reactive the metal, the more easily it will lose electrons, and the more reactive it will be with acids.

Explanation: The answer is **Aluminum.**The reactivity of metals can be arranged in a series called the activity series. The metals at the top of the activity series are the most reactive, and the metals at the bottom of the series are the least reactive.

Aluminum is at the top of the activity series, so it is the most reactive metal. When aluminum is added to dilute hydrochloric acid, it reacts vigorously to produce hydrogen gas. The reaction is exothermic, so the solution will become hot.

The other metals in the answer choices are less reactive than aluminum. Iron will react with dilute hydrochloric acid, but the reaction will not be as vigorous as the reaction with aluminum. Lead and silver will not react with dilute hydrochloric acid at all.

Q: What mass of magnesium (Mg) is required to react completely with 50 mL of 2.0 M hydrochloric acid (HCl)? (options not available)
Explanation: The answer is **1.5 g.**

The balanced chemical equation for the reaction of magnesium with hydrochloric acid is:

Mg + 2HCl → Mg${Cl}_{2}$ + ${H}_{2}$

This means that 1 mole of magnesium reacts with 2 moles of hydrochloric acid. We are given that 50 mL of 2.0 M hydrochloric acid is used. The molarity of a solution is the number of moles of solute per liter of solution. So, 50 mL of 2.0 M hydrochloric acid contains 50/1000 * 2 = 1.0 moles of hydrochloric acid.

Since 1 mole of magnesium reacts with 2 moles of hydrochloric acid, 1.0 moles of hydrochloric acid will react with 1/2 * 1.0 = 0.5 moles of magnesium.

The molar mass of magnesium is 24.305 g/mol. So, 0.5 moles of magnesium has a mass of 0.5 * 24.305 = 12.1525 g.

Therefore, 1.5 g of magnesium is required to react completely with 50 mL of 2.0 M hydrochloric acid.

1.0 g is incorrect because it is less than the mass of magnesium required to react completely with 50 mL of 2.0 M hydrochloric acid.
2.0 g is incorrect because it is more than the mass of magnesium required to react completely with 50 mL of 2.0 M hydrochloric acid.
2.5 g is incorrect because it is more than the mass of magnesium required to react completely with 50 mL of 2.0 M hydrochloric acid.

Q: Oxides of non-metals are said to be ________ in nature when they react with bases. (options not available)
Explanation: The answer is **Acidic.**

Oxides of non-metals are acidic in nature. When they react with bases, they form acidic solutions. This is because the oxides of non-metals contain oxygen atoms, which can donate electrons to the hydroxide ions from the base. The resulting hydrogen ions make the solution acidic.
When these oxides react with bases, they form acidic solutions. For example, when carbon dioxide reacts with sodium hydroxide, it forms carbonic acid, which is a weak acid.

C${O}_{2}$ + NaOH → NaHC${O}_{3}$

NaHC${O}_{3}$ is a salt of carbonic acid, and it is also a weak acid. When it dissolves in water, it forms a solution that is slightly acidic.

The incorrect options are incorrect because they do not describe the nature of oxides of non-metals. Basic oxides are oxides of metals that react with acids to form salts and water. Neutral oxides are oxides that do not react with acids or bases. Alkaline oxides are oxides of metals that react with acids to form salts and water, and they also turn litmus paper blue.

Q: What is the primary mode of nutrition for organisms in the Plantae kingdom? (options not available)
Explanation: The answer is **Photosynthesis.**Plants are autotrophs, which means that they can make their own food. They do this through the process of photosynthesis, which uses sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water to produce glucose and oxygen.

The other options are incorrect:

Absorption: Absorption is the process of taking in nutrients from the environment. Plants do absorb nutrients from the soil, but this is not their primary mode of nutrition.

Respiration: Respiration is the process of using oxygen to break down glucose and release energy. Plants do respire, but this is not their primary mode of nutrition.

Q: What is the primary role of plants in maintaining the ecological balance? (options not available)
Explanation: The answer is**Carbon sequestration.**

Plants play a vital role in maintaining the ecological balance by absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and storing it in their tissues. This process is called carbon sequestration. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change. By sequestering carbon dioxide, plants help to mitigate the effects of climate change.

The other options are incorrect:

Oxygen production: Plants also produce oxygen as a byproduct of photosynthesis. However, oxygen production is not the primary role of plants in maintaining the ecological balance.
Decomposition of organic matter: Decomposition of organic matter is an important process in the ecosystem, but it is not primarily carried out by plants. Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers in the ecosystem.
Predation of other organisms: Plants do not usually prey on other organisms. They are autotrophs, which means that they produce their own food. Some insectivorous plants do eat insects to meet additional nitrogen requirements, but the main ecological role of plants is to produce food by fixing carbon into usable forms of energy.

Heterotrophic nutrition: Not all living organisms are heterotrophs. Some bacteria are autotrophs, which means that they can make their own food.

Q: How do plants benefit from their symbiotic relationship with mycorrhizal fungi? (options not available)
Explanation: The answer is **Fungi supply plants with essential nutrients, such as phosphorus and nitrogen.**

Mycorrhizal fungi are a type of fungi that form a symbiotic relationship with plant roots. This means that both the fungus and the plant benefit from the relationship. The fungus provides the plant with essential nutrients, such as phosphorus and nitrogen. In return, the plant provides the fungus with carbohydrates that the fungus needs to survive.

Fungi do not provide plants with additional carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is a gas that plants need for photosynthesis, but they can obtain it from the atmosphere.
Fungi do not protect plants from herbivores. Herbivores eat plants, and fungi cannot protect them from being eaten.
Fungi do not produce oxygen for plants. Oxygen is a gas that plants need for respiration, but they can obtain it from the atmosphere.

Hence rest of the options are incorrect.

Q: What is the main function of seeds in the life cycle of plants? (options not available)
Explanation: The answer is**Reproduction and dispersal of offspring.**Seeds are the reproductive units of plants. They contain the genetic material that will be used to grow a new plant. Seeds are also encased in a protective layer, which helps to protect them from the environment. When seeds are dispersed, they can travel to new locations and germinate, giving rise to new plants.

The other options are incorrect:

Production of flowers is not the main function of seeds. Flowers are the reproductive organs of plants, but they do not produce seeds.
Protection of roots is not the main function of seeds. Roots are the underground organs of plants that absorb water and nutrients from the soil. They are not protected by seeds.
Absorption of water is not the main function of seeds. Seeds do not absorb water. They absorb water after they have germinated and started to grow into a new plant.

Fibrous roots is incorrect because fibrous roots are the type of root system that is found in monocots. Fibrous root systems are made up of a network of thin, branching roots.

Q: The circulation and recycling of nitrogen gas into different compounds is known as: (options not available)
Explanation: The answer is **Nitrogen cycle.**The nitrogen cycle is a biogeochemical cycle that involves the transformation of nitrogen gas into various forms, such as ammonia, nitrates, and nitrites. These forms of nitrogen are then used by plants and animals, and eventually returned to the atmosphere through a process called denitrification.The nitrogen cycle is essential for life on Earth, as it provides plants and animals with the nitrogen they need to grow and survive. The cycle also helps to regulate the amount of nitrogen in the atmosphere, which can have a significant impact on the climate.

Oxygen cycle is incorrect because oxygen gas does not undergo a recycling process. Oxygen cycle is incorrect because water does not undergo a recycling process. Option (d) is incorrect because carbon dioxide gas undergoes a recycling process, but it is not the same as the nitrogen cycle.

Q: Assertion: The carbon cycle is one of the important bio-geo-chemical cycles on Earth.

Reasoning: Carbon is continuously passed on from one living organism to another through the processes of photosynthesis and respiration. (options not available)
Explanation: The answer is both assertion and reasoning are true, and the reasoning is the correct explanation of the assertion.

The carbon cycle is a biogeochemical cycle that describes the movement of carbon through the biosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere. Carbon is continuously passed on from one living organism to another through the processes of photosynthesis and respiration.

During photosynthesis, plants use sunlight to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. The glucose is used by the plants for their own growth and reproduction, and the oxygen is released into the atmosphere.

During respiration, animals and other organisms use oxygen to break down glucose and release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. The carbon dioxide is then taken up by plants during photosynthesis, and the cycle continues.

So, the assertion that the carbon cycle is one of the important biogeochemical cycles on Earth is true, and the reasoning that carbon is continuously passed on from one living organism to another through the processes of photosynthesis and respiration is also true. The reasoning is the correct explanation of the assertion because it explains how the carbon cycle works.

Option (b) is incorrect because the reasoning is the correct explanation of the assertion.

Option (c) is incorrect because the assertion is true.

Option (d) is incorrect because the reasoning is true.

Explanation: The answer is **photosynthesis and decomposition.**Photosynthesis is the process by which plants use sunlight to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.Decomposition is the process by which dead organisms are broken down by bacteria and other organisms.
Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, while decomposition releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. These two processes work together to maintain a relatively stable concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

Combustion and respiration, are also processes that release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. However, these processes are not as important for balancing the carbon cycle as photosynthesis and decomposition.

Evaporation and condensation, are processes that are involved in the water cycle, not the carbon cycle.

Weathering and erosion, are processes that break down rocks and minerals, releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. However, these processes are not as important for balancing the carbon cycle as photosynthesis and decomposition.

The reasoning states that fungi release mycotoxins into the food during their growth, but this does not explain why food items on which fungi have grown cannot be safely consumed. The reasoning does not mention the fact that mycotoxins are poisonous chemicals.

Option (c) is incorrect because the assertion is true. Food items on which fungi have grown cannot be safely consumed because fungi can produce mycotoxins.

Q: Imagine you are at a crowded public event when you notice a person suddenly collapsing and becoming unresponsive. Describe the step-by-step actions you would take to provide effective first aid and assistance in this situation. Justify each action based on your understanding of first aid principles. (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is check for breathing and if absent, begin chest compressions, then call for medical help.

Here are the step-by-step actions you would take to provide effective first aid and assistance in this situation:

Assess the scene for safety. Make sure the area is safe for you to approach the collapsed person. If there is any danger, such as traffic or a fire, call 911 or your local emergency number first.
Check for responsiveness. Gently shake the person's shoulders and ask them loudly if they are okay. If they do not respond, call 911 or your local emergency number immediately.
Check for breathing. Place your ear over the person's mouth and nose and look for their chest to rise and fall. If you do not see their chest rise and fall, or if you do not hear any breathing, begin chest compressions.
Perform chest compressions. Place the heel of your hand on the center of the person's chest, just below their collarbones. Place your other hand on top of your first hand and interlock your fingers. Lock your elbows and straighten your arms so that your shoulders are directly over your hands. Press down on the person's chest with a smooth, steady motion, using your body weight to generate force. Compress the chest at least 2 inches (5 centimeters) and allow it to come back up completely before the next compression. Continue chest compressions at a rate of 100-120 per minute until help arrives.
Check for a pulse. After 30 chest compressions, check for a pulse on the person's neck. If you do not find a pulse, continue chest compressions and rescue breaths until help arrives.
Give rescue breaths. If the person is not breathing, give them rescue breaths after every 30 chest compressions. To give rescue breaths, pinch the person's nose closed and cover their mouth with yours. Blow into their mouth until their chest rises. Give two rescue breaths, each lasting 1 second.
Continue CPR until help arrives. Continue CPR until help arrives. If someone else arrives to help, have them take over chest compressions while you give rescue breaths.
The other options are incorrect:

(a) Performing CPR immediately is not the most critical step in this situation. The most critical step is to check for breathing. If the person is not breathing, they need rescue breaths immediately. Chest compressions are important, but they are not as important as rescue breaths in this situation.
(c) Offering the person water to drink is not appropriate in this situation. The person is unconscious and may have a serious medical condition. Giving them water could make their condition worse.
(d) Applying a tourniquet is not appropriate in this situation. The person is not bleeding heavily and there is no obvious source of bleeding. Applying a tourniquet could cause more harm than good.
It is important to remember that first aid is a temporary measure to stabilize the injured or sick person until professional medical help arrives. If you are unsure of what to do in a first aid situation, it is always best to call 911 or your local emergency number immediately.

Q: The two plane mirrors are placed, making an angle $\theta^{\circ}$ in between them. When an object placed in between the mirrors, an angle gradually increased from $0^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$, how will the number of images change ? Will it increase, decrease or remain unchanged? (options not available)
Explanation: When two mirrors are kept parallel to each other,i.e $\theta={0}^{^{\circ}}$then,

$n=\frac{360^{\circ}}{0^{\circ}}=\infty$

Therefore, for object placed in between the two mirror parallel to each other, the number of images formed will be infinity.

When the angle between them increases to $\theta={180}^{^{\circ}}$

then $n=\frac{360^{\circ}}{180^{\circ}}=2$

Therefore, for an object placed in between the two mirror parallel to each other, the number of images formed will be $n-1=2-1=1$.

Thus, if an angle is gradually increased from ${0}^{^{\circ}}$ to ${180}^{^{\circ}}$ then the number of images decreases.

Q: A student observes the following while experimenting with a spherical mirror:

1. When the object is far from the mirror, the image appears small and inverted.

2. As the object moves closer, the image becomes larger and remains inverted.

3. When the object is very close, the image appears upright and enlarged.

Based on these observations, which type of mirror is the student using? (options not available)
Explanation: These observations correspond to the behavior of a concave mirror:

Far object: Forms a small, inverted, real image.

Closer object: Forms a larger, inverted, real image.

Very close object (within focal length): Forms an enlarged, upright, virtual image.

This progression is characteristic of concave mirrors, which can produce both real and virtual images depending on the object's distance from the mirror. Convex mirrors, in contrast, always produce virtual, upright, and diminished images regardless of object distance.

Q: The focal length of spherical mirror is the distance between __________ (options not available)
Explanation: Pole (P): The geometric center of the mirror's surface.
Focus (F): The point where parallel rays of light converge (for a concave mirror) or appear to diverge from (for a convex mirror).
Focal Length (f): The distance between the pole (P) and the focus (F) of the mirror.

Why "Focus and Pole"?

By definition, focal length (f) = PF (distance from the pole to the focus).
This is a fundamental property of spherical mirrors (both concave and convex).

Why Not Other Options?

Centre of curvature (C) and pole (P): This distance is the radius of curvature (R), not focal length.

Relationship: R=2f (radius is twice the focal length).
Optical centre and focus: Relevant for lenses, not mirrors.

Q: If the incident ray passes through the centre of curvature of a spherical mirror, the reflected ray will __________________. (options not available)
Explanation: When an incident ray of light passes through the center of curvature of a spherical mirror, the reflected ray retraces its path because the incident ray is normal to the mirror surface at the point of incidence. This means the angle of incidence is zero, and according to the laws of reflection, the angle of reflection is also zero. Consequently, the reflected ray will travel back along the same path as the incident ray.

The incorrect options are explained as follows:

Pass through the focus: Rays passing through the focus do not generally pass through the center of curvature.

Pass through the principal axis: While the principal axis is important, the ray passing through the center of curvature does not simply pass through it after reflection.

Pass through the pole: The pole is the geometric center of the mirror's surface, and rays do not typically pass through it after reflection unless they strike it directly.

This means the angle of incidence is zero, and according to the laws of reflection, the angle of reflection is also zero. Consequently, the reflected ray will travel back along the same path as the incident ray.

The incorrect options are explained as follows:

Focus: Rays passing through the focus reflect in a different direction and do not retrace their path.

Pole: The pole is the geometric center of the mirror's surface, and rays passing through it are reflected at angles, not retracing their path.

Vertex: The vertex is the point where the principal axis intersects the mirror surface, but this does not guarantee retracing the light's path.

Q: A ray of light passing through the focus or appear to pass through the focus, after reflection from a spherical mirror _________________ (options not available)
Explanation: Becomes parallel to the principal axis:
This is the correct rule of reflection for spherical mirrors (specifically concave). A ray that passes through the focus (or appears to, in convex mirrors) reflects and travels parallel to the principal axis. This behavior is one of the standard rules of image formation by spherical mirrors.

Incorrect Options Explained:

Passes through the focus:
This describes the opposite of the correct situation. A ray that comes in parallel to the principal axis passes through the focus after reflection (in concave mirrors), not the other way around.

Retraces its path:
This only happens if the ray strikes the mirror along the normal (through the center of curvature), not when it passes through the focus. Therefore, this is not relevant in this case.

Will pass through the center of curvature:
This is incorrect because a ray passing through the focus reflects parallel, not toward or through the center of curvature. The center of curvature is involved in a different rule (a ray through the center retraces its path).

Explanation: Equal to: If a ray of light is incident at the pole of a spherical mirror, the angle of incidence (the angle between the incoming ray and the normal to the mirror at the point of incidence) is equal to the angle of reflection (the angle between the reflected ray and the normal). This follows the law of reflection, which states that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
The incorrect options are explained as follows:

Less than: The angle of reflection is not less than the angle of incidence. The law of reflection ensures they are equal.

Greater than: Similarly, the angle of reflection is not greater than the angle of incidence.

Bigger than: This option is not correct for the same reason; the angles are not different in size. They are equal according to the law of reflection.

Q: An extended object is placed in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature $20cm$ at a distance $15cm$ from the pole. Find the lateral magnification produced. (options not available)
Explanation: Using the cartesian system for sign convention

Given,$u=-15cm$, $f=-10cm$ (using $f=\frac{R}{2}$)

using the formula for mirror

$\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f}\ \frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{(-15)}=\frac{1}{(-10)}\ \frac{1}{v}=-\frac{1}{(-15)}+\frac{1}{(-10)}\ \frac{1}{v}=\frac{-2+3}{(-30)}=\frac{1}{-30}\ \$

we get,

$v=-30cm$

and lateral magnification is given by

$m=-v/u\ =-2$

Q: A convex mirror has a focal length f. A real object is placed at a distance f in front of it from the pole, produces an image at (options not available)
Explanation: $\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{u}$
Here:

$f$= focal length (positive for a convex mirror)

$u$ = object distance (negative since the object is in front of the mirror)

$v$ = image distance (positive for virtual images behind the mirror)

When the object is placed at a distance $u=-f$:
$\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{-f}\ \frac{1}{f}+\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{v}\ \frac{2}{f}=\frac{1}{v}\ v=\frac{f}{2}$

Thus, the image is formed at a distance $\frac{f}{2}$behind the mirror.

Q: A diminished image of an object is obtained on a screen $1m$ from it. This can be achieved by appropriately placing (options not available)
Explanation: A convex mirror and a concave lens always produce semi image for the objects. The image by a convex lens is diminished when the object is placed beyond 2f.

Let u = 2f + x

Using $\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f}$,

$⇒\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{-\left(2f+x\right)}=\frac{1}{f}\ ⇒\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{f}-\frac{1}{\left(2f+x\right)}\ =\frac{2f+x-f}{f(2f+x)}\ =\frac{\left(f+x\right)}{f\left(2f+x\right)}$

But u=v=1 (given) $\left(2f+x\right)+\frac{f\left(2f+x\right)}{f+x}\le1\ ⇒2f=x\left[1+\frac{f}{f+x}\right]\le1\ ⇒{\left(2f+x\right)}^{2}\lef+x$

The above is true for f<0.25 m

Q: The change seen in case of sound waves in the region where the pressure is high is called as_____ (options not available)
Explanation: Compression
Explanation:

In sound waves, compression refers to the regions where the air particles are pushed together, resulting in high pressure. These regions are followed by areas of rarefaction, where particles are spread apart and pressure is lower. Compression and rarefaction alternate as sound waves travel through a medium.

The incorrect options are explained as follows:

Rarefaction: Rarefaction is the opposite of compression, where the pressure is lower due to the spreading apart of particles.

Collision: While collisions occur between particles in sound propagation, they are not specifically related to the change in pressure in sound waves.

Dilation: Dilation refers to expansion, but in the context of sound waves, the term used for high-pressure regions is "compression."

Explanation:

In sound waves, rarefaction occurs in regions where the pressure is decreased. This happens when the particles of the medium are spread apart, creating an area of low pressure. Rarefaction alternates with compression, where particles are closer together, resulting in high pressure.

The incorrect options are explained as follows:

Compression: Compression refers to regions of high pressure, where the particles are compressed together.

Collision: Collision refers to the interaction between particles but does not describe a region of decreased pressure in sound waves.

Condensation: Condensation typically refers to the phase change of a substance from gas to liquid, not a concept related to sound wave pressure variations.

Q: A boy shouts towards the mountain and hears his echo 4.5 seconds later. If the mountain is 765 m away from the boy, calculate the speed of the sound in the air. (options not available)
Explanation: Let the speed of sound in the air be v m/s.

The distance travelled by the sound to the mountain and back = 2d

$\begin{matrix} 2d=2\times765 \\ =1530m \\ 2d=v\timest \\ 1530=v\times4.5 \end{matrix}$

Therefore,

$\begin{matrix} v=\frac{1530}{4.5} \\ =340{ms}^{-1} \end{matrix}$

Hence the speed of the sound in air is 340 m/s.

Wavelength (λ): Changes to compensate for the velocity change (since v=fλ).
Frequency (f): Remains constant (depends only on the source).

Liquids are less rigid than solids → slower sound speed.
Oil is slightly less stiff than water → marginally slower.

Why Not Air?
Air has very low elasticity and low density → slowest sound propagation.

Q: Which component is used for the production of ultrasound energy? (options not available)
Explanation: Transducer
Explanation:

Transducers are the components used to convert electrical energy into ultrasonic waves (sound waves) and vice versa. In medical ultrasound, the transducer both emits high-frequency sound waves and detects the echoes that return from the body to create images.

The incorrect options are explained as follows:

Screen: The screen is used to display the images produced by the ultrasound waves, but it does not generate ultrasound energy.

Receiver: A receiver detects the returned ultrasound waves, but it is not responsible for producing them.

Cable: The cable transmits signals between components, but it does not generate ultrasound energy either.

title: applications of ultrasound
text:
Study Of Sound › Uses of ultrasonic sound › applications of ultrasound — Practice question

Q: What is effect of using a narrow beam in ultrasound machines for lateral resolution? (options not available)
Explanation: The lateral resolution is good
Explanation:

Using a narrow beam in ultrasound machines improves lateral resolution. A narrow beam allows for more precise imaging of structures in the body by focusing the ultrasound energy in a smaller area, thus enhancing the ability to distinguish between objects that are close to each other laterally.

The incorrect options are explained as follows:

Penetration is increased: A narrow beam does not necessarily increase penetration. In fact, narrower beams often have less energy in them, which can limit the depth of penetration.

Penetration is decreased: While a narrow beam may reduce the overall penetration depth, the primary effect is on lateral resolution, not penetration.

No effect: This is incorrect because a narrow beam does indeed affect lateral resolution.

title: applications of ultrasound
text:

Q: Which frequency sound is used to remove the cataract and in kidneys to break the small stones into fine grains? (options not available)
Explanation: Ultrasonics
Explanation:

Ultrasonic waves (sound waves with frequencies higher than $20kHz$) are used in various medical procedures, including cataract removal and breaking kidney stones (a procedure known as lithotripsy). Ultrasound waves can generate high-intensity vibrations that help break down stones into smaller fragments or help with soft tissue disintegration like cataracts.

The incorrect options are explained as follows:

Infrasonic: Infrasonic waves are below the human hearing range (less than $20Hz$) and are not used in medical procedures like cataract removal or lithotripsy.

Sonics: This term is not specific enough. "Sonic" generally refers to sound waves in the audible range ($20Hzto20kHz$), which are not used in these medical applications.

Ultraviolet: Ultraviolet (UV) light refers to electromagnetic radiation and is not used for breaking stones or removing cataracts.

Q: The animal/s that use sound for navigation - (options not available)
Explanation: Explanation:

Bats and whales both use echolocation (sound waves) for navigation.

Bats emit high-frequency sound waves (ultrasonic) and listen for the echoes to determine the distance and direction of objects around them, aiding in navigation and hunting, especially in low-light conditions.

Whales use a similar method called sonar, emitting sound waves and listening to the echoes that bounce back from objects in the ocean, allowing them to navigate through dark or murky waters.

Q: Calculate the minimum distance between the source of the sound and the obstacle so that the echo will be heard? [assume an air to be the medium] (options not available)
Explanation: Let d be the distance of the observer from the obstacle and V is the speed of the sound in the medium, then the total distance travelled by the sound to reach the obstacle and then to come back, 2d. The time is taken to hear the echo is

t = total distance travelled / speed of sound =$\frac{2d}{V}$

$d=\frac{Vt}{2}$

We know that the sound sensation in our brain persists for about 0.1 s, the time interval between the original and the reflected sound must be at least 0.1 to hear a distinct echo and V=340 m/s

hence $d=\frac{(340\times0.1)}{2}=17$ m

and, Distance = 1500 $\times$ 2 = 3000 m

Q: What is the name given to the property of elements occurring in more than one form with different physical properties but the same chemical properties? (options not available)
Explanation: The answer is **Allotropy.**

Allotropy is the property of elements occurring in more than one form with different physical properties but the same chemical properties. For example, carbon can exist in the form of diamond, graphite, and fullerenes. These allotropes of carbon have different physical properties, such as density, melting point, and electrical conductivity, but they have the same chemical properties.

Isomerism, is the property of molecules having the same molecular formula but different structural formulas. For example, ethane and propane are isomers, but they have different physical and chemical properties.

Polymerization, is the process of joining together many small molecules to form a larger molecule. Polymers can have different physical properties, but they always have the same chemical properties as the small molecules that they are made up of.

Sublimation, is the process of a substance going directly from the solid state to the gas state without passing through the liquid state. Sublimation does not affect the chemical properties of a substance.

Q: Which of the following rays is not emitted by a radioactive substance? (options not available)
Explanation: Radioactive nuclei emit three different types of radiations.

Physicists have named the three types of radiations emitted by nuclei as alpha, beta, and gamma radiations.

Alpha radiation is the term for the emission of an alpha particle from nuclei.

In fact, helium nuclei are identical with an alpha particle.

Beta radiation involves the emission of electrons or positrons, and gamma radiation is the term used for the emission of energetic photons.

Cathodic rays are not produced by a radioactive substance, they are named as cathode rays because they are produced by negative electrode or cathode.

Oxygen reacts and a layer of hydrated aluminium oxide is formed on the anode, i.e. the iron article.

Q: Which of the following is responsible for generating impulses in the human body? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Nerve cells.**Nerve cells, also known as neurons, are responsible for generating impulses in the human body. Neurons are specialized cells of the nervous system that transmit electrical signals, known as nerve impulses or action potentials. These impulses are the basis for communication within the nervous system and are responsible for transmitting information between different parts of the body, allowing for sensory perception, motor control, and various physiological processes.

a) Muscle cells: Muscle cells are responsible for generating contractions and movements in response to nerve impulses. While muscle cells are electrically excitable and respond to signals from nerve cells, they do not generate the initial impulses themselves.

b) Blood cells: Blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, are involved in functions such as oxygen transport, immune response, and blood clotting. They do not generate nerve impulses.

d) Skin cells: Skin cells, or keratinocytes, make up the outer layer of the skin and are involved in protecting the body from the environment. They do not play a role in generating nerve impulses.

Q: The ability of body cells to respond to impulses depends on: (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is**The body's temperature**

Explanation:

The ability of body cells to respond to impulses depends on various factors, and one of them is the body's temperature. The rate of chemical reactions and the functioning of cellular processes are influenced by temperature. Enzymes, which play a critical role in many cellular reactions, have optimal temperature ranges at which they function efficiently. If the body's temperature is too high or too low, cellular processes, including the ability of cells to respond to impulses, can be affected.

The incorrect options are:

The color of the surroundings: The color of the surroundings does not have a direct impact on the ability of body cells to respond to impulses. Cellular responses are primarily governed by biochemical and physiological factors.

The complexity of body structure: The complexity of body structure does not directly affect the ability of individual body cells to respond to impulses. However, the organization and interactions of different types of cells within the body contribute to overall physiological processes.

The time of day: While the time of day can influence certain physiological processes due to the body's circadian rhythms, it is not a primary determinant of the ability of body cells to respond to impulses. Circadian rhythms can affect functions like hormone release and sleep-wake cycles, but they don't directly control cellular responses to impulses.

Q: Which type of animals have a nervous system for responding to stimuli? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Multicellular animals.**Multicellular animals,have a nervous system for responding to stimuli. The nervous system is a complex network of specialized cells called neurons that transmit electrical signals throughout the body. This allows multicellular animals to detect and respond to changes in their environment, enabling behaviors and physiological responses that are crucial for survival and adaptation.

The incorrect options are :

a) Plants: While plants do exhibit various responses to stimuli, they lack a centralized nervous system like animals. Instead, plants have evolved different mechanisms for responding to environmental cues.

b) Unicellular organisms: Unicellular organisms, such as bacteria and protozoa, lack a nervous system as observed in multicellular animals.

c) Invertebrates: Invertebrates, which include animals without a backbone, do have a nervous system for responding to stimuli.

Q: Nervous control enables humans to respond to: (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Changes in both internal and external environments.**Nervous control enables humans to respond to changes in both their internal and external environments. The nervous system processes sensory information from both the external environment (such as temperature, light, sound, and touch) and the internal environment (such as blood pressure, blood glucose levels, and hormone concentrations). This information is integrated, and appropriate responses are generated to maintain homeostasis and ensure the body's survival and proper functioning.

The incorrect options are:

a) Changes in their internal environment only: While the nervous system certainly responds to changes in the internal environment, it is not limited to internal stimuli alone. It also responds to external stimuli to help the body adapt to its surroundings.

b) Changes in their external environment only: This option is also not accurate. The nervous system responds to both external and internal stimuli. External stimuli allow humans to interact with their environment, while internal stimuli help regulate physiological processes.

d) Changes in their dreams: Dreams are experiences that occur during sleep and are primarily a function of brain activity, particularly during the rapid eye movement (REM) sleep phase.

Q: What do unicellular organisms like amoebas lack in terms of control and coordination? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Nervous system.**Unicellular organisms like amoebas lack a nervous system in terms of control and coordination. The nervous system is a complex network of specialized cells (neurons) that transmit electrical signals to coordinate responses to stimuli. Since unicellular organisms are single-celled and lack specialized tissues and organs, they don't have the same level of complexity found in multicellular organisms. Instead of a nervous system, unicellular organisms rely on simpler mechanisms for responding to stimuli, such as chemical and physical processes.

The incorrect options are:

a) Muscles: Some unicellular organisms, including amoebas, do exhibit movement, but they lack specialized muscles like those found in multicellular animals. Their movement is typically achieved through extensions of their cell membrane called pseudopodia.

c) Cellular structure: Unicellular organisms do have cellular structures, as they consist of a single cell. However, their lack of complex tissue and organ systems is what sets them apart from multicellular organisms.

d) Eyes: Unicellular organisms lack specialized sensory organs like eyes. While some unicellular organisms may have light-sensitive structures that allow them to respond to changes in light intensity, these structures are not as complex as the eyes of multicellular animals.

Q: What role do nerve cells play in the control and coordination of the body? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Transmit impulses and signals.**Nerve cells, also known as neurons, play a crucial role in the control and coordination of the body by transmitting impulses and signals. Neurons are specialized cells of the nervous system that are capable of generating and transmitting electrical signals called nerve impulses or action potentials. These impulses travel along the length of the neuron and are transmitted from one neuron to another at synapses.

The incorrect options are :

a) Produce red blood cells: Nerve cells do not produce red blood cells. Red blood cells are produced in the bone marrow of certain bones and are responsible for carrying oxygen to tissues and removing carbon dioxide.

c) Synthesize nutrients: Nerve cells are not primarily responsible for synthesizing nutrients. Nutrient synthesis is typically performed by various cells throughout the body, including specialized cells in organs like the liver and intestines.

d) Store genetic information: Nerve cells, like all cells in the body, contain genetic information in the form of DNA, but their main role is not to store genetic information. Nerve cells are more specialized for transmitting and processing electrical signals.

Q: Impulses in the nervous system are similar to: (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Electrical signals.**Impulses in the nervous system are similar to electrical signals. Nerve impulses, also known as action potentials, are the means by which nerve cells (neurons) communicate with each other and transmit information throughout the nervous system. These impulses are based on changes in the electrical potential across the cell membrane of neurons.

The incorrect options are :

b) Chemical reactions: While chemical processes are involved in the functioning of neurons and the nervous system (such as neurotransmitter release at synapses), impulses themselves are primarily electrical in nature.

c) Mechanical movements: Impulses in the nervous system are not similar to mechanical movements. Mechanical movements involve the physical displacement of objects or parts of the body, whereas nervous impulses involve the transmission of electrical signals within neurons.

d) Sound waves: Impulses in the nervous system are not similar to sound waves. Sound waves are a form of mechanical energy that propagates through a medium (like air or water) and are typically associated with auditory perception.

Q: Nervous control is a vital mechanism that allows organisms to respond to changes in their environment. Consider the following scenarios:

Scenario 1: A deer senses the approach of a predator and swiftly darts away into the forest.

Scenario 2: A single-celled organism moves away from a region with a high concentration of harmful chemicals.

Which of the following statements best reflects the significance of nervous control in these scenarios? (options not available)
Explanation: **Nervous control is essential for both the deer and the single-celled organism, as it enables rapid responses to environmental changes** is the correct options.Nervous control is not limited to complex organisms like the deer; it's a fundamental mechanism that allows organisms to respond to changes in their environment, regardless of their complexity. Both scenarios involve organisms responding to external changes – the deer's quick escape and the single-celled organism's movement away from harmful chemicals – highlighting the importance of nervous control in facilitating these responses.

Option A: Nervous control is crucial only for complex organisms like the deer, as they possess advanced nervous systems.

This option suggests that nervous control is only relevant for complex organisms like the deer. However, this is not accurate. Nervous control is essential for a wide range of organisms, including both simple and complex ones. Even unicellular organisms can exhibit simple forms of responses to environmental changes without possessing advanced nervous systems.

Option C: Nervous control is unnecessary for the single-celled organism, as it relies on simpler mechanisms for survival.

This option implies that single-celled organisms do not require nervous control since they rely on simpler mechanisms for survival. While it's true that single-celled organisms have less complex structures compared to multicellular organisms, they still exhibit responses to changes in their environment, often through basic mechanisms like chemotaxis (movement in response to chemicals). Nervous control may not be present in the same way as in multicellular organisms, but these organisms do show responsiveness.

Option D: Nervous control is primarily responsible for maintaining the balance of chemicals in the environment.

This option suggests that the primary role of nervous control is to maintain the balance of chemicals in the environment. However, this is not accurate. The primary function of nervous control is to facilitate communication and coordination within an organism's body, allowing it to respond to external stimuli effectively. While nervous systems can influence certain aspects of an organism's interactions with its environment, their primary role is not to maintain the balance of chemicals in the external environment.

Q: What is the role of neuroglia in the nervous system? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Supporting nerve cells.**Neuroglia, also known as glial cells, play a crucial role in the nervous system by providing support and maintaining the overall functioning of nerve cells (neurons). While neurons are responsible for transmitting electrical signals and conducting impulses, neuroglia have several important functions that contribute to the proper functioning of the nervous system.

The other incorrect options are :

Conducting impulses: Neuroglia are not responsible for conducting impulses. This role is primarily fulfilled by neurons, which have specialized structures (dendrites and axons) that enable the transmission of electrical signals.

Producing hormones: Neuroglia do not produce hormones in the same way that endocrine glands, such as the pituitary gland or thyroid gland, do.

Generating energy: Neuroglia do not play a significant role in generating energy within the nervous system.

Q: Which part of a neuron collects information from the surroundings? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Dendrites.**Dendrites are the part of a neuron that collects information from the surroundings and other neurons. They are specialized, branched structures that extend from the cell body of the neuron. Dendrites contain numerous synaptic receptors that receive signals in the form of neurotransmitters released by other neurons.

Other incorrect options are:

Cell body: The cell body (soma) of a neuron contains the nucleus and most of the organelles necessary for the neuron's survival and functioning. It integrates the information received from dendrites and determines whether to generate an action potential. However, it doesn't directly collect information from the surroundings.

Axon: The axon is a long, slender projection of a neuron that carries the generated action potential away from the cell body and transmits it to other neurons or target cells. The axon's main function is to transmit signals, not to collect information from the surroundings.

Terminal: The terminal branches (axon terminals) are located at the end of the axon and are responsible for transmitting signals to other neurons or target cells through synapses.

Q: Where does the chemical process begin in a neuron? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Dendrites .**The chemical process in a neuron begins in the dendrites. Dendrites are the specialized projections that extend from the cell body of the neuron. They contain synaptic receptors that receive chemical signals in the form of neurotransmitters released by other neurons.

The correct options are:

Spinal cord: The spinal cord is a part of the central nervous system and serves as a pathway for transmitting sensory and motor signals between the body and the brain. However, the chemical process that initiates the neuron's activity begins at the dendrites, not in the spinal cord.

Axon: The axon is responsible for transmitting the electrical signals generated by the neuron, but the chemical process that initiates the signal starts in the dendrites. The axon carries the electrical signal away from the cell body and toward the axon terminals.

Terminal: The terminal branches (axon terminals) are located at the end of the axon and are involved in transmitting the signal to other neurons or target cells through synapses. They release neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft, which then bind to receptors on the dendrites of other neurons.

Q: How are impulses transferred from one neuron to another? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Through the synapse.**Impulses are transferred from one neuron to another through a specialized junction called a synapse. A synapse is a tiny gap between the axon terminal of one neuron and the dendrite or cell body of another neuron. The transfer of information (impulses) across this synapse involves a complex process:

Other incorrect options incorrect options :

a) Through blood vessels: Blood vessels primarily carry blood, oxygen, nutrients, and waste products throughout the body. While the circulatory system is vital for the overall function of the body, it does not directly transmit impulses between neurons.

b) Through the spinal cord: The spinal cord serves as a conduit for transmitting sensory and motor signals between the body and the brain. It plays a role in communication within the nervous system, but impulses are not directly transferred between neurons through the spinal cord. Instead, the spinal cord helps relay and process signals.

d) Through skin contact: While physical touch or skin contact can stimulate sensory receptors and generate electrical signals in the nervous system, it is not the primary mechanism for transmitting impulses between neurons. Impulses are mainly transmitted through synapses, as described above.

Q: What is the role of the chemicals secreted by nerve cells at the terminal of an axon? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is**They generate impulses in the dendrites of the next neuron.**The chemicals secreted by nerve cells at the terminal of an axon are neurotransmitters, and their primary role is to transmit signals from one neuron to another across synapses. When an action potential (nerve impulse) reaches the axon terminal of the presynaptic neuron, it triggers the release of neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft, which is the small gap between the axon terminal and the dendrite or cell body of the postsynaptic neuron.

Other Incorrect options are:

They create a physical barrier: Neurotransmitters do not create a physical barrier. Instead, they facilitate communication between neurons by acting as signaling molecules that traverse the synaptic cleft.

They stimulate muscle growth: While some neurotransmitters can affect muscle contractions, their primary role is in transmitting signals between neurons, not stimulating muscle growth.

They prevent nerve impulses from reaching the synapse: Neurotransmitters do not prevent nerve impulses from reaching the synapse. In fact, they are released by the presynaptic neuron specifically to transmit the nerve impulse's signal to the postsynaptic neuron.

Q: How are impulses finally conveyed to muscle cells or glands? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Through direct contact.**Impulses are conveyed to muscle cells or glands through direct contact between nerve cells and the target cells (muscle cells or glands). This communication occurs at specialized junctions known as neuromuscular junctions (for muscle cells) and neuroglandular junctions (for glands). These junctions enable the transfer of signals from nerve cells to the target cells, allowing for coordinated responses.

Other incorrect options are:

Through blood circulation: While blood circulation is involved in the transport of nutrients, oxygen, hormones, and other substances throughout the body, impulses are not conveyed to muscle cells or glands directly through blood circulation. The communication between nerve cells and target cells occurs at specific junctions.

Through the spinal cord: The spinal cord is an essential part of the nervous system, but it primarily serves as a pathway for transmitting signals between the body and the brain, and for processing certain reflex responses. Impulses are not conveyed to muscle cells or glands through the spinal cord itself.

Q: What is the role of muscular tissue in the body? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Responding to nerve signals.**The role of muscular tissue in the body is to respond to nerve signals by contracting and generating force. Muscular tissue, also known as muscle tissue, is one of the four primary tissue types in the human body and is responsible for movement, stability, posture, and generating heat.

Muscles play a crucial role in a variety of bodily functions, including: Movement, Stability and Posture and Heat Generation.

Other Incorrect options are:

Conducting electrical impulses: Muscular tissue itself does not conduct electrical impulses like nerve cells (neurons) do. Instead, muscular tissue responds to electrical impulses by contracting. Nerves conduct impulses, and when these impulses reach muscles, they trigger contractions.

Producing hormones: Muscular tissue is not primarily responsible for producing hormones. Hormones are mainly produced by endocrine glands, such as the thyroid gland, adrenal glands, and pancreas.

Collecting information: Muscular tissue does not collect sensory information from the surroundings like sensory receptors do. Sensory information is typically collected by sensory neurons and specialized sensory structures, while muscular tissue responds to nerve signals and contracts to create movement.

Q: What type of protein allows muscle cells to change shape? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Contractile proteins.**Contractile proteins are the type of protein that allows muscle cells to change shape by contracting. These proteins are essential for muscle contraction, which is the process by which muscle cells generate force and shorten in length. There are two main types of contractile proteins found in muscle cells: actin and myosin.

Other incorrect options are :

a) Enzymes: Enzymes are biological molecules that facilitate chemical reactions in the body. They do not play a direct role in allowing muscle cells to change shape by contracting.

b) Antibodies: Antibodies are proteins produced by the immune system to help defend the body against pathogens. They do not have a role in muscle contraction or shape change.

c) Hormones: Hormones are signaling molecules that regulate various physiological processes in the body. While hormones can influence muscle function, they do not directly allow muscle cells to change shape.

Q: How do muscle cells respond to electrical impulses from nerves? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is**By contracting and changing shape.**Muscle cells respond to electrical impulses from nerves by contracting and changing shape. The contraction of muscle cells is a result of the interaction between the contractile proteins actin and myosin within the muscle fibers.

Other incorrect options are:

By releasing chemicals: While nerves release neurotransmitters that initiate muscle action potentials, muscle cells themselves do not release chemicals in response to nerve impulses.

By generating heat: Muscle cells do generate heat as a byproduct of contraction, but heat generation is not the primary response to nerve impulses.

By dividing and multiplying: Muscle cells do not typically divide and multiply in response to nerve impulses. Muscle growth and repair occur through a process involving the activation of satellite cells and protein synthesis, not direct division and multiplication of muscle cells.

Q: Which type of neurons conduct impulses from sensory organs to the brain and spinal cord? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is**Sensory neurons.**Sensory neurons, also known as afferent neurons, are responsible for conducting impulses from sensory organs (such as the skin, eyes, ears, nose, and taste buds) to the central nervous system, which includes the brain and spinal cord. These neurons play a crucial role in transmitting sensory information from the external environment to the brain and spinal cord, where further processing and interpretation of the sensory input occur.

a) Motor neurons: Motor neurons, also known as efferent neurons, are responsible for conducting impulses from the brain and spinal cord to muscles and glands, enabling the execution of voluntary and involuntary movements as well as secretion of various substances.

b) Association neurons: Association neurons, also called interneurons, are located entirely within the central nervous system and are responsible for processing and integrating information. They connect sensory neurons to motor neurons and play a vital role in relaying and modulating signals within the nervous system.

d) Peripheral neurons: There is no specific category of neurons referred to as "peripheral neurons." The peripheral nervous system consists of both sensory and motor neurons that connect the central nervous system to the rest of the body, including sensory organs and muscles.

Q: What is the main function of motor neurons? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is **Conduct impulses from the brain to effector organs.**Motor neurons, also known as efferent neurons, are responsible for conducting impulses from the brain and spinal cord to effector organs, which can be muscles or glands. These neurons play a crucial role in transmitting signals from the central nervous system to the periphery, allowing for voluntary and involuntary muscle movements as well as the release of substances from glands.

Incorrect options:

a) Conduct impulses from sensory organs to the brain: This describes the function of sensory neurons, not motor neurons. Sensory neurons transmit sensory information from sensory organs to the brain and spinal cord.

c) Perform integration in the nervous system: This is the function of interneurons or association neurons, which are responsible for processing and integrating information within the central nervous system.

d) Protect the spinal cord: Neurons do not serve the primary function of protecting the spinal cord. The spinal cord is surrounded and protected by bony structures (vertebrae) and various layers of tissue.

Q: Which part of the nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord? (options not available)
Explanation: The correct answer is the **Central nervous system.** The central nervous system (CNS) consists of the brain and spinal cord. It is responsible for processing and integrating sensory information, coordinating motor functions, and performing higher-order cognitive processes. The brain and spinal cord play a crucial role in receiving, interpreting, and responding to various signals from the body and the environment.

Incorrect options:

a) Peripheral nervous system: The peripheral nervous system (PNS) includes all the nerves and ganglia outside the central nervous system. It connects the CNS to the rest of the body, including sensory organs, muscles, and glands.

b) Autonomic nervous system: The autonomic nervous system is a division of the peripheral nervous system responsible for regulating involuntary bodily functions such as heart rate, digestion, and respiratory rate. It includes the sympathetic and parasympathetic branches.

d) Sensory nervous system: There is no specific "sensory nervous system." Sensory neurons are part of the peripheral nervous system, and they transmit sensory information from the body's sensory organs to the central nervous system.
